en: Om, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

The *Mañjūṣā-kuñjikā*, a commentary on the *Laghumañjūṣā*— the established doctrine of grammar— which is an extraction of the Śabdabrahman through the craftsmanship of the *Mañjūṣā* and the *Kuñjikā*.
"O quarters of space, grant us eternal and supreme protection in every direction! || 1.1 ||

Regarding "Nāgeśa": he is called *bhaṭṭa* because he is a *bhaṭ*, meaning eloquent; the suffix *ṭan* is applied to the root *bhaṭ* (to speak). He is called *mañjūṣā* because he "sinks" (*majjati*) [into knowledge]; the suffix *ūpaṇ* is added to the root *masj* according to the rule *masjer ūc ca*. According to Vātsyāyana, a collection of objects known in such a manner is "established" (*siddha*); the systematic arrangement of that which is established, consisting of its various states, is the "tenet" (*siddhānta*). Because it is the cause for liberation, the supreme human goal, he introduces the preliminary discussion (*upoddhāta*). The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "among the tenets of the Grammarians. The word "principal" (*mukhya*)...

The meaning is that the primary purpose of grammar is the knowledge of the Śabdabrahman (the Absolute as Word) consisting of the sentence-sphoṭa. Since the Brahman consisting of the sentence-sphoṭa alone is ultimately real, and any entity distinct from it is not ultimately real, alternative doctrines are considered secondary. Although the internal sphoṭa is the signifier and has no usage in the world, nevertheless, the phrase "of that very [Brahman]" means "of the sentence itself. And thus, there is the establishment of the sentence-sphoṭa which is manifested by that [internal sphoṭa].

Now, one might ask: "How can there be understanding from [the word] *dvāram* alone? To this he says: *tena* ("by that"). The sense is that even in that case, understanding arises precisely through the recollection of the sentence. *Arthasamāptiḥ* means the completion of the meaning. Although, according to our own view, it will be stated that even a single word like *dvāram* constitutes a sentence and is itself the conveyor of meaning, nevertheless, this is presented according to the perspective of others. He introduces that very other view with the words: *padasamūhaḥ* ("a collection of words").

Although the established doctrine is that the sentence is a single, partless *sphoṭa* and that the meaning of the sentence is the *pratibhā*, nevertheless, this [analysis] is undertaken by means of the conceptualization of words (*pada*) for the purpose of explaining the sentence. As it was said by Hari: "Just as in a word, the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth are divided, so too is the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of words described in the case of a sentence."

However, rules such as "a sentence consists of one finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*) have been defined as *paribhāṣās* (technical conventions) specifically for the purpose of prescribing accents (*anudātta*, etc.); thus, it has been stated that [a sentence] is a collection of words (*padasamūha*). As it has been said: "That which is defined in the treatise for the sake of establishing the arrangement of accents and so forth is a *paribhāṣā*. By this, those who explain [a sentence] as "a sentence is that whose primary qualificand is the meaning of a single finite verb" in order to avoid the over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) are refuted. Furthermore, because the word *pada* here refers to its fitness (*yogyatā*), there is no over-narrowness in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*).

Now, if it is held that "a word (*pada*) is that which is meaningful," then it would follow that even a collection such as a verbal root (*prakṛti*) and so forth would possess meaning as a compound; therefore, he says: "In this context. Thus, Gautama’s sūtra states: "Those [elements] ending in case-terminations (*vibhakti*) are words (*pada*). An example of a collection of *subanta* (nominal) elements is "tvayā bhoktavyam" ("it is to be eaten by you"); an example of a collection of *tiṅanta* (verbal) elements is "pacati bhavati" ("he cooks, [it] exists"). If it is argued: "In a case where only 'dvāram' ('the door') is uttered, comprehension does not arise even through the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the word 'pidhehi' ('close'), because according to the Bhāṣya, only what is actually articulated is expressive."

In this regard, it will be explained that even a single word possesses the power [to convey] the meaning of a sentence. However, because of partial similarity, parts of sentences are also employed in place of whole sentences; in such cases, there is indeed *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with respect to fire based on its association with smoke. But when the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is present, there is simply inference (*anumiti*). As for the claim of the ancient logicians that the word "pada" refers to mental presence (*upasthiti*), since comprehension occurs even from "silent verses" (*mauniśloka*) and the like—that is incorrect.

"A word produced by the knowledge of the reality of the meaning that serves as the cause for its application is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By thus grasping that which is delimited by the property of being produced by the knowledge of the reality of the sentence-meaning—which serves as the cause for its application—the definition from the *Cintāmaṇi* avoids the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of a verse composed by a silent sage (*maunī*). (1.1)

[Objection: "Since a sentence is partless (*niravayava*), the cognition of individual words must be an error; why then is there an analysis of them? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). He states that, just like the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*), the knowledge of the word itself is also the result [of analysis], by saying: "Of its grammatical exposition" (*tadanvākhyānasya*). This means: "of the grammatical exposition of the sentence. Regarding the phrase "by means of conceptual construction" (*kalpanayā*): having conceptually constructed words within the sentence, and having conceptually constructed the division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) within the word, the meanings of the bases and suffixes are conceptually constructed through the imagined methods of agreement (*anvaya*) and difference (*vyatireka*). This is the meaning.

Although there is no possibility of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) because the understanding of "offspring" occurs even in the absence of the suffix *aṇ*—as it does through suffixes such as *phiñ*—nevertheless, a negative concomitance exists here, just as in the case of grass, flint, and gems being causes for fire. Since the division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth is merely conceptual (*kalpita*), both positive and negative concomitance are likewise conceptual. Similarly, because sentences such as "bring the jar" are indivisible wholes (*akhaṇḍa*), the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*) as described by the logicians (*tārkika*) is not possible. This is what is meant by "merely the scripture" (*śāstramātra*).

The meaning is that this conceptualization is useful only within the context of grammatical procedure (*prakriyā*), because in the world it is the sentence alone that conveys meaning. "This very [point]" means that it pertains specifically to the subject matter of the technical treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding Kaiyaṭa: having cited the Bhāṣya—"the mention of *sub* (inflected word) is so that [the suffix] might not apply to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)"—he raises the objection: since only a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) possesses the function of expressing "partial non-completion" (*īṣadasamāpti*), and the nominal stem lacks that function, how could there be any possibility [of the suffix applying]? This is the sense. Regarding "positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatireka*): the sense is that it is precisely the possession of meaning as conceived through positive and negative concomitance established by means of the technical treatise that is useful for the grammatical procedure.

[Objection: "But surely, if unreal parts and their meanings are postulated, the sages would lack authority. To this, he says: "By the cognition of each respective part... The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by the cognition of each respective part, the whole is cognized; and by the cognition of the meaning of each part, the meaning of the whole is cognized.

Regarding the statement "in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa": for there, since the meaning of a sentence consists in the relation between word-meanings (*padārtha-saṃsarga*), the sentence alone possesses the expressive power (*śakti*). However, because of similarity, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are merely postulated. And thus, it is clear that the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) which would have accrued to the sentence is precluded by the restrictive rule established through the mention of *samāsa*. [This refers to] the phrase "śruti-vākya" (scripture and sentence).

Regarding the statement, "One should worship the *gārhapatya* fire at the end," the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger; however, the worship of Indra is weaker because it is based on the consideration of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), namely, "Indra is the deity of this [rite]. This is what is meant by "relative strength" (*balābala*). For the meaning of a sentence, characterized by the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), is stronger because it presents itself first.

The point is that if the sentence were an indivisible whole expressing only an indivisible meaning, then meanings obtainable through indicators (*liṅga*) and other means would be impossible, resulting in their total abolition. (1.2)

Now, one might object that if the sentence-sphoṭa (vākyasphoṭa) is primary, other types of sphoṭas would be abolished; to this he says: "In that regard, by the scripture" (*tatra śāstreṇa*). Some maintain that a *prakṛti* (base) is so called because it is "practiced" (*prakriyate*), meaning it is formed prior to the suffix (*pratyaya*); but that is not correct, as it would fail to apply in cases such as *bahupaṭuḥ*. Therefore, the proper meaning is that it is that which is the "object of reference for the suffix" (*pratyayoddeśyatā*). In this very way, it is merely imagined for the sake of the grammatical procedure (*śāstraprakriyā*) of the treatise. *Lāghava* is the state of being light (*laghoḥ bhāvaḥ*), which is to say, proceeding with ease; its application (*vṛtti*) in the means of achieving that [ease] is used figuratively (*upacārāt*). [The phrase] "stated explicitly" (*kaṇṭhata uktāḥ*) refers to this.

By the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) and so forth; "by that logic" means that the meanings of the substitutes have been stated according to the aforementioned logic. "By such an assumption" means having postulated the base and the suffix through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the meaning is assigned] to the word in the form of their aggregate.

Regarding the phrase "in the definition": the words "being formulated" (*kriyamāṇe*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding "when the suffix exists": the meaning is that when the suffix has arisen, its status as denoting an action (*bhāvavacanatva*) is understood, and from that which denotes an action, the suffix occurs. [The opponent objects: Since the entire complex (*samudāya*) does not exist prior to the linguistic usage of the treatise (*śastra-vyavahāra*), there is an absence of the distinction of meaningfulness obtainable through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); therefore, it is incorrect to say "having resorted to its status as denoting an action. To this, he provides the intended sense: "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*).

The meaning is this: the primary denotative power (*vācakatva*), which is accessible through linguistic usage and resides either in the word (*pada*) or the sentence (*vākya*), is not accepted here. Regarding the phrase "imagined" (*kalpita*): since the author of the Bhāṣya has stated—on the basis of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—that the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone expresses action, the intention is that the denotative power is accepted as residing only in the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth. If it is objected: "If the distinction produced by suffixes is imagined, does this not contradict scriptural statements such as 'What is the root? and so on?", [the reply is: True; however, such a statement was made precisely with the intention of what is imagined. Furthermore, even this imagination is eternal because its usage is eternal.

"And thus" (evañca): he refutes the view that direct denotative capacity resides only in the word (*pada*), because the substituends (*sthānin*) vary according to different grammatical systems (*vyākaraṇa-bheda*) and therefore lack a fixed denotative capacity. [He says] "of grammars" (*vyākaraṇa*) and "of scripts" (*lipīnām*); the meaning is: just as there is a means of cognition even for various different scripts. || 1.3 ||

Regarding the term "pramāṇa" (means of valid cognition): the point is that when a word denoting one object is employed to denote another object, even though the listener gains an understanding of the meaning, it does not possess the status of a *pramāṇa*, which consists in being a generator of valid knowledge (*pramā*). As for the claim that the cognition arising even from a silent verse (*mauniśloka*) and the like proves that the knowledge of the word (*padajñāna*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the word itself—that is incorrect; for, by accepting that the internal *sphoṭa* is the expressive agent (*vācaka*), it is the written characters themselves that serve as the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of that *sphoṭa*.

As for the claim that the word (*pada*) is not the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by the recollection of the word-meaning (*padārtha*), that is not correct; for in that case, since there is no operation (*vyāpāra*), the status of being an instrument is impossible. Others, however, hold that the recollection of the word-meaning itself is the operation. As for the Veda, which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), its authority is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) even in the absence of being spoken by a trustworthy person (*āpta*); whereas in the case of what is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), its authority arises precisely from being composed by a trustworthy person. In common worldly usage, however, the inference of authority is based on the speaker’s being the utterer of a sentence that generates purposeful activity consistent with reality.

In the case of the Veda, however, since there is no corroboration for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, whose fruits are restricted to other worlds, its authority must be accepted as intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the reality of things" (*vastutattva*): the word *tattva* is conventionally used for that which is non-superimposed. Regarding "passion and so forth" (*rāgādi*): passion (*rāga*) has its cause in the volition (*saṅkalpa*) consisting of the cognition that something is a means to a desired end; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hatred is included. Regarding "one who does not speak otherwise": the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that a person who does not speak otherwise is an authoritative person (*āpta*). Authority (*āpti*) is the knowledge of the reality of the matter; one who is recognized through that is an *āpta*. (1.4)

"Ungrasped" (agṛhītā): the meaning is that no comprehension of the object is observed from a word whose *vṛtti* (conventional relation) has not been grasped. He states that there is also a power (*śakti*) regarding the property-aspect (*dharma-aṃśa*). "Not indeed" (*na hi*): the meaning is that no cognition having "sweetness" (*madhuratva*) as its qualifier is observed. "Determined by that property" (*taddharmāvacchinna*): the meaning is a *vṛtti* having as its object that which is delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). The qualification of the *vṛtti* in the cognition [is established] through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); the status of being the locus of the cognition is [established] through the relation of being the object (*viṣayatā*).

Logicians maintain that the knowledge of the word-meaning relation (*vṛtti*) and the knowledge of the word are separate causes [of verbal cognition]. However, here, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the causality of the qualified [cognition] alone is stated. Even there, since it would involve complexity (*gaurava*) if the cause were a cognition of the word as the locus of the *vṛtti*, which is co-located with an awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the *vṛtti*, the inclusion of co-location and other such factors within the scope of the relation [of the cause] is avoided. Thus, the inclusion of co-location and so forth occurs within the scope of the relation [of the cause].

For when the function (*vṛtti*) of a word such as "pot" is known, both the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding that function and the cognition (*jñāna*) itself exist as objects within that word; furthermore, that cognition has as its object the word which is the locus of the function. As for the claim that the "presentation of the word-meaning produced by the word through its function" (*vṛttyā padajanyapadārthopasthitiḥ*) is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), that is not correct. This is because it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to hold that the cognition of the word is the cause through the relation of "presentation of the word-meaning produced by itself," rather than positing the status of being such a presentation as the heavier delimitor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

"By another means of knowledge" (mānāntara) means that sweetness is presented through inference and so forth. Logicians, however, say it is produced by the *jñānalakṣaṇā* [perceptual cognition]. Poeticians, on the other hand, say it is produced here by *vyañjanā* (suggestion). [Objection: But since there is no grasp of the word's power (*śakti*) with "sweetness" as the qualifier, how can such a cognition arise when only a part [of the word] is used, namely "guḍa"? To this, he says: "But where... [and] "But not... The meaning is that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) such as "the guḍa possesses sweetness. This is what is indicated by the term "suggested" (*dhvanitam*).

For in that regard, in the expression "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*), the cognition of rice sprinkled with curd arises through the word "curd" itself; and in the case of "jaggery" (*guḍa*), although sweetness is perceived by means other than verbal expression, it is clear that it does not constitute the denotation of the word.

Now, one might object: in the case of the sentence "He eats jaggery" (*guḍaṃ bhuṅkte*), since sweetness (*madhuratva*) is also a qualifier (*prakāra*) just like jaggerness (*guḍatva*), one must prevent a verbal cognition that has sweetness as its qualifier. To this end, it is argued that a verbal cognition having jaggerness as its qualifier and jaggery as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is caused by the knowledge of the word-potency (*sakti*) having that [jaggerness] as its qualifier. This is because, in that case, the delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) of ākāśatva—which is of the nature of being the substratum of sound—is undelimited (*niravacchinna*). If this is said, we reply: no. For we accept that from the word *ākāśa* there arises only an indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) presentation; therefore, such a causal relation is not postulated in that instance.

Furthermore, this is because even "spaciousness" (*ākāśatva*) is a universal (*jāti*). By this, the objection that—if one accepts indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*)—there would be no cognition of non-difference in the case of the judgment "space is a substance" due to the absence of a presentation of distinct modes, is refuted. As for the claim that, since space consists of only a single individual, even if it does not depend on a pervasive property (*anugamaka-dharma*), the property of being the substratum of sound (*śabdāśrayatva*) constitutes the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "space" for the sake of its fixed presentation—that too is incorrect; for even if the Grammarians (*Śābdika*) admit spaciousness, it is still a universal.

If it is objected: "But since a non-conceptual cognition such as 'the jar and jar-ness' lacks the property of having 'jar-ness' as its qualifier, how can it be produced by the knowledge of the referents of words such as 'jar'? We say no; for since non-conceptual cognition is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), we do not admit that it serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the effecthood [of the subsequent conceptual cognition]. 1.5.

"By way of inversion" means for the purpose of preventing a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) having "pot-ness" as its qualifier from arising immediately after the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) which has "pot-ness" as its qualificand. Regarding the phrase "limited by that property" (*taddharmāvacchinna*): [an objection]—if this were so, since the apprehension of the potency of words such as *tad* ("that") occurs with respect to what is limited by being present in the mind, then when it is said "bring that," the resulting cognition would be "bring what is present in the mind" alone, and not in a specific form such as "pot-ness" and so forth.

If it is argued that for this very reason, there is an over-extension of the definition of inference (*anumiti*)—since the verbal cognition produced by the sentence "That [mountain], which possesses smoke pervaded by fire, is fiery," is generated by a reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*)—as stated in the *Dīdhiti*, the following is said in response: Even though the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the word as a general form, the presentation (*upasthiti*) from pronouns such as *tyad* occurs only in a specific form. The traditional maxim that the presentation and the apprehension of denotative power must have the same objective form applies only to cases other than pronouns; thus, in the case of words like "pot," the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is indeed a specific property such as "pot-ness."

Others maintain that it is indeed accepted that words such as *tat* have multiple meanings. Regarding the phrase "having its own object" (*svaviṣayaka*): the meaning is that there is a co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between an awakened latent impression (*udbuddhasaṃskāra*) whose object is the linguistic function (*vṛtti*), and the state of having as its object the word that is the substratum of that function. Furthermore, there exists an awakened latent impression whose object is the function as determined by the referent of the word "jar," and there is also the cognition of the word "jar" as its [the impression's] object. This is the intended sense.

The word "ghaṭa" (pot) has its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is qualified by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Immediately after a cognition whose qualificandum is such a relation (*vṛtti*), a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises having that very same form. A cognition of the word, as qualified by such an impression, is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). [This is expressed in the rule: "Not for one who has not grasped the relation. Because there is an absence of an impression whose object is the relation, the requirement of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is introduced to exclude verbal comprehension from another word, even though a relation pertaining to that other word may exist.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is to be understood not only through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*), but also through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Consequently, after the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word "cow" [in the case of the word "cow"], there is no verbal cognition for Maitra [if he does not know the word]. The phrase "of one whose function is distinct" is to be construed with the word "cognition. The sense is that this is because of the absence of an awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*). The phrase "of one who lacks knowledge of the word" is used because there is an absence of knowledge [of the word] as an object therein. The term "word" (*pada*) is employed to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as gestures of the hand, which also possess meaning.

He states the result of incorporating the condition of being the locus of the relation as determined by that [property]. [The phrase] "by way of being the locus" means as follows: since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), although space is presented through words such as "pot," the word "pot" does not convey that [space], because the relation determined by [the property] delimited by "spatiality" (*ākāśatva*) is absent in the word "pot. This is the meaning.

Although it is true that in the absence of either a mental state (*vṛtti-jñāna*) or the cognition of a word (*pada-jñāna*), the production of the effect is impossible precisely due to the lack of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the collection of causes, nevertheless, the inclusion of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is for the sake of the cognition of the relation that constitutes that totality. It might be argued: "Experience alone is the cause of memory; since non-remembrance is possible simply because no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises from a cognition that is indifferent (*upekṣā-ātmaka*), what is the use of [positing] a mental impression as the cause?"

If it is argued that, because there is no rotation by another [cause], the status of causes such as the staff would not apply to the production of jars and the like, we say: no. For while it would be cumbersome to regard the various specific instances of those [causes] as causes due to their being excitants (*udbodhaka*), it is simpler to postulate the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) itself as the cause. Furthermore, the popular maxim that "the possessor of an operation is not rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*) by the operation" is entirely baseless. Here, by the word *saṃskāra*, a specific type of mental trace (*vāsanā*) is meant, and not the one well-known to logicians (*tārkika*) as the producer of memory.

Because it will be refuted later that verbal cognition is of the nature of memory. Regarding the phrase "of Caitra and so forth": for Caitra and others are indeed presented [to consciousness] by virtue of being manifested by words.

[Objection: But surely, there would be no resulting cognition immediately after the experience of the word-meaning relation (vṛtti) regarding a jar or the like, because the latent impression (saṃskāra) would not exist prior to that; therefore, he says: "from the latent impression [left by] the non-cognitive [experience]. The point is that since experience is momentary, even in that case, cognition arises only from remembrance. [Objection: But surely, since no latent impression is produced after an experience of power (śakti) that is of the nature of indifference (upekṣā), there would be no resulting verbal cognition; therefore, he says: "by that. [Objection: Since a latent impression is beyond the senses, there is no evidence for its existence; therefore, he says: "and that which postulates the latent impression."

Because the cause, which is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), is inferred solely through its effect, which is memory. Although a cause produces an effect only when it exists in its own nature and not when it is merely known, nevertheless, the term "kalpikā" means that which causes the postulation of the cause. Now, since a latent impression is destroyed by its fruit, and because the impression would have been destroyed once the mental modification (*vṛtti*) has become memory, there would be no occurrence of verbal comprehension; therefore, he says: "Or rather, the verbal cognition itself [is the destroyer]. The sense is that only the final fruit is the destroyer of the latent impression.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, a further recollection would not occur immediately after a recollection; for in that case, the recollection itself is what generates the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). As it is stated in the *Dīdhiti*: "And from repeated recollection, an even firmer impression is produced. (1.8)

"Vṛtti is threefold. The suffix *dhā* in "threefold" (*tridhā*) denotes manner. A "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is that which differentiates an existing universal (*sāmānya*). Here, "being a function" (*vṛttitva*) is the universal, while "being a power" (*śaktitva*) and so forth are the particulars. Thus, the meaning is that a function possesses three such particulars. This, however, is merely a description of its essential nature; as for the causal relationship between the cognition of power and the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is indeed one and the same.

For instance, the causality for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) resides in a cognition that has as its qualificandum an object residing in a word, which is itself a qualifier residing in a word, and this qualifier is defined by a subject-object relation (*viṣayatā*) that is delimited by power (*śakti*). This is because power is the relational connector (*saṃsarga*) in a cognition where the word is the qualifier, whether through the relation of power (*śakti-sambandha*) or the relation of denotability (*śakya-sambandha*). As for the claim that "vṛtti-ness" consists in being either power or indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that is not correct, because it would result in the failure to include particles (*dyotaka*) such as *eva*. [The author] restates the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*): "From this word... and so forth.

Objection: If the desire of God, which has "being cognizable" as its qualifier, were the *śakti* (power), it would follow that it is a property of the object (*arthadharma*). Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he says: "This... (*idam iti*).

Regarding the phrase "and of that": the meaning is that the desire of God (īśvarecchā) obtains its status as *śakti* (denotative power) everywhere—in the word, in the object, and in the relation between the produced and the producer. Although primary qualificandhood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) resides only in the object, nevertheless, because when the *śakti* is grasped—as in the case of "an animal is to be understood from the word 'paśu' (animal)"—there is a cognition even of the hair and so forth which lack primary qualificandhood, it was not stated in that way [as being restricted to the object]. Regarding the phrase "in that": the meaning is that the denoter (*vācaka*) is the object of the [divine] desire by virtue of being the generator of cognition, and so forth. There is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); that is, there is no contingency of denotative power (*vācakatva*) applying to the relation and other such factors.

"First apprehension of the power [of words]" (*prathama-śakti-graha*) refers to the fact that children acquire knowledge of meaning from sentences alone. "Insertion" (*āvāpa*) is the addition of another word; "exclusion" (*udvāpa*) is its removal. Examples include "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) and "take the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ naya*), and so forth. The phrase "by the author of the treatise" (*śāstrakṛt*) implies that since the division of words is merely conceptual, in reality a sentence such as "bring the jar" or "take the jar" is indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). Even though, according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), a sentence is not indivisible, nevertheless, the division of meaning is only imagined through the division of words;
for it has already been stated that the completion of meaning occurs only in the sentence as a whole.

[Objection: Is it not improper to say that "power" (śakti) is simply the will of God (īśvarecchā), since—due to a lack of decisive evidence—it is equally possible for God’s knowledge and action to be of the nature of power? To this, he states the acceptance of the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) with the words "yadā hi" ("when..."). That [will] is the power. [Response: "tanna" ("that is not so"). A child, seeing a jar brought by a person who has heard a sentence such as "bring the jar," infers: "This person possesses the cognition that the jar-bringing is the effect [to be accomplished], because he possesses an activity directed toward the jar."

Then, because an effect does not arise without a cause, one determines that the indivisible sentence possesses the capacity to produce that effect. Consequently, since there is no relation between the sentence and its meaning—because [otherwise] cognition would be impossible—and because the postulation [of such a relation] occurs only after the knowledge that it generates cognition, the question arises: how can the capacity to generate cognition itself be the relation? The sense is this: first, the apprehension of the capacity to generate cognition occurs, and only afterwards is the relation postulated. (1.9)

"By the activity of the person to be prompted"—that is, by the bringing of a jar or the like—"his knowledge [is inferred]"; the meaning is that one infers that this knowledge of the sentence-meaning has arisen in the person to be prompted. Regarding "of the knowledge": the meaning is that for the knowledge residing in the person to be prompted, that very sentence is the cause; and since there could be no capacity to convey meaning if there were no relation between the sentence and its meaning, a relation between the two is postulated. "Because it is itself untenable" means because it is impossible at the outset. "Apprehended" means known.

The point is that the relationship characterized as "being a producer of cognition" cannot be known [prior to the cognition itself]. It is therefore rejected, because the status of being a relationship is only postulated immediately after the knowledge of its being a producer of cognition. Furthermore, if "denotative power" were defined simply as "the capacity to produce cognition," there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to phonemes such as *sparśa* which manifest qualities like sweetness.

"Due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāviraheṇa*) means that there is no deciding factor (*vinigamanā*) as to whether the power (*śakti*) resides in the will of God or in the knowledge of God. Furthermore, "if this were so" (*kiñcaivam*) means that the causality of the staff and other such instruments would consist merely in their being the object of a desire such as, "Let a jar be produced from the staff. Therefore, the sense is that a distinction is necessary: the power residing in the staff and so forth produces the effect by its very existence (*svarūpasatī*), whereas the power residing in words is useful for verbal comprehension only when it is known (*jñātā*).

Furthermore, one must state that the very nature of being a producer of heaven and so forth constitutes the causality (*kāraṇatva*) in sacrifices and the like; and since there has been no prior apprehension [of such causality] by way of its being a producer of heaven, it would follow that there could be no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) from the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. This is what is meant by the phrase "there would be many difficulties" (*bahūpaplava*); the meaning is that causality as a distinct entity (*atirikta*) could not be established in other cases either. Therefore, the intention is that the Lord’s will (*īśvarecchā*) alone is the regulator of causality. [This applies to] "all cognitions" (*pramāṇām*).

The meaning is that, since it is observed that the eyes and other sense organs produce the cognition of a jar and so forth only when they are related to the jar through a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is likewise inappropriate here for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) to stand in a [causal] relation.

"Otherwise" means: if a relation such as being a producer (*janakatva*) were accepted; "when the smoke is being known" means: intending to show that smoke itself is the cause and not the cognition of smoke, he said "from smoke. "Annihilation of pervasion (*vyāpti*)" means: pervasion is the rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*); its status as a cause would be destroyed. Therefore, the intention is that a relation consisting of being a producer is not appropriate.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "of desire or of being a generator," that which exists in both relata—just as the conjunction exists in both the pot and the ground—is alone considered a relation; however, since properties such as being a generator reside only in one term (the pot), they lack the quality of being a relation because they do not subsist in both. He demonstrates the absence of desire's subsistence in both by the word "desire": the meaning is that the objectivity belonging to the cognition which is the object of desire does not serve as the regulator for the locus of that desire.

For in that case, neither the word nor its meaning is the object of the desire; rather, it is consciousness itself. And the fact that consciousness is the locus of the desire must be stated as being solely by virtue of its being the object of consciousness. But that is not possible, because there is no such cognition as "this word" or "this meaning possesses the desire. This is the intended sense.

In order to state the absence of relation, he first demonstrates the nature of relation with the words "For relation... Although the quality of being the regulator of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) belongs to both the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), they are excluded because they are objects even in an unqualified cognition (*aviśiṣṭabuddhi*). He states that in the present case there is no such qualified cognition—as there is in the case of a qualified cognition such as "the floor possesses a jar"—with the words "For not... The word "therein" (*tatra*) means: in the object of that cognition which is the object of desire.

[Objection: Since the object, like the word, is also a cause for verbal cognition, there exists a relation called "the capacity to generate cognition" in both cases; therefore, [the author] says: "Even though it exists," etc. [He states the reason: "Because it is difficult to establish," etc. The meaning is that although both the staff and the wheel are causes of the jar, there is no mutual relation between them. This same meaning applies even if the reading is "due to the absence of a relation. He states this very point in the words: "In the case of cognition," etc.

Otherwise, since both the object and the person are causes of cognition, it would follow that when there is a relation between the person and the object, a specific cognition of those two would arise—this is the meaning. [Objection: Since the object also exists as the locus of the property of being a producer of cognition and as its determiner (*nirūpaka*), let it be considered a related term. [Reply: No, because the relation of being a determiner (*nirūpakatā*) is not a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*). 1.10.

Regarding the phrase "the denoted and the denoter": the capacity in the form of causality is well-established in the word, while the capacity in the form of being the denoted belongs to the object. Regarding the term "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*): superimposition is the appearance of the attributes of one thing in another; the identity based upon that is [merely] conceptual, not real—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: let it be explained that identity itself is the convention (*saṅketa*), since the superimposition of identity occurs immediately after the apprehension of the convention. This is not so; for the convention is simply the identity [itself], as in the case of "This is Devadatta. Regarding the phrase "of that too": this means "of that identity as well."

The sense is that the superimposed identity between the word and its meaning functions as the apprehender of the expressive power (śakti), and thus it is the expressive power itself. Now, [the opponent] asks: "Of what kind of identity? [The author] explains the absence of its being a relation by saying: "Because of difference and non-difference. The sense is that when there is real difference, the superimposed non-difference alone constitutes identity; and for such [an identity], the status of being a relation is impossible. He states the reason for this very point: "Of that which constitutes it," and so forth.

The meaning is that the relationhood of either difference (*bheda*) or non-difference (*abheda*), which constitutes identity (*tādātmya*), has not been observed elsewhere. Now, one might object: even if difference lacks relationhood, non-difference is seen to possess relationhood in cases such as "the pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*); to this he replies: "it will be refuted. The sense is that a relation is necessarily restricted by the difference between the relata (*sambandhin*). || 1.11 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that if there is a convention (*saṅketa*) in the form "this word is the designator of this meaning," the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning is destroyed? To this, he says: "But the convention... [The phrase] *itaretarādhyāsaḥ* means the superimposition (*āropa*) of mutual identity. [The term] *itaretarādhyāsa* is derived from the sense "that by which mutual superimposition is manifested. [The compound] *smṛtyātmaka* means "that whose self is memory," which signifies "the object of memory. For this very reason, he will say later: "of cognition itself," and so forth. [The phrase] *śaktibodhakatvam* means "the state of being the grasper of the expressive power (*śakti*). He states another meaning for the word *smṛti*: "Furthermore (*kiñca*)."

Regarding the position that the three types of words function [in this way], he says "And thus" (*evañca*). Since only the name itself is etymologically derived (*vyutpanna*), there is indeed a power (*śakti*) in that case consisting solely of the superimposition (*āropa*) of actions obtainable through etymological analysis (*yoga*), because there is no convention (*saṅketa*) by God made known through the recollection of [the word] *pāminī* and so forth. He shows the relationship which is the cause for such superimposition with the words "By its own power" (*svaśakteti*). The meaning of "Govinda" is that the usage of the modern Govinda occurs through the superimposition of the well-known qualities of [the ancient] Govinda. He demonstrates the connection that serves as the basis for the superimposition. "By its own power" [means]: [it functions] by its own inherent capacity.

One who is capable of censuring cows is a "go-vandin"; the modern *hovinda* is the object of that convention (*saṅketa*). Now, if one resorts to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for words such as *govinda*, there would be no need for a convention; to this he replies: "Precisely for this purpose. This means: precisely for the sake of knowing the aforementioned relationship.

And by means of superimposition (*āropa*), he shows his agreement. "For this very reason" means: because of the absence of an objective referent (*pratyayārtha*). The sense is that in the case of an arbitrary word (*yadṛcchāśabda*), since only the speaker's intention (*puruṣecchā*) is the cause [of its application], there is no dependence on any specific ground for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*); therefore, the abstract suffix (*tva-pratyaya*) would not apply. "Ending in an abstract suffix" (*bhāvapratyayānta*) means: occurring as something ending in a suffix whose meaning is an abstract state (*bhāva*). (1.12)

Regarding the term *prāthamakalpika*: a *prāthamakalpika* is the primary [individual], such as Ḍittha; he who performs his actions or possesses his qualities is called "Ḍittha. When one says, "The Ḍitthas perform such actions, and you do so too," the meaning is that your "Ḍittha-ness" consists in the performance of such actions. Thus, the point is that upon observing the actions associated with Ḍittha, the basis for the application of the name (*pravṛttinimitta*) is precisely those actions, qualities, and so forth. This is the essential truth here.

According to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, which holds that "the application of a word to a substance occurs due to the existence of a certain quality (*guṇa*)," one must follow this very definition: a quality is that which differentiates, and a substance is that which is differentiated. Consequently, an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to a quality—which is merely a qualifier—derived from a word that denotes only the qualified substance. Thus, when the word *go* (cow) denotes a substance delimited by a genus (*jāti*), the abstract suffix in *gotva* (cowness) refers to the genus. However, when it denotes the genus alone, the abstract suffix refers to the phonetic form of the word itself, which is co-extensive (*samaniyata*) with that genus.

For that which colors another by its own nature is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). And thus, since a word conveys its meaning by coloring it through its own form, its own form alone is the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*); and the cognition of the object occurs through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that form. Consequently, in the case of *ḍitthatvam*, because of the superimposition of action and quality elsewhere [than the name], the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refers to the action and quality co-occurring with "Ḍittha-ness. Thus, the expression *ḍitthatvam* intends the superimposition of non-difference between the action and the quality.

"How so?"—the meaning is: how can there be a function [of the suffix], since superimposition is impossible in the case of the first *ḍittha*? He provides the answer: "Just as... [and] "occurring in some instances. The suffix *ṭhak* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule for words beginning with *vinaya*. The meaning is that because there are different states (*avasthā*), one may even postulate a genus (*jāti*) there; thus, just as there is a cognition characterized by that [genus], so too is there the suffix *-tva*. With the intention that, due to the absence of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there is no evidence for postulating a genus there, and therefore a cognition devoid of any qualifying mode (*niṣprakāraka*) is more appropriate, he says "somehow" (*kathañcit*). "Therein" (*tatra*).

The meaning is as follows: when the apprehension of a word's expressive power (*śakti*) arises through inference—namely, "this word is capable of this meaning because it is employed by the elders for this meaning"—it is necessary that there be a delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*). Consequently, just as there is a cognition where the word is the qualifier (*prakāra*) due to the superimposition of the word upon the object, so too does the suffix *tva* [denote] the word-form itself as the occasion for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). *Tat* = the word-form itself. *Prakāram* = the qualifier. *Pravṛttinimittam* = the occasion for application.

"In that view" means in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. "There is no natural consistency" means that since even from words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) there is observed a cognition having "word" (*śabda*) as its qualifier, this method is universal; therefore, the word found in the Bhāṣya cannot be taken in its natural sense in any way. "Elsewhere" [refers to the following].

The meaning is that even if the name-form (*saṃjñāsvarūpa*) of a modern object were intended to be expressed, since the suffix *tvap* could still occur, the application [of the suffix] by superimposing the action belonging to the original object would result in the *Bhāṣya* being rendered useless. However, if one explains that because the word-form itself is the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the case of a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), the suffix occurs only there, then the use of the word "even" (*api*) in the *Bhāṣya* would somehow be inconsistent. Thus say others.

The meaning is that, for the reason of the aforementioned defect, others explain the Bhāṣya differently. Regarding the phrase "by way of two objective relations" (*viṣayatādvayena*): here, the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the referent of the word *ḍittha*; it appears both as the qualifier (*prakāra*) and as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, the meaning is that the individual qualified by the state of being a qualifier is the referent of the suffix *-tva*. The sense is that the expression "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*) used in the Bhāṣya is appropriate because this method is not observed elsewhere.

By the words "prayogādī" (from usage, etc.), [the author] indicates the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) and the cognition of existence (*bhāvapratyaya*). The "discomfort" (*asvarasa*) here is that for people like us, [the apprehension of power] is difficult to grasp. Regarding the word "tatra" (therein): the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is comprehension even in the absence of power and so forth. He refutes the view that power does not exist therein because, since there is no non-conceptual apprehension of power or verbal comprehension from the word, [power] would be absent. Regarding "tattad" (that respective): he states the fault that would arise if one does not accept [these] as being functions (*vṛtti*). [He says this in the phrase] "vṛttijanyā" (produced by a function).

If it is asked, "How then is there verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) regarding that which is to be imitated?"—the answer is that because it consists of recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is indeed verbal comprehension; and as for its being connected with other word-meanings even though it is presented in that way, this occurs precisely because of the grammatical rule *bhūsattāyām* and so forth. Now, one might raise the objection: "In cases of modern names (*nāmadheya*), although there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*), there certainly is such power in the case of [Vedic] names, as evidenced by the statement *dvādaśe 'hani* (on the twelfth day). Therefore, the previously stated claim that there is only indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in those cases is incorrect. To dispel this doubt, he says: *dvādaśe 'hani* and *tattadrūpeṇa*. [The meaning is: Even in the case of the statement *dvādaśe 'hani*, the name applies to the child in its specific form [as a particular individual], and thus it is a primary denotation (*śakti*). However, in the case of modern names, since there is no established relationship [between the name and the object], there can be no primary denotative power. Therefore, the previous position remains correct.

The meaning is "by means of [the universal] *caitratva* and so forth. Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), because even when pronouncing them as such, they would be considered corrupt according to the rule *nāpabhāṣitavai*. Therefore, the point is that being uttered by God (*īśvara*) in its respective form is precisely what determines the possession of expressive power (*śaktimatva*); and this does not exist in the case of proper names. Regarding the phrase "there too": the meaning is "even in the case of proper names, unlike modern technical designations. Others hold that since God is omniscient, a specific utterance is postulated even in the case of proper names.

[Objection: But what is the proof for the existence of that capacity (*śakti*) there? Is it because it is well-known in the case of words ending in nominal suffixes (*subanta*), or because one grasps only the expressive word (*vācakaśabda*)? There is a capacity [in the form of] the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth; therefore, he says: "In this regard, the word is the cognizer. And thus, the sense is that in the absence of capacity, there would be no cognition. (1.13)

He states that it is the relation of power (*śakti*) that regulates the relationship between the signifier and the signified, but not power itself; this is expressed in the words "of power also. The meaning is that because the power to produce a jar exists [in the staff], the staff’s status as a producer of the jar is due to the power residing in the staff. Furthermore, there is no other power belonging to power, for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding "assistance" (*upakāra*): where there is a relation whose nature is assistance, there the property called "power" is inferred, because there can be no assistance for things that are unrelated.

Furthermore, power (*śakti*) itself is not the relation, because even in the case of powers, it is the relation alone that acts as the regulator for their dependence on a substratum and for the production of an effect. Moreover, it is the relation itself that regulates the subsistence of qualities (*guṇa*) within a substance (*dravya*), since even those things that are dependent can still provide assistance; this is the meaning.

The object (*artha*) is that which is assisted; the word (*śabda*) is that which assists. Here, the state of being an assistant belongs to both of them reciprocally. [The term] "kāryam" [means] "upakāram" (the assistance). This relation is called "assistance" (*upakāraka*). [The phrase] "of the capacities (*śakti*) also" means that it is only when a relation exists that even a capacity can produce an effect. [The term] "definition of the object" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) which conveys the meaning. By the words "by this" [in the commentary], the sense is that it is improper to state that the word possesses a capacity for indicating meaning, because the mention of "capacity" was intended to define the sentence (*vākya*) for the purpose of grasping the convention (*samaya*). || 1.14 ||

"By this [it is meant]: even words, though they depend on the apprehension of the relation between word-meanings, do not depend on the apprehension of the relation between sentence-meanings; for, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, the sentence-meaning is understood precisely because it is otherwise impossible. [The view] is refuted: because when the sentence-meaning is understood through expectancy and other factors inherent in the two constituent words, the existence of the *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-absolute) is unavoidable. 'By way of the meaning of the parts' means by way of the meanings of the stems (*prakṛti*) and so forth. 'It is indicated'..."

By the statement "it is the grasper of the aggregate characterized by the word," the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of the word is indicated; and by the mention of its being a grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), the conceptualization of the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth is indicated. That [is] repetition. He establishes this very point with the words "of the word *iti*. Since the word *ghaṭa* is referred to by the word *iti*, the meaning is that there is no difference between the word and the cognition [of it]. This non-difference exists precisely because of the distinction in their forms. [The phrase] "hear the object" means that the object is merely superimposed upon the verbal [cognition], since the verbal [cognition] itself is what is heard. This is the intended sense.

"Om, the single syllable. Now, one might object: since the scripture states, "He who is the bull among the Vedas, whose form is the universe, arose from the Vedas out of the immortal"—and thus the syllable Om, the bull among the Vedas, is heard to have arisen from the Vedas—how can it have the nature of Brahman? True; however, the phrase "he arose" means that he appeared [as such]. 1.15.

Now, if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its meaning, would it not follow that upon the utterance of the word "fire" (*agni*), one would suffer burns from a frying pan, and that the conventional usage "this is the designator of that" would be impossible? To this, he says: "And identity... [referring to] those two, namely difference and non-difference. "Its designator is the *praṇava*"—this is a *sūtra* of Patañjali. The meaning is that the *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, is the designator of that Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the passages cited, such as "The single-syllabled *om*," etc.; "being a property of the word" means being perceived through hearing and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of words denoting a relation" (*sambandhaśabdāde*): here, the meaning of the locative case is "being denotable" (*vācyatva*). In the expression "having understood the fitness" (*yogyatāṃ pratītya*), there is the status of a *karmapravacanīya* with respect to the relation of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*). Thus, the relation denoted by the word "relation" is indeed fitness itself. And this is ascertained solely through fitness, based on the linguistic usage: "this [word] is fit for this [meaning]. The meaning is that fitness alone is the relation between word and object.

For this very reason, Helārāja explained that the word *sambandha* (relation) denotes the capacity for relation precisely by means of its fitness (*yogyatā*). Now, one might object: "In that case, there would be no utility for linguistic convention (*saṅketa*. To this he says: "From convention" (*samayāt*). Through convention—which is synonymous with the continuous tradition of the usage of elders—the innate capacity itself is ascertained; for this [capacity] does not exist merely because of its being expressed. Thus it is said: "being" (*satī*).

The meaning is this: since the status of being the cause of a determinate cognition regarding a fixed object is only logical when a relation exists and not otherwise, therefore, from the effect—which is the communication of the meaning—it is concluded that a relation between word and meaning exists. According to the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*, the ascertainment of fitness (*yogyatā*) arises from the usage of the word that makes the relation known—such as "this word has a relation to this meaning"—and from the usage "this meaning possesses the fitness for this [word]."

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of this": in this view, the expression "the relation of fitness" (yogyatāṃ prati sambandhaḥ) means "the relation of fitness. Thus, the meaning is that the very relation which fitness has within the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) is itself fitness. The reading "the relation characterized by identity as defined by fitness" (*yogyatānirūpitastādātmyalakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ*) is a corruption. For identity is the locus (*āśraya*) of fitness, not its defining correlate (*nirūpita*). [The phrase] "of those like us," etc. [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that [the object] is inferred by means of that convention of God which is grasped through our own convention, which is itself a succession of the conventions of the elders. For this very reason—namely, because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and object—the threefold [cognition] is understood through words manifested in usage: the nature of the word, the object, and the intention of the speaker. And since this is not possible in the absence of a fixed relation, the relation is real and not merely conventional.

The meaning of "established" (*samavasthita*) is that it is rooted by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), not introduced by treatises (*śāstra*). In that regard, the relationship between the object (*artha*) and the word (*śabda*) is that of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*); however, with respect to the intention of the speaker (*prayoktr-abhiprāya*), there is a relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). As they say: "That object which appears in the intellect as a specific operation of the speaker is the basis for the multiplicity of meanings of words. Thus, identity (*tādātmya*) has been stated. [This refers to] superimposed identity (*adhyasta-tādātmya*). Regarding "difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda*):
the meaning is that while there is indeed difference in reality (*vastutaḥ*), there is non-difference through superimposition (*āropita*). (1.16)

"Buddhist indeed" means that the word and its object are merely the denoter and the denoted as objects of cognition (*buddhi-viṣaya*), and not real entities. For this very reason, [the author] establishes the reality of their difference by means of the non-difference between word and object. "Inherent," etc., refers to *yoga*, which is the relationship (*sambandha*). For this very reason, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "of those that are unrelated," and so forth.

"Yoga is [the relation] between word and meaning. Following this, there is the text: "Therefore, even reality (tattva) is designated [as such]. The meaning is that because the use of the genitive case—in the form "this is the denoter of this meaning" and "this is the denoted of this word"—would otherwise be inexplicable, there must exist an inherent (svābhāvika) connection between word and meaning, even though they are unreal. For this very reason, the reality of word and meaning is treated as non-different [from each other], such that one says, "This is a cow. He begins to refute the view of others—that the apprehension of convention (saṅketa) occurs through the linguistic usage of elders and so forth—by stating: "The synonyms... etc.

The meaning is that even though there are four synonyms, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through such linguistic usage. "A collection of objects" (*arthajātam*) refers to the generality of objects (*artha-sāmānyam*); by this, the exclusion of the individual (*vyakti*) is intended. He says "this belongs to this" (*asyedam*) because it is impossible to grasp a previously mentioned convention regarding something whose name is unknown. He says "this is also an injunction" (*ayam api niyogaḥ*) because, in an instruction such as "this is the moon," it is impossible to grasp the power [of the word] through mere usage; thus, this too is an injunction. He says "and the injunction" (*niyogaś ca*) because the word "injunction" (*niyoga*) is well-known in the sense of establishing a specific state.

[Objection: But surely, because there is no cognition such as "the pot has sound" or "the pot is the object," there is no relation between word and object; consequently, the cognition of an object would arise without restriction. To this, he says: "conventional" (*sāmayika*). This means "dependent upon convention" (*saṅketa*). The implication is that, by virtue of this, the cognition of an object from words does not occur without restriction. "This is this" means having the form "that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is a cow. "Because of the non-attainment of convention" means that there would be no convention of the form "this word has its denotative power (*śakti*) in this object. As for what was stated in the *Kusumāñjali*:

"The production of a scorpion from cow dung is like [the production of] illusion (*māyā*) through convention (*samaya*), and so forth. Just as a scorpion is produced from both a scorpion and cow dung at the beginning of creation solely from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), whereas now the birth of a Brahmin occurs [through convention]; and just as a magician, having created an illusory object to be employed, employs it by saying "bring the jar" and so forth, and thereby causes one to grasp the power [of that convention], so too the Lord, having created two bodies, causes one to grasp the power—this he demonstrates with the phrase "by observation in the world. And such a convention exists for the Lord, because in the world we observe exactly such a convention.
Therefore, the meaning is that convention (saṅketa) merely reveals the [inherent] power [of the word]. || 1.17 ||

For this very reason—that is, precisely because convention (*saṅketa*) is the grasper of expressive power (*śakti*). The meaning is that the convention was directly revealed by the Lord (*īśvara*) to the Great Sages (*maharṣi*) and others. "That convention" means the convention of the Lord. [Objection: But surely there could be no convention for a relationship between word and meaning that already exists [prior to the convention]. To this he says: "And all words... [and] "...with all meanings. For this reason, [the relationship is eternal] with all meanings. "Eternal" (*nitya*): the sense is that if it were created by the Lord, it would follow that it is non-eternal due to being something produced (*janya*).

*Tantra* is so called because by it things are woven (*tantryante*) or explained (*vyutpādyante*). "Supreme in both forms" means that because both mere sound and mere meaning have Brahman as their material cause (*upādāna*), there is no difference between them and it. "Of both" refers to both the word and its meaning. "From Prakṛti, which has the power of action predominant" means from Prakṛti which is oriented toward the act of transformation. As it is said in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: "This universe is the power of action; you are its cause, and [it arises] from that. "In the form of the Bindu" means consisting of a mixture of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*).

The meaning is as follows: In the view that Brahman unconditioned by *māyā* is *nirguṇa* (devoid of attributes) and Brahman conditioned by *māyā* is *saguṇa* (possessing attributes), and that this [latter] Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, it is that very [Brahman] which is denoted by the term *bindu*. However, when *prakṛti* is the material cause, then *prakṛti* itself is the *bindu*. That *bindu* is subtle in its causal form, but in its effected form it is threefold: *bindu*, *bīja*, and *nāda*. *Bindu* is Brahman; the sense is that because there is no difference between word and meaning, Brahman—which is the essence of all objects—possesses the nature of sound.

Because the world is manifested as being pervaded by the word whose essence is Brahman. Now, one might object that if the *sphoṭa* is thus produced, it would follow that it is non-eternal; therefore, he says: "And because of its eternity. Regarding the phrase "with the meaning": the meaning is that its true nature, which is the form of the word, is not divided—that is, it is absolutely not distinct—from the meaning. Regarding the word "one" (*ekām*): this is because that [word-essence] in the form of the *sphoṭa* is unitary.

Regarding the phrase "prāṇāpāna": within the interval between the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths of all beings, the Goddess whose form is speech (*vāk*) abides. From her alone arise the various states such as *vaikharī* and the rest. In the "places" (*sthāneṣu*), that is, in the palate and other articulatory organs; "when opened" (*vivṛte*), meaning when she has attained the state of manifestation. Regarding "by the function of *prāṇa*" (*prāṇavṛtti*): it is through the operation of the *prāṇa* wind that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are manifested. As it is said in another Smṛti: "This very [speech], nourished by *prāṇa*, is the basis for worldly transaction."

And thus, that which is restricted to the domain of the sense of hearing, designated by others as "revelation" (*śruti*), and whose form is audible, is the *Vaikharī* speech. The *Madhyamā*, however, has cognition alone as its material cause; it possesses a sequential order and follows the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The *Paśyantī*, moreover, has its form withdrawn and its power of sequential order internalized. [The phrase] "having cognition as its material cause" [is used].

[Objection: Is it not the case that, during the commentary on the *Vārttika* stating "the relationship between word and meaning is eternal," Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that because the meaning is non-eternal, an eternal relationship with it is impossible, and therefore the relationship is characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*)—is inconsistent? For if the meaning is non-eternal, even fitness characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) cannot possibly be eternal. To this, he says: "Of Kaiyaṭa. The intention is that since the word is eternal, that which delimits its causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), residing in it, is also eternal.

[Objection: But surely, since it begins with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and one understands from this that the purport of the Vedāntas is the Brahman devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), how can they have as their object the meaning of a sentence consisting of the relation between word-meanings? To this he says: "The [sentences] such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*)," etc. "By means of an indivisible sense" (*akhaṇḍārthena*). The point is this: because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the referents of the words *tat* (That) and *tvam* (thou)—which are respectively qualified by mediacy and immediacy—is impossible, there arises the cognition of the substratum alone, through the abandonment of the qualifying portions. Herein lie the views of the Vedāntins.

The operation of words occurs by presupposing either the relation of action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) or the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*); however, that relation of attribute and substrate does not fall within the scope of Brahman, because Brahman is devoid of attributes. Therefore, they maintain that without any analysis of words and their meanings, a sentence such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) expresses the undivided Brahman as an indivisible whole. The meaning of a sentence is that which constitutes the intended object of the sentence's purport (*vākyatātparya*).

Thus, the sense is that because the indivisible Brahman, as it is being realized, is the very capacity of the sentence, there is non-difference between the sentence and the meaning of the sentence. Here, this should be understood: perception is of two kinds—determinate (*savikalpaka*) and indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*). That which does not apprehend a relation, such as "I know the jar," is determinate. That which does not apprehend a relation, produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), is indeterminate.

This [consciousness] is perceptible because there is non-difference between the consciousness delimited by the object, as in the case of "this is Devadatta" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even by the pure [consciousness]": the sense is that just as a sense organ, even when not producing a cognition of "that-ness" (tattā), can produce a cognition of "that-ness" through the assistance of something else, so too a sentence that expresses a qualified entity (sakhaṇḍa) can also express an unqualified meaning (akhaṇḍārtha). || 1.18 ||

[Objection: "But surely, upon hearing such statements as 'That thou art,' even people like us would attain the realization of the undivided Brahman. To this, he says: "And the comprehension of that [is required]. This refers to reflection on the sentence (*vākya-manana*), which is reflection on the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-manana*). And that consists of repeated contemplation through logical arguments (*yukti*) in the form of presenting supporting and subverting proofs. *Śama* is the restraint of the internal organs; *dama* is the restraint of the external organs. Regarding the phrase "of one who is endowed": "Just as a bird moves through the sky by means of both wings, so too is the eternal goal attained through both knowledge and action."

Because of this statement, it is established that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) accompanied by action alone is the cause of liberation. Now, one might ask: how can the knowledge produced by a sentence (*vākya*) have as its object a relation (*saṃsarga*)? This is true; however, what is essential for the knowledge produced by a sentence is simply that which constitutes its intended meaning (*tātparya*). And here too, the Vedāntas have their intended meaning in the pure Brahman; this very thing is what constitutes "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Now, if Brahman is the object of the knowledge arising from the meaning of the Great Sentences (*mahāvākya*), does this not contradict the Śruti texts such as "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer"? No, it does not.

It is precisely because the nature [of the Self] is veiled by ignorance that knowledge produced by the Great Sentences (*mahāvākya*) serves to remove that veil, as it becomes the object of such knowledge. However, for that which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), since there is no veil, there can be no connection with the knowledge produced by the scriptures. Now, one might object: even by the Vedāntins, the postulation of word-meanings must necessarily be accepted within the path of conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*). Otherwise, since the meaning of a sentence is something entirely new (*apūrva*), and because there would be no prior apprehension of the convention (*saṅketa*) regarding the sentence-meaning, there could be no comprehension at all.

Therefore, because the relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is not possible between two indivisible [entities], he says "Or else" (*yadvā*) out of dissatisfaction with that view. Indivisibility of meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) consists in being the producer of a cognition of reality that does not involve a relation. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the Advaita tenet that sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) produce the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Brahman, he says "Or else. Regarding the principle that "the difference in words follows from the difference in meanings," one might object: "In the case of a word recited in the Veda, since it is employed for a different meaning at the time of its ritual application (*viniyoga*), would this not result in a difference in the word? To this, it was stated by Bhartṛhari:
Mantras, however, acquire their distinct forms through specific application, much like modifications;
some of these are indeed recited in other Vedic traditions, while others are not.

Thus, all mantras possess the very status of being Veda; however, the meaning [of the term "Veda"] is that only certain [portions] among them are recited as mantras. Now, one might ask: "In this view, how is the Bhāṣya passage—'A single word has multiple meanings, such as *ajñāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*'*—to be justified? To this, he says: "Because of having an identical form. It is incorrect to claim that there is a difference in words because there is a difference in their actual referents (*artha*). *Note: The Bhāṣya passage refers to the fact that the same word-form can denote different things (e.g., *ajñāḥ* as "unwise people," *pādāḥ* as "feet" or "quarters of a verse," and *māṣāḥ* as "beans"). This objection challenges the definition of Veda as a specific collection of mantras by pointing out the polysemy of linguistic units.*

If it is argued that in the case of *kuṭībhārya*, because there is an absence of "having been previously used as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) within a common form (*samānāyām ākṛtau*), the rule of "masculine-like substitution" (*pumbat*) does not apply—and thus there is no inconsistency with the Bhāṣya; and that there is no reason to establish identity [of the word] through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) and so forth—this is true. However, the author of the Bhāṣya himself has demonstrated the identity of the word by stating, "Because the gender is made manifold by the object [of reference]," and so on. Furthermore, he has demonstrated the difference between words by stating, "But there is a change of state (*ānyabhāvya*) due to the intervention of time and words," and so on. [The term] *tasya* refers to that [identity], while *tadānantaryasya* refers to its immediate proximity.

Therefore, the first position is that there is a difference in words and a difference in their identity (*tādātmya*). The meaning is that the word is the locus of the power (*śakti*), while the object is that which is characterized by the power; the difference arises from the distinction between these two. As for what was stated in the *Kusumāñjali*: "The difference in powers is not non-different, for an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is difficult to transcend. The meaning of this is: "The difference in powers is not [non-existent], because [the powers] are not non-different [from the object], since there is no difference between the power and the possessor of the power (*śaktimat*)."

Now, it might be argued that the capacity of a single entity to produce various effects is due to its very nature (*svabhāva*), as it has been said that "nature is difficult to overcome. However, if the nature of producing an effect were to persist [unchanged], then it would follow that a single cause must produce other effects as well; thus, according to that view, a single staff could not produce multiple effects such as a jar or injury. Furthermore, regarding the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) expressed as "this is that," if similarity alone were the basis for it, then in the case of "this is that letter *ka*," the same would apply, resulting in the undesirable consequence that letters such as *ka* would also be identical. (1.19)

"The identities are distinct. Even though there is a difference in the objects, there is no difference in the word, because that would entail the postulation of an infinite number of individual instances (*vyakti*). Therefore, the sense is that, like many fruits on a single stalk, multiple meanings are connected to a single word. In this view, having superimposed the word "village" (*grāma*)—which applies to both a settlement with boundaries (*sīmaka*) and one without (*sāraṇyaka*)—there are two positions regarding the theory of word-identity: either the power (*śakti*) is one and the same despite the difference in the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), or the power is indeed distinct due to the difference in the delimiters of the denotable capacity.

And the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is the locus of the complete inherence (*paryāpti*) of the property of being a delimitor of denotability; therefore, because of the difference between the sun and the moon, there is no polysemy (*nānārthatā*) in the word *puṣpavanta*. In the first alternative (*pakṣa*), just as even though the inherence of color (*rūpa-samavāya*) exists in air, the cognition "it possesses color" does not arise because there is no inherence qualified by being specified by color, so too, at the time of cognizing one meaning, there is no cognition of the other meaning due to the absence of the recollection of the expressive power (*śakti*) qualified by being specified by that [other] meaning.

They say that because there is a distinction of powers (*śakti*), the conventional usage of multiple meanings occurs for those functions (*vṛtti*) determined by all objects; therefore, since they are conveyed by a single word, their unity is logical.
