Furthermore, one should understand that there is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in assuming a plurality of powers. Regarding the phrase "by all types [of persons]": the meaning is that whether they are conventions (*saṅketa*) made by God or by ourselves and others, and regardless of their various specific forms, they are related as such simply by virtue of being conventions.

"By way of equal pervasion" means by way of being co-occurrent. The sense is that the word *ānaya* (bring) conveys the meaning of bringing as connected with the jar because it is connected with the word *ghaṭa* (jar); thus, there is an inference of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) from the pervaded (*vyāpya*) word. For this very reason, Gautama stated: "And because burning and cutting would [otherwise] be impossible, there is no relation [of pervasion]. The meaning of that is that since the mouth would be burned upon the utterance of the word "fire," there is no relationship of pervader and pervaded between the word and its object.

In the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), however, since sound resides in space (*ākāśa*), it is located in a different locus [from the subject]; therefore, no inference can be made by means of it—this is the sense. Regarding the term "pakṣa": a *pakṣa* is that which possesses a doubtful probandum (*sādhya*). "Cognition of the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*) is the cognition that the logical reason (*hetu*) subsists in the subject. The sense is that this [proposition] is not an inference because verbal comprehension occurs even without the "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*) in the form: "This [subject] possesses a word that is pervaded by the object. Now, one might object: "But this [verbal] inference is indeed distinct, as it does not depend on the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth."

Otherwise, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of having to postulate two separate instances of obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatā*)—one for the verbal causal complex (*śābda-sāmagrī*) and one for the inferential causal complex (*anumiti-sāmagrī*)—with respect to a perception whose object is different [from their own]. Therefore, he says: "when certainty has already arisen" (*siddhasattve*). The point is that after the certainty "there is fire on the mountain," an inference of fire on the mountain occurs only through the desire "let there be an inference of fire on the mountain"; whereas verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), however, occurs even when certainty exists, without any such desire, and thus there is a disparity (*vaiṣamya*).

Although an inference is possible—namely, that words such as "bring the jar" are preceded by a cognition of the connection between the objects recalled by those words, because they constitute a collection of words possessing expectancy and so forth, since there is no lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in this inference—even so, because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is more immediately present when there is identity (*tādātmya*) between word and object, this refutation is directed against that [position of identity]. (1.20)

One might object: "Surely, even when the existence of the object is already established, just as there is no inference, so too there is no verbal cognition; for when the conditions for perception are equally present, that [perception] is stronger. Consequently, after the recollection of word-meanings, let there instead be an inference: 'These word-meanings possess a mutual relation, because they are recollected from words possessing expectancy and the like. Anticipating this objection, he says: "From the word alone. The sense is: "Even without the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth."

In verbal cognition, the recollection of word-meanings (*padārtha-smaraṇa*) is the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*). Thus, [the author] refutes the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), who hold that since it is merely the recollection of word-meanings, it does not constitute a distinct means of valid knowledge (*atirikta-pramiti*). [The verse says: "It is merely recollection," because the cognition of one related member (*ekasambandhi-jñāna*) causes the recollection of the other related member (*aparasambandhi-smāraka*). Now, one might ask: once the meaning has been recollected from the words, why would there not then be an inference (*anumiti*)? To this, he replies: "That is not tenable."

Furthermore, in this view, the recollection of word-meanings alone is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Consequently, since that recollection has perished at the time of the cognition of the meaning of a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākyārtha*), the cognition of the meaning of the major sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*) would not arise from it. Therefore, the cause is simply the mental presence (*upasthiti*) brought about by the words; and since that very presence takes the form of the cognition of the subordinate sentence’s meaning, there is no fault. The phrase "because of the non-inclusion of 'that-ness' (*tattā*)," means that recollection arises only when 'that-ness' has been made an object of the intellect. The phrase "even from a sentence" [is explained as follows].

And thus, the meaning is that if recollection were to result even from a sentence, there would follow the total abolition of inference and verbal cognition. Nor should it be argued that in the case of a sentence whose meaning has never been experienced before, recollection is impossible because there was no prior experience; for it is possible to recollect word-meanings and their relations when they are already well-known in their individual parts.

The phrase "tathānuvyavasāyeti" means that because of such a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), the universal property of being verbal (*śābdatva-jāti*) must indeed be postulated; and since the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth must necessarily be postulated as the cause for that which is delimited by it, what is the point of postulating [the universal] of being an inference (*anumititva*) and so on? The sense of "siddhisattve 'pi" is that even when there is already a proof (*siddhi*), an inference does not arise after the cognition of fire on the mountain, whereas a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), following upon the use of words, is difficult to avoid.

If it is argued that even when there is already a proof (siddhi), verbal cognition (śābdabodha) can still occur just like the inferential cognition of an object, we say no. This is because inferential cognition arises only when there is a desire to infer (anumitsā). Furthermore, in the case of inferring for the sake of another (parārthānumiti), a five-membered syllogism—such as "The mountain possesses fire because it has smoke; whatever has smoke has fire"—is employed. Verbal cognition, however, occurs to oneself from a sentence uttered by another; thus, there is a distinction between the two. Regarding the term "pratibadhyatva" (the state of being obstructed):
the meaning is that one must state that proof (siddhi) acts as an obstructor with respect to cognitions other than verbal cognition.

"From destruction alone" means that because cognition is momentary, there is an inference of a [subsequent] moment upon the destruction of the perception. Now, one might object that there is no contradiction with experience even if there is a delay of a single moment; to this he says: "In all cases. The meaning is that since the inference would necessarily occur in the very moment immediately following the destruction of the proof (the middle term), there would be no inference even at the time of the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā).

For this very reason, the logicians (tārkikas) maintain that where there is a perception such as "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire; it possesses fire," followed by a desire to prove [the conclusion], the non-existence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove must be postulated for the arising of inference. It was established previously that the apprehension of word-meaning (śaktigraha) occurs through the usage of seers (ṛṣis) and others. Furthermore, since the usage of seers and others pertains only to correct words (sādhavaḥ), only correct words possess denotative power (vācakatva). 1.21.

Now he states another opinion: "And that... [sā ca]. But how can the observation of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) be the grasper of word-potency (*śakti*), given the absence of a word that makes it known? For if there is no grasping of potency, there will be no grasping of its being a means to achieve the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and consequently, no inclination toward suckling at the breast would occur; therefore, he says: "The observation of worldly activity... The meaning is that the observation of worldly activity is merely a reminder by way of an awakener (*udbodhaka*), and thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*); the awakener is simply the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) from living. For this very reason...

This is precisely because of the acceptance of the recollection of experiences from previous births; otherwise, in the absence of the knowledge that [an action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), there would be no inclination toward activities such as suckling at the breast. Furthermore, even in the case of animals and the like, who are almost insentient, a certain fixed intuition (*pratibhā*) is perceived according to their specific species; therefore, the point is that for them too, beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone are the seed. "At that very time" means at the very moment of the first awakening of cognition. "The possibility of that" means the possibility of grasping the expressive power (*śaktigraha*). The phrase "and not" is to be construed with the word "to be stated" (*vācyam*). This was stated by Hari: "Some maintain that the incorrect form is expressive through inference."

The term *vācaka* means "that which causes understanding. The underlying point is this: learned persons do not perceive the meaning directly from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) alone; therefore, there is no direct relationship between corrupt words and their meanings. Regarding the statement that corrupt words lead one to infer the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) through similarity and the recollection of the correct word, he provides the authority for that very point by saying: "They [corrupt words] [lead to the recollection] of the correct ones. [Corrupt words are] "incorrect" (*asādhavaḥ*). "[They lead to the recollection] of the correct ones" (*sādhuṣu*). "[This occurs] through the recollection of the correct word" (*sādhusmaraṇena*). The meaning is: a child speaks indistinctly, but for those who know the correct language, a clear determination arises. "Knowledge of that" (*tajjñānam*) refers to the recollection of the correct word.

"Even without [correct words]"—this is the underlying point: the employment of words is for the sake of communicating meaning; and since the comprehension of meaning occurs without distinction even from corrupt words (*apaśabda*), they too possess a connection with that meaning. This refutes the view that comprehension arises from the inference that "there must be some correct word (*sādhupada*) here that conveys this meaning. [The author states: "Not [from] the meaning," etc.; the meaning is that the denoted object is presented only when the *ānupūrvī* (the specific sequence of phonemes) which delimits the expressive power (*śakti*) is known. He also refutes the notion that comprehension arises from the recollection of words such as *tad* and so forth, which denote that [object].

"And because of non-experience. Now, one might object: since common people lack the apprehension of the word-potential (*śakti*) for words such as "ghaṭa" (pot), how can there be an error regarding the word "gagarī" based on its similarity to that [word]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "pūrvapūrva... (the preceding preceding...). The meaning is: like one for whom an error is preceded by the cognition of the word-potential. Regarding the phrase "qualified by pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvaviśiṣṭa*): an error regarding the word-potential residing in the word "ghaṭa"—as determined by the object "pot"—is not possible in the case of the word "gagarī," because the perception of a specific difference in the phonemes exists. Indeed, after the certain determination of the possession of hands and feet, an error of "man-ness" does not arise with respect to a post.

Regarding the phrase "yadi ca" (and if): the meaning is that when a first person knows, "This word *gagarī* was uttered by him due to inability [to pronounce the correct form]," then for a second person there arises the delusion that the word *gagarī* itself is the signifier. Regarding the phrase "tādātmyam upagamyaiva" (having attained identity): the meaning is that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) reveal the object as if they were non-different from the correct words (*sādhuśabdās*). Regarding the term "tādātmya" (identity): this is the underlying point; because of the conventional usage of non-difference in the form "this is the object," identity between word and object—characterized by superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—is the primary one.

But if one were to postulate another relation [between the word and its meaning], then yet another relation would have to be postulated for that one as well; thus, because of this infinite regress (*anavasthā*), even when there is cognition, the object cannot be established as being the content of that cognition (*viṣayabhāva*). Therefore, the conventional usage of "relation" (*sambandhatva*) is merely figurative (*ivaśabdena*), like the case of the universal (*sāmānya*) which is not [inherently] posterior. Furthermore, if the identity (*tādātmya*) between the correct and incorrect words were real, then it would follow that even incorrect words possess the capacity to convey meaning; this very point was stated by the author of the treatise in the second half of the verse. He says "by means of the word *iva*" with the intention of explaining that it is precisely by accepting such identity that words are the illuminators of the meaning. The meaning is that by the word *iva*, the error regarding the [existence of a real] power (*śakti*) is indicated. (1.22)

"Then there is incapacity (*aśakti*). This means that the incapacity regarding that correct word (*sādhu-śabda*)—due to a lack of ability, that is, a deficiency in the organ of articulation (*karaṇa*), resulting in an incorrect pronunciation because [the speaker] possesses the same phonemes (*samāna-varṇavatva*) [as the standard]. Regarding "it is called *śaba*": the root *śabadhātu* has the sense of "going. However, in the Kamboja country, among the Ārtha tribes, it is used in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*), as in "a corpse is *śaba*. Regarding "the expressive [word] functions as a suggester (*vyañjaka*)," for example: "O traveler, spread your bedding here in this village of Arthagrāma; having seen my swelling breasts, if you wish to stay, then stay."
"O traveler, there is not even a slight matting here in this village on ground strewn with stones;
if you see a cloud with uplifted breasts [or a woman with high breasts], then you may stay"—this is its meaning.

In this village made of stones, there is no bedding (*āstaraṇa*); *payodhara* means both "cloud" and "breast"—this is a pun (*śleṣa*). Here, by the word *payodhara*, the capacity for enjoyment (*upabhogakṣamatva*) is suggested; the usage of its corrupt form, *paohara*, serves as the expressive power (*vācakatā*) in that context. This demonstrates the absolute impossibility of mistaking [the corrupt form] for the primary expressive power (*śakti*). Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "when a correct word has been employed, and women, Śūdras, or children have a doubt regarding the meaning."

[Objection: But surely, by the word *yava* (barley), only a specific kind of long-awned grain (*dīrghaśūka*) should be understood and not *kaṅgu* (millet); this would render the discussion of that section (*tadadhikaraṇa*) incoherent, because the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) is equal in both cases. To this, he says: "This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). As for the claim that the determination [of the meaning] is made from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "In spring, the falling of leaves occurs for all crops," that is not correct. For in the case of the rule, "The staffs of a Vaiśya are of *pīlu* and *audumbara* wood," since there is no supplementary statement, it would follow that the word *pīlu* could refer even to an elephant; consequently, it would follow that a staff made of an elephant's bone could also be accepted. || 1.23 ||

"From what has been stated in the Bhāṣya": the meaning is that, because of this, one should not suspect a misconception regarding the primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that case. "Of both": of both the Āryas and the Mlecchas. "In both places": in the case of *kaṅgu* (millet) and *dīrghaśūka* (long-awned barley). "As being correct": the meaning is that in the country of the Mlecchas, the word *yava* is correct only when it refers to *kaṅgu*. "An option": the meaning is that an option (*vikalpa*) would arise due to the two-fold established usage.

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya, Śabarasvāmin, established the conclusion that by the word *yava* (barley), only a specific type of long-bearded grain is to be understood, based on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "where other plants wither. However, the author of the Vārttika does not accept this, because since the determination [of meaning] arises from the superior authority of the usage of the Āryas alone, the citation of a supplementary statement would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, it is only in cases where there is a doubt regarding the denotation of a word's meaning among the Āryas themselves that a resolution is reached through a supplementary statement.

In reality, however, the word *yava* must refer to long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*) specifically in the context of the *karambha-pātra* vessels used in the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice, because the supplementary explanatory passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) exists only there; it does not apply to the injunction prescribing the substance for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as no such supplementary passage exists there. Therefore, with the intention of stating that the supplementary passage is mentioned merely as a corroboration, he says: "On account of the usage of the Āryas. He says: "On account of the usage of the Āryas."

"In the sacrifice, it is indeed barley"—this is because only those [barley grains] possess the capacity to produce the *apūrva*. The "true nature of the word" (*śabdatattva*) is the identity between a specific word and its specific meaning. The "learned ones" (*śiṣṭāḥ*) are those who perceive supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadarśinaḥ*). For they perceive the relationship between word and meaning even without the operation of the sense organs; and through the traditional lineage of their instruction, for people like us as well, there occurs the manifestation of the object by means of the manifestor (the dewlap, etc. acting as a cooperative factor. "They are established"—the remainder of the sentence is "as a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇatvena*). But not so among the non-Aryans (*anāryeṣu*).

The meaning is that the word *yava* has no denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the *kaṅgu* plant, nor is it ungrammatical (*asādhutva*). Regarding the phrase "because it is not observed in those [cases]," the *Vārttika* states: "In a conflict between traditional law (*smṛti*) and custom (*ācāra*), when there is doubt as to their equality or inequality, the disagreement should be regarded as equal, because both have an identical basis."
The meaning is that, since the world is the authority regarding the meaning of words, there can be no contradiction; thus, the disagreement would be equal [on both sides].

"Of those remaining" means "uninterrupted," which signifies "transmitted through tradition. "In words and in the Vedas" means that while the word *yava* denotes a specific type of long-bearded grain in common usage, it is understood in the Veda to denote that very same thing; such is the sense. "One [usage] is secondary" means that because the usage for *kaṅgu* (millet) is based on similarity, there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) since there is an inequality between the two due to one being secondary. "Where other plants [do not flourish]" refers to the spring season, when such a possibility exists. "In the same way" means precisely at the time of the exhaustion of the previous crop. "Otherwise" [means otherwise than this].

The meaning is that if one were to accept *priyaṅgu* as something other than [the intended grain], the similarity stated by you would be inconsistent. Now, an objection is raised: "If *dīrghaśūka* is accepted based on the usage of the noble ones (*āryaprasiddhi*), then the aforementioned supplementary statement is redundant"; to this, he replies with the words "by the stated reasoning. This means [the acceptance is not based] merely on the form of the statement regarding the usage of the noble ones. 1.24.

"Valid instruction" (*āptopadeśa*) means that the instruction of one who is authoritative—that is, free from error and the like—is verbal testimony (*śabda*). "That" (*sa*) means: the word which an authoritative person employs with respect to a certain object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object. "Just as" (*yathā*) means: in whatever manner an object has been seen—that is, by whom such a vision was obtained—such is the meaning. "Similarly" (*samānam*) implies: because [the authoritative person] is the employer of those specific words that convey those respective meanings. He refutes the charge of redundancy by the first term [of the definition]. "The seer is the Veda" (*ṛṣirvedaḥ*).

"By way of being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvena*): the meaning is "of the cognition produced from that word which is characterized as a means of valid cognition. The implication is that in this way, even that which arises from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) possesses an equal status as being based on convention (*sāmayikatva*). Now, one might object: "It is possible for the meaning of the Veda to be revealed through convention; yet, even if the expressive power (*śakti*) is grasped through the linguistic usage of elders, because a Vedic sentence constitutes a unique collection [of words], its relationship with the meaning remains unknown. Consequently, if one were to postulate such a relationship, it would result in the fallacy of it being a mere convention (*saṅketa*), and thus, due to its dependence [on human agency], it would incur the loss of its status as a means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). To this, he says: "Grasped through convention" (*samayagṛhīta*).

Because there is no difference in meaning between worldly usage and the Veda, and because even a Vedic sentence is rooted in worldly linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), it does not depend on human convention; thus, its authority is indeed independent. Regarding the phrase "of the sages": this means that [the Veda] would contradict the fact that Vedic sentences convey meanings established by convention. Now, one might object: in the verse, "Your pair of breasts entreats you in distress, do not speak a falsehood," there is no fault even if the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is ungrammatical, because it is outside the context of a ritual (*kratu*). To this, he says: "In poetry."

[Objection: But surely, since the word *aśva* with a dental *a* in the middle is not seen to convey the meaning of "horse," the knowledge that it is incorrect (*asādhutva*) must be an obstacle [to comprehension]. To this, he says: "Even when that exists. The point is that even when there is a certainty of incorrectness, comprehension of the meaning from an apabhraṃśa word does occur; therefore, [incorrectness] is not an obstacle. He says "of the object-qualified" because the word *aśva* lacks correctness (*sādhutva*) when applied to a horse. "In the manner stated in the Śikṣā" means by way of being free from defects such as nasalization (*ambūkṛta*). "And of that" means and of correctness (*sādhutva*). || 1.25 ||

[Objection: But surely, since correctness (*sādhutā*) is restricted to specific meanings—as in the word *aśva* being correct only when it denotes a horse—it would follow that words such as *gaṅgā* could not be correct when applied to a riverbank and the like. To this, he says: "Even in the case of metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) [words]. [Objection: But how is the cognition of the bank produced? To this, he says: "The words [denote] the other. The point is that in that case, the state of being a stream (*pravāhatva*) is superimposed upon the bank; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the relationship between word and meaning being non-eternal (*anitya*).

Thus, it should be understood that "primary" (mukhya) status consists in having a well-known meaning as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the state of being a continuous flow (*pravāhatva*), whereas "secondary" (*gauṇa*) status consists in having such an unknown meaning. Now, an objection is raised: since the word *gopa*, which is based on the act of protecting cows, does not apply to a woman, and since there is no basis for the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* to one who possesses only a superimposed cowherd-ness (*āropitagopatva*), how can there be an injunction [of the feminine form] for it? To this, he says: "In cases such as *gopī*," etc.

For one who herself tends cows is called a *gopī* (cowherd woman); however, the word *gopī* is applied to the wife of a cowherd (*gopa*) even though she lacks the act of tending, because she possesses that status (*taddharmalābha*). By this, those who claim that the suffix *ajī* applies in the sense of "union with a male" (*puṃyoga*) are refuted; for in that case, since the genus (*jāti*) alone is the cause [of the application], there is no basis for the acquisition of that status, and thus union with a male is impossible. Now, an objection is raised: "Since there was previously no cognition of her being female, how can the suffix *ṅīṣ* apply? To this, he says: "In the process of derivation" (*prakriyā*).

The meaning is that, in the case of the feminine form [of *gopa*], the capacity to convey the sense of "female" is the cause for the application of the suffix *ḍīṣ*, and this capacity is inferential during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Now, one might ask: since there is no indicator of intended meaning (*tātparya*) here—unlike in the case of words such as *tīra*—what is the basis for the implied denotation (*ākṣepa*)? To this, he says: "From the scripture" (*iti śāstrataḥ*).

Regarding what was stated—that the understanding of femininity arises from the grammatical rule *puṃyogāt*—he states the proof for that: "The gender (*liṅga*). The meaning is that the rule *puṃyogāt*, which prescribes the suffix, serves as the *liṅga* (logical mark) that leads to the cognition of the feminine gender. Herein lies the essential point: when the word *gopa* is applied to a *gopī* who is not the wife of a cowherd (*gopāla*), the sole cause for its application is the relationship of being husband and wife.

For just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the term applies to the bank through the relation of proximity; in "the platforms are shouting," the relation is indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*); and in "clarified butter is life," the relation is that of being a producer (*janakatva*), so too in "Devakī" and similar cases, the application to the daughter occurs solely through the relation of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*). Since this usage is well-established (*nirūḍha*), one need not postulate another relation, nor should an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) be invoked. It is precisely in this manner that usages such as "Jagadīśī" (referring to the wife of Jagadīśa) and others are explained.

Thus, since words such as *devadatta* can function in the feminine by their own nature, there is no connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), and therefore the suffix *ṭāp* alone is applied. However, when the word *śūdra* is applied to a wife of a Śūdra belonging to another caste, the relationship with a Śūdra is indeed the cause [of its application]. He states the proof for the fact that, in the case of the masculine word *gopa*, which denotes a male, its capacity to convey meaning during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) is merely inferential (*ānumānika*). This is expressed by the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

The meaning is this: if the purpose of grammar were restricted solely to the prescription of *tiṅ* (tense) suffixes and so forth, then its status as a teaching on correctness (*sādhutva*) would be undermined; therefore, *asti* and the other suffixes are prescribed as qualified by correctness. If it is asked, "But since there is no usage of *laṭ* and the other [suffixes], how can they be prescribed as qualified by correctness?", the answer is: in that case, the rule "the *laṭ* occurs in the sense of the present" implies that whatever is established by that [rule] is correct. Regarding the term "presumption" (*arthāpatti*): it is the postulation (*kalpanā*) of a supporting fact (*upapādaka-artha*).
Just as in the case of "Devadatta is fat," nocturnal eating is inferred because fatness would otherwise be inexplicable. ||1.26||

"What more? [The meaning is as follows: After the sublating certainty that "this is not silver" regarding a word's capacity (*śakti*), the erroneous nature of the prior cognition is postulated; however, since no sublation whatsoever is observed regarding the portion of the capacity residing in the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*), its erroneous nature is impossible. "From the ascertainment of its absence" means: from the ascertainment of the absence of capacity on the part of the sages, due to their lack of error. "Of the means of knowledge" means: of words as they are being cognized. "Even of those" means: even of the corrupt forms. "For this very reason."

The meaning is that even for *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt) words, their status as *dharma* (meritorious/authoritative) exists precisely because they possess a connection with meaning; however, it is not said that they possess the capacity for [correct] cognition (*bodhakatva*). "They are used for the sake of meaning" means that these words are uttered for the purpose of conveying meaning. Regarding the *Jaimini-sūtra* as well: for there, the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra—"Because it is not a scripture regarding usage and origin, there would be no fixed rule among words"—means that there would be no restriction on usage. He states the final (*siddhānta*) sūtra: "It is improper that there be many [words]," [referring to] "among words."

The word "to be employed" (*prayoktavye*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. It has been stated that "employment" (*prayoga*) is the production of another effort, which is an error resulting from the completion of a previous effort. || 1.27 ||

"Of *gagara* and so forth as well" means by virtue of being corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *go*. "Of words such as *goyā*" means by virtue of being corruptions of the word *go*. "But in the Veda it is correct" implies that this is due to a transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). "By Patañjali" means by him while commenting on the *Vārttika*: "When the comprehension of meaning is the same, [it matters not whether] words or corrupt words [are used]. (1.28)

"Yarvāmaḥ"—this means those who have that name. Now, one might object that the suffix *su* would also arise after words such as *gagarī*; therefore, he says: "Of the base and the suffix. [The phrase] "in being within the scope of the grammatical treatise" means "possessing the property that serves as the delimiting condition for the objective of the rule (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) according to the Śāstra. [The phrase] "only of the word *ghaṭa*" implies that although it possesses the capacity to convey meaning, the suffix *su* does not arise from it because the meaning qualified by singularity is already encompassed by the suffix itself; this is the sense. [The word] "it is simply incorrect" means...

The point is that in the *Śruti*, there is no fault even in the imitation of what is incorrect (*asādhu*), because such imitation is itself correct. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of having meaning" (*arthavattvena*): the meaning is that only those forms which are correct (*sādhavaḥ*) and possess meaning are the objects of the technical designation *prātipadika*. Regarding the phrase "for this very reason": since a suffix is correct only when employed after a base (*prakṛti*) that has been prescribed by rule, it is for this very reason [that the rule applies]. Regarding the phrase "even though there is similarity arising from word-formation" (*vṛttijasādṛśye’pi*): the intention is that the expression "not merely a suffix" means "one belonging to the same class as a suffix. Regarding the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*): [it refers to the restriction that a suffix must follow a base].

Although the subsequent position (*paratva*) of suffixes is already established by the very mention of the ablative case in the rule *ṅy-āpprātipadikāt*, [the author] says "even though" (*api*), and so forth. "In those who lack wealth" (*asve*); "in the poor" (*daridre*). That which makes this known; that which makes known their correctness (*sādhutva*). A restriction of dharma (*dharmaniyama*); a restriction whose purpose is dharma. In the first half of the verse, having stated that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are not expressive—based on the view of some who maintain that "an incorrect form is expressive through inference"—Haribhadra states another opinion: "Even though there is no difference in their being expressive," and so forth.

Or, let it be that meaning is understood from corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa); however, the scripture establishes a rule regarding merit and demerit: "The meaning must be expressed only by correct words (sādhu), not by incorrect ones (asādhu); for when this is done, it becomes conducive to prosperity. (1.29)

"Confusion" (*saṅkara*) means: [the presence of] mere correctness in a correct *ga* sound, mere incorrectness in an incorrect *ka* sound, and both together [in one instance]. "Of which two universals" (*yayor jātyoḥ*) means: just as the nature of being a man-lion (*narasiṃhatva*) is distinct because of the coexistence of humanity and lionhood in a single locus. "Only the collapse of difference" (*bhedabhaṅga eva*) means: that the very proof of difference—namely, that the substratum of humanity is one thing and the substratum of lionhood is another—is simply not established. For this very reason, it was not resolved by claiming that confusion regarding universals residing in qualities (*guṇagatajāti*) is not a fault. "In the case of a mule" (*aśvatara*).

In that case, there is a confusion (*saṅkara*) between the states of being a horse and being a donkey. As for the phrase "of which two," the intention is that the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and substanceness (*dravyatva*) is not a defect. Corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is a genus (*jāti*) because it is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of motion; due to its confusion with that [corporeality], "element-ness" (*bhūtatva*) is not a genus. The conventional usage of the term "element" (*bhūta*) with respect to space (*ākāśa*), however, is figurative (*bhākta*), being prompted by the possession of a specific quality perceptible by an external sense organ. This is because there is a lack of evidence [for it being a genus].

The sense is that the statement made [by the opponent] is devoid of reason, because it would entail the violation of the rule that, with respect to the property of being a genus (*jātitva*) qualified by a genus through the two relations of "coexistence with itself" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and "coexistence with its own absence" (*svābhāvasāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is a necessary absence of being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of an absence coexisting with itself. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of corporeality" (*śarīratve ca*): Logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that corporeality is not a genus (*jāti*) due to the defect of over-extension (*sāṅkarya*). This is because pure earthiness (*pṛthivītva*) exists in a jar and the like, pure corporeality exists in bodies composed of fire (*taijasa*) and so forth, and both exist in our own bodies; thus, they overlap.

[The opponent says: "There is a royal decree [to that effect]. [We reply: This is because the reasoning based on parsimony (*lāghava*) is equal [in both cases]. For this very reason, Vardhamāna maintains that *jātitva* (the property of being a universal) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word 'water' (*jala*). As for the claim that *bhūtatva* (the property of being an element) is a universal because it serves as the delimitor of the causal obstruction (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka*) for preventing the production of another substance within a pot-sherd (*kapāla*) which already exists as a substance—that is not correct, because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) to prefer it over *mūrtatva* (the property of being corporeal). 1.30.

"It is indeed incorrect," because names are assigned solely through the conventional path of grammatical treatises (*śāstra-vyavahāra*). Now, one might object: if one holds the view that "all words denote all meanings," then rules such as *vṛddhir ādaic* would lack the status of injunctions (*vidhi*) since they would merely serve as restrictors (*niyāmaka*); consequently, it would be inconsistent to call them "modern technical terms" (*ādhunika-saṃjñā*). To this he replies: "Even though [words] denote all meanings. The underlying intention is as follows: the relationship between word and meaning is intended here to be characterized by "fitness" (*yogyatā*). For every word, when employed as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), is connected to every possible meaning by virtue of its fitness.

The operation of the creator of a technical name (*saṃjñākāra*) consists merely in delimiting a power (*śakti*), because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. And thus, due to the delimitation of power, it possesses the character of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and because it reveals a power that was previously unknown, it also possesses the character of an injunction (*vidhi*). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of usage" (*vyavahārāya*): the meaning is that the restriction of a name to a named object is for the purpose of linguistic usage. The connection of words such as *ḍittha* with their respective referents is indeed eternal, just as the connection of words such as *go* (cow) with their referents is; this is the meaning. The word *tat* (that) connects with the phrase "intended as a restriction" (*niyamapara*).

Regarding the phrase "by the speaker's intention": if it is objected that this would result in the contingency of the relationship between word and meaning being non-eternal (*anitya*), we say no; for the meaning is that the power (*śakti*) is merely manifested by the speaker's intention. The application of *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) and so forth in words such as *aij* is brought into harmony [with the system]. He says "only the Veda" because words such as *vṛddhir ādaij* lack the quality of being "worldly" (*laukika*), which consists in their being employed in common worldly usage. He says "because of being worldly" with the underlying sense that the operation of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is necessarily required for worldly usage. Regarding the term *sūktavāka*: [it refers to the ritual formula].

The application of the *sūktavāka* formula in sacrifices, such as "May Amukaśarman desire long life," and likewise the *saṅkalpa* (vow), are indeed mental operations; nevertheless, the employment of words is required precisely because they are so prescribed. Regarding the phrase "having the semi-vowels within": "within" means in the middle; that which has the semi-vowels (*antasthā*)—namely *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—in its interior [is so described]. 1.31.

"Agnyādi" means that Agni and the others are the deities of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). "By these" refers to names such as *Agnidatta* and so forth. "Stated in the Jyotiṣa" means that names such as *Cūḍāmaṇi*, which are formed by the syllables of the feet of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, are intended for use in sacrificial rites (*yajña-karma*). "In the same way it has been stated" means that this very [method] is what is called the asterismal name (*nākṣatra-nāma*). "In the context" connects with the word "stated. "And the name" indicates the inclusion of other names by means of the word "and" (*ca*). "He points out" means he writes. "The secret" (*rahasya*)... [end of fragment].

"Because it is not to be made public. Regarding the phrase "and that very same [name]": the grammatical connection is that Āśvalāyana has stated, "and that which is to be used for salutation," and so forth. Having assigned a conventional name, the name intended for salutation—the purpose of which is salutation—should be performed in a whisper; and that [name] should be known only by the mother and father until the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*). Furthermore, at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), the boy should be told: "Salute with this name."

"He utters the name" refers to the practice in Śrauta rituals where this sacrificer, having sat down in the middle of the altar during the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), utters the names of his sons using such formulations as, "May [Name] Śarman attain long life. And that is how it is employed: "May [Name] Śarman continue the lineage," and so forth. As for the phrase "asau" (so-and-so): the meaning is that after uttering two names immediately following the words "this sacrificer," the Hotṛ priest should say, "he desires long life. The expression "asau asau" (so-and-so, so-and-so) is an illustration of these two names.

"Uncertain" (*saṃdigdham*) means because there is no certainty as to what kind of two names [should be used]. "By Devatrāta" means the sense is that the meaning of Āśvalāyana’s statement is that one should employ the two names in this manner: "This one is Devadatta; this one is Ānurādha. "In the words of the Sūtra" means that such a pair of names is not obtained by the force of that Sūtra. "Of the Āśvalāyanas" connects with the phrase "they practice" (*ācaranti*) according to the statement in the *Kārikā* spoken by Devatrāta. "Conventional" (*sāṃvyavahārikam*) means designated for the purpose of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

In this regard, the following is the procedure: one should write the name "Devotee of [Name]" according to one's own family deity in a bronze vessel and thereby assign a name for the month. And those names are:
Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Acyuta, Vaikuṇṭha, Janārdana, Upendra, Yajñapuruṣa, Vāsudeva, and Hari.

In this regard, the sequence begins with Caitra and so forth, or Mārgaśīrṣa and so forth; then the name of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra); then a two-syllable or four-syllable name, and so on, ending in the conventional suffixes such as -śarman, which should be written down. || 1.32 ||

Regarding the phrase "the truth here" (*atra tattvam*): it is indicated by the performance [of rituals] according to one's own respective *gṛhya-sūtra*. For this very reason, Kātyāyana stated otherwise, saying, "One should cause [the mantra] to be heard in the right ear of the boy," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the state of being external": because this [term *saṃjñā*] is also a technical name (*saṃjñā*), like the words *ai*, *au*, etc. [which are taught as substitutes]. As for the phrase "that is not so": the intention is that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the words *ai*, *au*, etc., has been established elsewhere. Now, if one asks: "In the view that there are four types of words, since there exist names (*saṃjñā*) that are unanalyzable (*avyutpanna*), how can those [names] be taught by the science [of grammar]?"—to this he says:

Regarding the phrase *śiṣṭaprayuktasya ca*: the meaning is that only that which is used by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and characterized by a conventional designation (*saṃjñā*) that is not etymologically derived (*avyutpanna*) is considered correct (*sādhu*). Regarding *lūtaka*: the question is how the word *lūtaka*—which is identical in form to the verbal noun *lūta*—is excluded when it is the action-word *lūta* (derived from the root √lū) that is intended as the referent. Regarding "also by other positions": this refers to how the rule concerning similar forms (*sarūpasūtra*) is formulated under the theory of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), whereas it is rejected (*pratyākhyāna*) under the theory of universals (*jātipakṣa*). Regarding "another solution": [this refers to a different way of resolving the objection].

The sense is that, when the fourfold view is rejected by the threefold view, since there is no such thing as an unanalyzed *lṛtaka* word, there is no purpose in teaching the phoneme *ḷ*. Regarding the term "superimposed" (*āropitatva*): the meaning is that even under the fourfold view, [the word] would be incorrect (*asādhutva*). The sense is that even though unanalyzed designations do exist, correctness belongs only to those words employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Furthermore, regarding "if this were so": the meaning is if even that which is not derived through grammar were considered correct. (1.33)

"Conventional meaning" (*rūḍhi*) means that when a word conveys only the collective sense of its constituent parts, that power [of the word] is called conventional meaning. Now, one might ask: since the division between base and suffix is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), how can there be a distinction between conventional and non-conventional meanings? To this he replies: "imagined by the author of the grammatical treatise" (*śāstrakṛtkalpita*). This was stated by Bhartṛhari: "When a sentence has reached another meaning through the conceptualization of similarity, the status of certain words as being based on convention is understood only within the treatise."

The meaning of this is as follows: When a similarity is conceived between a derivative form (*vṛtti*) and its analytical sentence (*vākya*), certain words are considered *rūḍhi* (conventional) because they convey a different meaning in their analysis (*vigraha*). In the word *maṇḍapa*, for instance, the analytical meaning—the "maker of a pavilion"—is present; yet all of this, including the division of the components and so forth, is merely imagined. Regarding the phrase *yadartha*: it means "of such a meaning. Regarding *maṇi*: it is called *maṇi* because it is praised (*maṇyate*). Regarding the word *nūpura*: it is called *nūpura* because it sounds (*nuvati*) or praises (*stuvati*) the city [the foot].

[Objection: But how can there be an understanding of the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) in the word *aśvagandhā*, given that convention (*rūḍhi*) is accepted as an inhibitor [of the etymological meaning] in order to prevent the cognition of a white lotus (*kumuda*) from the word *paṅkaja*? To this, he says: "Because it supersedes the etymological meaning. The reason for the strength [of convention] is simply its prior presentation compared to the etymological meaning, which is rooted in the recollection of the meanings of the constituent parts. However, where the etymological meaning is presented first, that alone possesses strength.

Just as in the case of the phrase "vājibhyo vājinam" (the whey for the *vājins*), the word *vājin* does not convey the meaning of "horses," but rather refers specifically to the Viśvedevas through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) "those to whom *vāja*—that is, food in the form of *āmikṣā*—belongs. This constitutes the connection with the *Āmikṣā-adhikaraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of context and so forth": the meaning is that where, by virtue of context and other factors, the etymological meaning presents itself first, there indeed occurs the cognition of that [etymological] meaning.

As for the claim that the status of *rūḍhi* (conventional meaning) as an inhibitor is necessary in order to prevent the understanding of a derivative (*yaugika*) meaning from various constituent parts, that is not correct; for it is impossible for that [conventional meaning] to act as an inhibitor because it does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped (*grāhyābhāva*). Furthermore, to assume such a function on the analogy of the "jewel-mantra" (*maṇimantra*) principle would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). There is no cognition [of the word *maṇḍapa*] as the agent of building a pavilion; rather, there is a cognition based on similarity, namely that a *maṇḍapa* is a particular kind of house. In this regard, since indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) rooted in convention (*rūḍhi*) is more powerful, the meaning is that the cognition occurs solely through *lakṣaṇā*.

Regarding the phrase "first cognized": because the meaning of being the agent of production from mud (*paṅkajanikartṛtva*) is construed with the word presented by the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) of the term *paṅkaja*, it is said to be "first cognized. For this very reason, there is no cognition of the white water-lily (*kumuda*) and so forth through mere etymological derivation (*yoga*). Regarding the phrase "by virtue of its strength": the sense is that conventional power (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymological derivation. Regarding the phrase "where": the meaning is "where the collective power is obtainable through the power of the constituent parts. For in such cases, the substantive word (*viśeṣyapada*) is indeed conjoined with the state of being the agent of production from mud. Here, this is considered:

If, in a case of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-lexical combination), the etymological meaning were also an object of verbal cognition, it would follow that from the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") there would arise the cognition: "the lotus is the agent of the act of being born from mud. However, this is not established by experience, because the usage *sthalapaṅkaja* ("land-lotus") would then be impossible, as would the usage *paṅkajaṃ paṅkajam* ("a lotus is a lotus"). [Objection: But surely, it is indeed accepted that sometimes from the word *paṅkaja* there is a cognition of a water-lily (*kumuda*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Thus, let there be only a power (śakti) common to all [words]; as for the restriction to specific word-forms, let there be only indication (lakṣaṇā). To this he says: "Of the word *padma*. He provides an example of the cognition of a meaning based solely on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*): "A lotus on the ground. Here, the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) is sublated. "Kalhāra" means a short lotus; "kairava" means a night-lotus. The meaning is that in these and similar cases—namely, in the case of various types of lotuses—the usage occurs by taking up the meaning of the individual parts [of the compound]. (1.34)

Regarding the term *nānārtha* ("having multiple meanings"): according to the position that "there is a difference in words due to the difference in their meanings," it refers to the state of being a word similar to one that expresses multiple meanings. Regarding the phrase *anekesām*: this [usage] contradicts [the author's own view], because the author himself will later establish the usage *aneko janaḥ* ("many people").

"Capacity alone" means "the state of being a cause alone. "Conjunction and so forth" means that these are merely manifesters of capacity. "With its calf" refers to the view that by the word *dhenu* (cow), any cow that has recently calved is included. "Without its calf": since a prohibition presupposes a prior application, even a cow without a calf is referred to as a *gauḥ* (cow). "There is no mutual dependence": otherwise, because of the association with Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa would have to be understood as the son of Daśaratha, and because of the association with Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma would have to be understood as the son of Daśaratha; this would constitute a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

He states that "co-occurrence" (*sāhacarya*) does not consist in moving together, because it is impossible in cases such as *dīdhī-vevī-ṭām*. He says "similarity" (*sādṛśya*). Regarding the example *rāmārjunau*: here, in someone's poetic comparison—where there is a similarity characterized by the phrase "the gait of those two is like that of Rāma and Arjuna"—there arises a cognition of Bhārgava (Paraśurāma) and Kārtavīrya (Arjuna), due to the contradiction [otherwise] with the literal meaning. On this point, some say: "The primary denotation (*abhidhā*) of the word 'Rāma' and so on would apply to Bhārgava and others; yet the restriction of that denotation occurs because of the contradiction. Thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). That is not correct.

Regarding the phrase "of those two" (*tayoḥ*): because of the mutual reflection of contradictory meanings within that word, at that very moment, a sense of contradiction also flashes forth in the expression "of Rāma and Arjuna. Regarding "with joined palms" (*añjalinā*): from the capacity of the *homa* sacrifice, a practice conducive to it is understood; however, in the case of the expression "he stands worshipping with joined palms," the meaning is entirely different. Likewise, the word *artha* here denotes purpose. Regarding "saindhava": the meaning is that there is no cognition of salt at the time of eating. *Śarkarā* refers to gravel consisting mostly of small stones mixed with clay.

Although in the case of "the [clarified butter] is smeared" (*aktā*), no specific meaning is expressed by the word, nor is an injunction to be inferred in the case of "clarified butter is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). And these [sentences] are set aside for the purpose of the *agnyādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires). Regarding the term *liṅga*: a *liṅga* is a distinguishing property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) that is connected through a relation other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For example, in the expression "the ocean-bannered one (Kāma) is angry," [anger] distinguishes Kāma from the ocean because of anger, which is a property distinct from their conjunction. As for the claim that *liṅga* means a "mark" (*cihna*), that is not correct; for a mark is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*), and anger is not such a property of Kāma.

Proximity (*sannidhi*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). By these, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "Hari with conch and discus" (*sa-śaṅkha-cakraḥ hariḥ*), because of the absence of coreferentiality between the conch and the discus [and the word *hari*]. Regarding "with an axe" (*paraśunā*): here it is understood that "[he] cuts. In the expression "Mitra shines," the masculine form is used for the Sun (*sūrya*), while the neuter form is used for a friend (*suhṛd*). In the case of "a cow with large spots" (*sthūlā pṛṣatī gauḥ*), there is doubt as to whether it means "a cow whose spots are large" or "a cow who has large spots. The meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is understood through the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).

He states another primary category [of suggestion] with the words "In this case" (*vatra*). In some instances there is the excellence of the speaker (*vaktṛ-vaiśiṣṭya*), and in others the excellence of the substance (*dravya-vaiśiṣṭya*). For example:
"O friend, having taken up an exceedingly large water-jar, I have come here quickly;
exhausted by the sweat of fatigue and gasping for breath, I shall rest for a moment."

In this context, the speaker is a passionate woman; by one who recognizes her specific characteristics, such as her immoral conduct, the concealment of secret amorous acts becomes manifest. An example for the person to be addressed is as follows: "Insomnia, emaciation, anxiety, lethargy, and sighing—alas, O friend, these afflict even you on my account, unfortunate as I am!"

And by the specific nature of that mischievous behavior, the enjoyment of the lover is manifested. That very latent impression (*vāsanā*), which consists of a wisdom characterized by ever-new manifestations, is what is called [the cause]; for it is only when that exists that there is the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). As they say: "For those who possess such impressions, there occurs the experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in drama and the like."
But those devoid of latent impressions (nirvāsana) are like the walls and stones of a house within a theater and the like.

Regarding the phrase *surabhimāṃsam*: the meaning is either "the meat of Surabhi" or "the meat of a cow (*go*) that is fragrant (*surabhi*). Regarding the cognition of the second meaning as well: here, the theorists of poetics (*ālaṅkārikas*) maintain that once the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) has been restricted by factors such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, the cognition of the second expressed meaning occurs only through suggestion (*vyañjanā*). For this very reason, they abandon the definition "that which possesses a direct convention (*saṅketa*) is the denotator (*vācaka*)" and instead formulate the definition: "that which expresses a meaning directly designated by convention is the denotator. Regarding the term *aślīla* (indecorous): [the text continues].

Because he possesses "aśrī" (lack of beauty), the suffix *lac* is applied according to the rule for the *sidhma* group; furthermore, by the rule beginning with *kapilakādi*, the *ra* of *aśrī* is replaced by *la*. Thus, it becomes *aślīla*, which brings about shame and the like. || 1.35 ||

Regarding the phrase "by way of being possible" (*śakyatvena*): the meaning is that it is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by that recollection of a possible relation which is preceded by the cognition of the impossibility of the syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*). The phrase "by way of being possible" is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). Since even the primary meaning (*mukhya*) can be conveyed through the relation consisting of denotation (*abhidhā*), the expression "impossibility of the syntactic connection," and so forth, was stated [to specify the context].

If it is objected: "But surely, once the word *gaṅgā* has presented the stream and then ceased its function, even if the bank is presented through its connection with the stream, there would be no *vṛtti* (denotative function) for the word *gaṅgā* [with respect to the bank]," the answer is: True. However, according to the principle that "the cognition of one related thing is the recollector of the other related thing," since the direct relatum is sublated, there is the apprehension of the relatum-of-the-relatum as well; this is the intended meaning. By this, the argument that "because there is no experience regarding the portion of the bank, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is impossible" is refuted, because the connection with the word *gaṅgā* exists there too.

Regarding the phrase "from usage": the sense is that because the Lord’s will has existence alone as its object, power (*śakti*) itself truly resides in the riverbank and so forth. By this, the claim that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting the well-established relation of denotatum and denoter (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists of a connection with the primary meaning, rather than postulating something additional in every instance, is refuted. As for the argument that the word "riverbank" (*tīra*) alone causes the cognition of the bank when the word "Gaṅgā" is used by itself—and that it is for this reason a common saying holds that a word possessing *lakṣaṇā* is not a producer of cognitive experience—that is not correct.

This is because the locative sense in "in the Gaṅgā" cannot be construed there [with the word *gaṅgā*], as it is not the meaning of the base form (*prakṛti*). As for the claim that—since the power (*śakti*) consists of God’s will and exists even in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), though it is distinct [from the standard form]—it is not established for the bank and so forth; that is incorrect, because it is more appropriate that even corrupt forms possess denotative power.

The refinement of capacity (*śakti-saṃskāra*): a refinement produced by capacity. [It exists] even in other births; for it is possible that infants possess a knowledge of the instrumental efficacy (*sādhanatā*) regarding the drinking of breast milk and so forth, precisely in that manner. He refutes the view that the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is the seed of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by saying "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). As for those who say that the impossibility of syntactic connection alone is the seed of figurative indication—and that even in cases such as "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), there is an impossibility of connecting the act of entering, which has eating as its object, with the sticks—he refutes that by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

Furthermore, since [the word] cannot be established as a part [of the primary meaning], it is not the case that the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in its being the producer of that [indicated meaning]; for indication, which takes the form of a possible relation, is not produced by that [meaning]. Nor does it consist in its being the grasper of the intention (*tātparya*) toward the indicated meaning, because such intention can also be established through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other means. Nor does it consist in its being the cause of the cognition of the indicated meaning, because there is a deviation in cases such as "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*). Regarding the phrase "in words such as *ghoṣa*": others hold that, since the meaning of a word is not something beyond the injunction (*vidhi*), indication resides in the word *Gaṅgā* alone. Regarding the term "conventional" (*rūḍhi*):...

The meaning is that in the case of the word *kuśala*, there is only conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) there is the cognition of coolness and so forth. For just as purity is cognized from the sentence "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," it is not so cognized from the sentence "the bank of the Gaṅgā. And thus, the three causes [of secondary indication] should be understood: the sublation of the primary meaning, the connection with the literal sense, and either conventional usage or a specific purpose. (1.36)

"Given that there is the apprehension of invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyagrahe sati*): the sense is that once the syntactic connection of the possible meaning has been established, it is impossible for a counter-consideration (*pratisañcāra*) of its inconsistency to arise there. "He sets aside the cognition": because it is impossible to have a cognition of an absence that is not qualified by its locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Now, one might object: even when the flow [of water] is presented from the word *gaṅgā*, there is no evidence for a cognition of its syntactic connection [with the bank]. To this he says: "In relation to the connection" (*saṃsarge*). The sense is that the cognition of syntactic connection occurs only upon the presentation of the relation with another word-meaning (*padārthāntara*).

[Objection: But then, since words such as "raṅga" (stage) also possess multiple meanings, would they not likewise result in being polysemous? To this, he says: "well-known" (*prasiddha*). The point is that although the bank is understood from the word "Gaṅgā," because it is not [the primary] well-known meaning, the word does not become polysemous. [Objection: But then, there would be the undesirable consequence of understanding fish and other things associated with the hamlet (*ghoṣa*) as well. Therefore, regarding the phrase "by means of the knowledge of the connection between the meanings," he states the form of that knowledge of the connection: "knowledge of the connection. Thus, the point is that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is precisely the capacity to produce a cognition whose object is the bank and so forth.

If it is objected that the common maxim—"that which is denotative of the bank [only] through the word *gaṅgāpāda* (the foot of the Ganges) is not a cause of cognition (*anubhāvaka*) by way of indication (*lākṣaṇika*)"—is inconsistent, we reply: true, provided there is no connection between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) according to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). For this very reason, there is the maxim: "In an injunction (*vidhi*), the primary meaning of the word is not something else. However, in the view of the Grammarians (*Śābdika*), since the bank is understood precisely as being struck (*prahata*), there is no doubt whatsoever. He states the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*): "It is simply the relation (*sambandha*)," and not the aforementioned awakened latent impression (*udbuddhasaṃskāra*).

[Objection: But surely, since there is no relation to the stream for either the bank or that which has passed beyond the bank, there could be no indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—in the form of a sentence-relation—in that case according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*). To this, he says: "In this view as well. By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that even in the first view, there is indication with respect to the delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). By this, the following [objection] is refuted: that indication, which consists in the presentation of the non-capable from the capable, exists even with respect to the delimitor of the capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), but that which consists in a relation to the capable does not exist [there].

[Objection: But surely, the relation [of the word] with the bank is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), whereas its occurrence in the state of being a bank (*tīratva*) is the property of residing in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktavṛttitva*); since these two are distinct, the use of the singular number in the phrase "the relation" (*sambandha*) is untenable. To this, he says: "In the universal" (*jātāv iti*). The intention is that they are one because they are both the relation (*sambandhatva*). In reality, however, since there is an identification (*abhedādhyāsa*) between the word and its referent, they are one; thus, let the word *gaṅgā* itself be the reminder of the bank by way of making known the related object. Even when the bank is remembered through invariable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*), there is no reason to postulate the occurrence of the word *gaṅgā* there [in the bank]. [This applies] even to the delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).

Otherwise, there would be no denotative power (śakti) even for the delimitor of capability (śakyatāvacchedaka). If it is argued that there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) in the case of the bank because there is no apprehension of a relation such as "the bankness belongs to the Gaṅgā," [we reply: just as in cases like "the pot is not," the state of being the delimitor of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedakatva) appears through the relation known as *saṃsargamaryādā* with respect to potness, so too it is the same here, because the indirect relation (*paramparāsambandha*) consisting in the state of being the delimitor of proximity exists with respect to bankness.

Regarding the qualifier, such as "bankness" (*tīratva*) and so forth, he states the view of the author of the *Dīdhiti*: "There is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the delimitor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). [This refers to] both [the views of the author of the *Śabda-kaustubha* and the *Dīdhiti*]. He explains: "By the qualifier," meaning "by the bank" and so forth. The meaning is that, with respect to a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having the bank as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and bankness as its mode (*prakāra*), the cognition of a relation residing in the bank is the cause. In this view, there is a lack of finality (*asvarasa*) because the rule "by means of a function (*vṛtti*)" is violated. He states the Mīmāṃsā view: "Such... This is because their established doctrine is that "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the presentation of the unexpressed (*aśakya*) through the expressed (*śakya*)."

By the word "Ganges" (gaṅgā), the stream is remembered; by the stream, the bank is remembered. And that [remembrance] alone is the cause of the cognition. For this very reason, there is the traditional saying that because the word "Ganges" lacks the capacity to directly present the bank, it is not an "experiencer" (anubhāvaka) when functioning through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā). If it is objected: "Since the presentation of the bank is not produced by the word, how can it be an object of verbal cognition (śābdabodha)?"—we reply: No. This restriction applies only to the cognition of the primary meaning (śakyārtha); in the case of the cognition of the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha), it is simply the presentation of the word-meaning (padārthopasthiti) itself that acts as the regulator.

According to this view, since the bank (*tīra*) lacks the status of being the referent of the word *gaṅgā*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the meaning of the locative case could not be construed with it. Furthermore, the *vṛtti* (linguistic function) is the cause of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*), but the mental presentation itself is not the *vṛtti*. Now, one might object that because the mental presentation resides in the object, it would follow that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is not a property of the word; to this he says: "svaviṣaye" (in its own domain). The meaning is: by way of the relation of being the denoter of the flow [of water] which is related to the bank, the domain of the indication.

[Objection: But surely, since *śakti* (denotative power) consists of will (*icchā*) and *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) consists of cognition (*bodha*), they belong to different classes; therefore, it is impossible for them to be functions (*vṛtti*). To this he says: "But as for being a function... [He explains: "Regarding the word and its meaning... The meaning is that the relation which the word *gaṅgā* has with the current and the relation it has with the bank are both its functions (*vṛtti*). Thus, although it is the relation with the bank alone that constitutes the function, because that very relation is the cause of the indicative function, it too is conventionally designated as "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*). This is the intended sense.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the statement beginning with "the generator of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhajanaka*) is incorrect, since from a word there arises only the recollection of the word-meaning (*padārtha*)? [The author] says: "Even from a word" (*padād api*). [He states the] intention (*āśaya*): otherwise, at the time of the cognition of the intermediate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*), the recollection of the word-meaning would have perished, and thus the cognition of the great sentence-meaning (*mahāvākyārtha*) would not occur. [Regarding the example] "kamalāni": one instance of the word *kamala* is the denoter of that which is qualified by fragrance. By this, the claim of the Logicians (*Tārkika*)—that words denoting a qualified entity do not possess secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the substratum (*viśeṣya*), because signification occurs only when [the object] is known under a form other than its own capacity (*śakya*)—is refuted; for that assertion is without foundation. (1.37)

Regarding the term *svanīrūpitā*: "its own" (*sva*) refers to the primary meaning (*śakya*). The meaning is that *gauṇī* (metaphorical indication) is that which conveys a relation to the primary meaning by way of the relation of similarity. That [indication] is *śuddhā* (pure). As for the claim that in the case of the theory of the universal (*jāti*), in the sentence "A cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), there is *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) because the individual (*vyakti*) is understood through the abandonment of the primary meaning—that is not correct. For in that case, the individual is merely implied (*ākṣipta*) due to its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), but it is not denoted (*abhidhīyate*) by the word. This is because secondary indication is impossible here, as there is neither a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) nor a specific purpose (*prayojana*) for it. *Lakṣaṇam* means "making known" (*bodhanam*).

[Objection: But how can there be the cognition of others from the word *chattrin* (umbrella-bearer) when it denotes a *chattrin*, and if there were no cognition of non-*chattrins*, there would be a total abandonment of its own meaning? To this, he says: "And there is no abandonment of that [meaning]. Thus, the meaning is that when both the denoted (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) meanings, by virtue of a form common to both, are construed with a single [predicate], [it is *ajahatsvārthā*]. Regarding the phrase "by whatever [means]": the Logicians (*Tārkika*) claim that when the connection with the action occurs through the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), it is *ajahatsvārthā*; whereas in cases such as "Bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), it is strictly *jahatsvārthā*. He speaks in order to refute this.

In the expression "kunțān" (spears), the word "kunța" is a qualifier for the person possessing spears (*kunțin*). Thus, just as the persons possessing spears are included by virtue of being qualifiers, so too are the spears themselves included in the application [of the sentence]. Sharpness, moreover, is the common property [shared between them]. By establishing that expressions such as "kākebhyaḥ dadhi" (keep the curd from crows) do not abandon their own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*), he refutes the claim that they constitute a third type [of elliptical compound or usage]. [The phrase] "by way of being a destroyer of curd" [is used].

Regarding this: the meaning is that even though "cow" is a qualifier when there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in something similar to a cow, [the word retains its primary sense]. Now, if it is asked, "In the view that it is only the universal *gotva* (cowness) that is superimposed upon the *bāhīka*, how can there be an abandonment of the primary meaning (*svārthasya tyāgaḥ*)?", [the answer is: because it will be stated later that although universals are each all-pervasive, they accomplish their function only where they are manifested; thus, by that principle, there is an abandonment of the primary meaning.

[Objection: But even in words such as *kuśala*, the word-meaning arises preceded by the cognition of its own [etymological] meaning; and since there is a connection when there is a process of discrimination (*vivecakatva*), does this not result in the status of being a "conventional indication" (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)? To this, he says: "when there is no purpose. For example, the bank is indicated by the word *gaṅgā* for the sake of conveying qualities such as coolness and purity; however, this is not the case in instances of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). [Regarding the phrase] "in the context of the connection": thus, in the word *kuśala*, if one reflects upon the meaning of the constituent parts, it is a conventional indication; but if one reflects upon the conventional usage itself, it is simply a conventional term (*rūḍhi*).

[Objection: But how can the pure [indication] alone be of two kinds, given that there is also the possibility of two types of figurative indication (*gauṇī*)? For instance, in the case of "The Bāhīka is a cow," there is *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) when the intention concerns both the cow and the Bāhīka; whereas in cases such as "Let these cows be brought," there is *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning). [Reply: True. In this regard, the relation is either similarity or something else. In the first case, since the similarity of the denotable object (*śakya*) does not reside in the denotable object itself, how could the denotable object be the indicated object (*lakṣya*), by virtue of which there would be the state of *ajahatsvārthā*?

In the second case, however, in the absence of a relationship based on similarity, there would be no figurative status at all. Regarding the example "the spears" (*kuntānām*): the syntactical connection is that because the entry of the spears themselves is not the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the application of the spears [to the men] is sublated.

Regarding the phrase "similarity to a cow": others hold that in a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), similarity itself is the delimiting factor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Now, one might ask: since the non-difference from a cow is sublated (*bādhita*), how can there be a cognition of it? To this he says: "produced by suggestion" (*vyañjanājanya*). A sublating cognition (*bādhajñāna*) is an obstacle only when it is of the nature of a certainty (*niścaya*). He states the reason why the presence of a sublating doubt does not obstruct the cognition of the property (*tadvattābuddhi*) even after the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*): "And thus," etc. The sense is that only a non-artificial (*anāhārya*) cognition is what is to be obstructed. Regarding the term "distinguishing," etc.: [The text continues: ...the word "cow" is used in its primary sense; however, because the non-difference [of the face] from a cow is sublated, the word "cow" is employed here in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) based on the similarity between the face and a cow. Therefore, the meaning is understood as "one who possesses a face similar to a cow. This is the view of some. Others, however, hold that the word "cow" is used in its primary sense, and the non-difference from a cow is cognized through the power of suggestion (*vyañjana-śakti*). In this case, the word "cow" is used in its primary sense, while the word "face" is used in a secondary sense. Thus, the meaning is understood as "one who possesses a face similar to a cow. This is because "cowness" (gotva) and "Bāhīka-ness" are mutually exclusive. Regarding the phrase "in the middle": it means prior to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. The sense is that once the denotation of the bank (*taṭa*) and so forth has been accomplished, and their identity [with the primary meaning] is perceived, qualities such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*) and the like are obtained.

Regarding the phrase "an act of kindness" (*upakṛtam*): one might ask, "What can be said of the many acts of kindness you have performed? Your goodness toward others is well-known.
