Therefore, he says, "having made [them] in the intellect," meaning that all proximity of priority and posteriority is merely conceptualized by the intellect. "In the intellect" (*buddhau*) means in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇe*). "Having performed the actions" (*ceṣṭāḥ kṛtvā*) means having produced sounds, that is, having produced their reflections.

The sense is that [the object] appears as a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), either because of the transparency of the internal organ or because it assumes the form of its own word. The meaning is that, having perceived all objects denoted by words within the locus that is the intellect (*buddhi*), one should apply the linguistic usage of priority and posteriority right there. Regarding the term *tattvanīti*: *tat* is "extension" (*tanana*); that which possesses this is *tatvatī*, meaning "pervading all objects. One whose intellect (*nīti*) is of such a nature is *tattvanīti*. There is also a reading: *kaccittanvannītiḥ*.

In that context, the meaning is: "one whose intellect (*buddhi*) extends throughout all objects. The author of the *Bhāṣya* states the meaning of the *kārikā*: "the object of the intellect" (*buddhiviṣayam*). He explains that very point with the words: "this which... The intellect that discriminates between the existent and the non-existent is the "discerning intellect" (*prekṣābuddhiḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the internal organ" (*antaḥ karaṇe*): it means that the internal organ itself receives the designation "intellect" during the state of its modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of ascertainment; [the objects] do not appear as reflections [there]. The meaning is that they do not appear as modifications of the internal organ. In that very place, [it is said] in the word "pertaining to the intellect" (*bauddha*) itself.

Since the priority and posteriority of cognitions will be refuted later, he says, "of cognition. "Precisely with reference to the speaker" means: precisely with reference to what resides in the cognition of the speaker; the sense is that this is because a grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is impossible for an external word. "Of that very [person]" means: of the speaker alone. "Because of hearing the fruit of dharma" means: because of hearing the dharma which is the fruit of the scripture. "For this purpose" means: since the employment of a word is restricted to specific meanings, it is stated that there must also be a perception of the meaning within the cognition.

"An illustration" (*upalakṣaṇam*): the meaning is that this also applies to the previously mentioned relationship between the signified (*bodhya*) and the signifier (*bodhaka*). "This [word]" (*ayamiti*): the meaning is that the word which is to be heard as a subtle utterance precisely by way of being reflected upon by the intellect (*buddhi*) is referred to by the word "this" (*idaṃ*) found in the *Bhāṣya*. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*): the meaning is if one were to refer to the word as it exists in the intellect. "The other" (*para*): the meaning is that which is manifested (*vyañjanīya*) by an utterance conducive to excellent cognition. "In the manifested" (*vyañjanīye*): [the meaning continues as above].

The sense is that phonemes (*varṇa*) possess only the capacity to manifest sound. "In the same way" means: just like the phonemes, because the cognitions of the phonemes are also impermanent, it is impossible for them to be made objects of reference by the word "this" (*idam*), which functions as a direct perception; such is the meaning. However, in my view, the manifested sound (*vyaṅgya-śabda*) is what is referred to by "this"; this is the sense. Now, if *i*-sounds and others reside in the intellect, how can there be a cognition of their being replaced by *ya*-sounds and so forth? To this he says: "The relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) also [exists]."

In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the state of being primordial matter (*prakṛti*) consists in the cause and effect existing as non-different within the intellect, while the state of being a modification (*vikṛti*) consists in their external form; this is likewise clear here. This is because it has been established therein that [the intellect] is a modification of the effect—the meaning being that the intellect is the effect, and its modification is the transformation.

"And this sound" means that it is accepted as the expressive [word] by virtue of being manifested by the resonance (*dhvani*). "Of the aggregate" (*samaṣṭeḥ*): the aggregate is the cognition of unity having the form "a forest. The body of the Virāṭ Puruṣa, extending from Māyā down to the world (*bhuvana*), is called Virāṭ through the aggregate of gross bodies; for it is precisely the region of the heart of the Virāṭ that is called space (*ākāśa*). "And situated in the place" means that because of its pervasiveness, it belongs to both places. "And that" means "and the sound. "Just as in one place," etc.

The point is this: where there is a difference in color due to the delimitation of distinct parts, there color exists only as non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). By this, the acceptance of a "variegated color" (*citrarūpa*) for that purpose is refuted. [As it is said: "That which is red in its color at the face, yet white at the tail..."

This is because it contradicts traditional authority (*smṛti*). Furthermore, in this case, one would have to assert that a jar produced from fragrant and non-fragrant potsherds is itself odorless; and if that were so, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the causal efficacy of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) with respect to odor. The phrase "likewise" (*tathā*) means that, just like color and other qualities, it is logical for sound also to be a "pervasive occurrence" (*vyāpyavṛtti*). For just as color, though pervasive, is perceived only when it is co-located with the contact of the eye, so too is the perception of sound in another location [only when it is co-located with the sense organ]. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "the word 'Indra'": [this refers to the specific instance of the word].

Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept a deity that is distinct from the word ending in the dative case or the word ending in the locative case. Even in the view of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), because of the non-difference between word and meaning, the mantra possesses the nature of a deity; however, having accepted that the deity has a physical form (*vigrahavattva*), it is stated in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* that deities lack qualification for ritual action (*karmānadhikāra*). This is because, since words generally have the meaning as their primary purport, the intention (*tātparya*) lies only in the recollection of the meaning inherent in the performance, and not in the physical form of an unknown deity and so forth—such is the underlying intent of the section on Mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*). [The phrase] "from the Commentary" (*bhāṣyāt*) refers to this.

Having begun with the position that the universal (*jāti*) alone is the meaning of a word, it was stated that "the single word *indra* assists in all sacrifices. And this pervasiveness of the word is only logical [if it refers to the universal]. Regarding the phrase "by means of *katva* and so forth": this is because the *katva* and other properties residing in the phonemes (*dhvani*) are superimposed upon it. Regarding the phrase "in the form of a word" (*padārūpeṇa*): the sense is that since there are no phonemes (*varṇa*) in the word itself, its status as a word is merely constructed by the intellect (*buddhi*). As for why this is clear in the *Bhāṣya*, he says: "For in that case... (*tattatra hi*). Regarding the phrase "perceived by the ear" (*śrotropalabdhi*): the meaning is that its perception occurs specifically through the auditory organ.

Furthermore, by means of auditory perception, it is established that sound occupies the same location [as its substratum]. Since the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is nothing other than the ether (*ākāśa*) delimited by the ear-cavity, the term "location" (*deśa*) should be understood as referring to the ether itself, with the intention that there is no entity distinct from the ether or the directions (*diś*). However, if [it is argued] that [sound] is indeed a quality belonging only to conch-shells and the like, [then the following applies].

In that case, it would be impossible for the sound—which performs an undesirable action—to travel as far as the ear, or for the ear to travel as far as that [sound]; thus, due to the absence of contact with the auditory organ, there could be no perception. By means of the three qualifiers found in the Bhāṣya, he demonstrates the three-fold nature [of the object]. He refutes the view of the Logicians (Tārkika) with the words "tatra" and so forth, and with the word "anyathā."

The meaning is that ten sounds, moving in the ten directions like *kadamba* flowers, arise and are perceived by the auditory organ (*śrotra*) once they have come into contact with it. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the analogy of waves and ripples is intended. Just as a first wave, having arisen, generates another wave, so too does the initial sound generate a subsequent sound, and that in turn generates another; in this manner, there comes to be a connection with the auditory organ. The phrase "due to the impossibility of perceiving that [initial sound]" implies that the first sound lacks a connection with the auditory organ.

[Objection: But if sound were a single entity, then even that which is situated at an extreme distance would result in being perceived directly; therefore, he says: "In that case. The meaning is that just as in the view of the Logicians (Tārkika) there is no production of sound up to the furthest limit, so too in our view there is no manifestation [of it]. For this very reason—namely, because sound is all-pervasive—one perceives it by means of one's own ear, i.e., by that auditory organ. (1.52)

He refutes the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) that space (*ākāśa*) is a distinct substance because it is the substratum of sound, by saying "and not" (*na ca*). Regarding the reason "because of non-establishment," he states the cause: "because it is intangible" (*asparśa*). The meaning is that sound is a quality of air, which is the specific [quality] among the four elements—earth and the others—that possess tangibility. The acceptance of a touch that is neither hot nor cold in earth, however, is due to the necessity of maintaining that touch is the cause for tactile perception (*tvācapratyakṣa*). Here, the Vaiśeṣikas [object]: "Sound is not a specific quality of that which possesses tangibility."

They argue that [sound] is not a quality of fire because it lacks the state of having conjunction with fire as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and because it does not originate from the qualities of its own cause; for whatever is a quality of earth and the like is produced by conjunction with fire, or else originates from the qualities of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), yet sound is not such. Nor is it a quality of air, because it lacks the property of being the counter-positive of a destruction caused by the destruction of its substratum. [The author] refutes them: "And it is not [lasting] as long as the substance."

"Every substance"; the meaning is that since a quality of earth and so forth exists only in its own substrate, there would be no perception of it elsewhere. "Of such a kind" means that there is a rule that a quality of earth and so forth must reside only in its substrate. "Because it is not accepted" refers to the observation that the fragrance of a flower is carried by the wind. Nor should it be argued that a particle of the flower itself comes there, for that would result in the flower becoming lighter than before. "From the substrate" means from the wind. "Elsewhere" means in space (ākāśa).

For it is well known among logicians that [sound] exists as long as its substance exists; therefore, the literal sense of the phrase "elsewhere than its substratum" is strained. By means of the three qualifiers in the Bhāṣya, he demonstrates three forms [of sound]: the meaning is that ten sounds, moving toward the ten directions like a *kadamba* flower, are produced and are perceived by the auditory organ once they have come into contact with it. By the word "etcetera," the analogy of waves on water is intended.

For example, just as a wave first produced generates another wave, so too the initial sound produces another sound, and that other sound [produces yet another], and in this way there is a connection with the auditory organ; the point is that direct perception [of the sound] would otherwise be impossible because the initial sound lacks such a connection with the auditory organ. Now, if there were only one sound, it would follow that even one situated at a great distance would be directly perceived; therefore, he says: "In that case."

The meaning is that just as in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) there is no production of sound at an extreme distance, so too in our own view there is no manifestation (*abhivyakti*). Regarding the phrase "for you also": since a sound produced in one location is perceived in another location, even for the logicians there is no restrictive rule that [sound] resides solely in its qualities (*guṇa*); this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "perceiving substance" (*dravyagrāhaka*): [the sense organ perceives the substance].

The meaning is that because the perception of the qualities of a jar occurs immediately after the perception of the jar by the eye—due to the relation of inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)—the quality and the possessor of the quality are indeed grasped by the same sense organ. Regarding the phrase "by its own latent impression" (*svavāsanā*): the point is that even though space is not perceived by the auditory organ, its quality, sound, is perceived. Regarding the phrase "the location of space": it means delimited by the location of space. Regarding the phrase "the power of support": the first half-verse of this [text] states:
"For some, space itself [is the locus], due to the conceptualization of distinctions of location."

Thus [it is said]. For some, because space is manifold due to the difference of its conjuncts (*saṃyogin*), the meaning is that space itself is the substratum (*ādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "of all conjuncts": this is the underlying intention. Just as space is the substratum for stars and so forth, likewise space is also the primary substratum for chariots and other objects located on the earth; however, for things that are inherent (*samavāyin*), their ultimate rest is in the atom (*paramāṇu*) by way of their own support, and since the atom’s own substratum is space, space possesses the power of being the support for everything.

Right here, he also cites worldly consensus as a means of proof: "it is from this, it is here. This is because, through the cognition "the bird is here, the bird is not here," space alone functions as the locus. As for the claim that—since space is beyond the reach of the senses—the object of the cognition "the star is here" is merely light, that is not so; for if that were the case, the cognition "light is here" would never occur. Regarding the term "designation": the meaning is that space is the cause (nimitta) of this conventional usage.

Regarding what was stated—that space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum of all things—that refers to objects that are already established; however, with respect to objects whose nature is yet to be proven, he states that time (*kāla*) is the substratum, saying "from time. The meaning is that time alone is the differentiator of action. The distinction between time, space, and so forth is merely conventional (*vyavahārika*); in reality, there is no difference at all. "The basis" (*nibandhana*) means the cause (*nimitta*). "Is divided" (*vibhajyate*) means it is treated as distinct. "All forms" (*sarvamūrtayaḥ*) means all entities (*sarvapadārthāḥ*).

The meaning is that space alone is the differentiator between the existence and non-existence of categories (*padārtha*). Regarding the phrase "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*): the meaning is that the status of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*) as determined by the stars and so forth, which were previously indicated, is not possible for the earth and other such elements. [The text] establishes its status as the substratum of all: regarding the phrase "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*): the meaning is that the earth and other elements ultimately rest within atoms through a series of dependencies, and the ultimate substratum of those atoms is space alone. Regarding the word "this" (*idam*): the meaning is that it is established by the aforementioned conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

In the explanation of the term "having the nature of the probandum," it says "action. [This refers to] birth and duration. Birth is the connection with the first moment; the meaning is that time alone is the efficient cause (nimitta) therein. Cessation is destruction.
Furthermore, those who know time understand time—which is distinct according to its various revolutions—as being the movement of the sun, the planets, and the lunar mansions.

Thus [it is said]. Some maintain that time is of the nature of action; he refutes them with the words "the substratum of action. The sense is this: from the cognition "this jar exists" and so forth, it is time itself that serves as the substratum, and not the solar motion (parispanda) and the like, because it is impossible for that which resides in the sun to be the substratum of such a cognition. Since the word *mūrti* is well-known among logicians (*tārkika*) to denote only the attributes of corporeal things, he says "immaterial" (*amūrtim*). Regarding the phrase "only conventional" (*vyāvahārika eva*): for this very reason it was stated in the *Dīdhiti*: "Space and time are not distinct from God, because there is no evidence [for their existence apart from Him]."

The point is that the distinction in conventional usage—such as "the pot now" and "the pot then"—is adventitious (*aupādhika*) for me just as it is for you. Regarding the phrase "the Lord alone": the meaning is that the Lord alone, as delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), constitutes the auditory organ. If one were to accept that sound inheres in the Lord with respect to every effect, then it must be stated that [sound] would also arise in the mind, because the inherence of the Lord—which is conjoined with the mind—is present there as well.

In order to exclude the perception of cooked rice and the like [from the definition of sensory perception], conjunction with a substance of that same class (*tajjātīya*) is posited as the cause; since God lacks such a [material] body, He is excluded. If it is asked: "Since the Śruti states 'Brahman has space as His body,' and thus there is no distinct entity called space, how can Brahman have a location?"—this is true. Just as one space exists within another space, so too does Brahman exist. However, what is intended by the Śruti is that His body is *like* space (*ākāśavat*). Thus, He is described as "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*).

The point is that time, consisting of moments, instants, and so forth, is postulated as being conditional (*aupādhika*) because its various conventional distinctions would otherwise be inexplicable. "Refutation" (*khaṇḍanam*) means that there is no indivisible time apart from the moment. "All" (*sarva*) means that since space is the substratum of all things, [sound] has that as its locus; or alternatively, since the region in the form of space is the substratum of all things, sound also has that region as its location. "Delimited by the ear-cavity" (*karṇaśaṣkulyavacchinna*).

The meaning is that, according to the doctrine that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇavāda*), the apprehension of sound—which is connected to the auditory organ whose nature is space—is established. "Consisting of those respective elements" means consisting of those respective elements which have the nature of their corresponding sense organs. Thus, the meaning is that only when sound is a property of space is its apprehension possible as being connected to the auditory organ, which has space as its essence.

Regarding this, the Buddhists say that because one perceives obstructed objects such as jars through the eyeball and so forth, the eyeball itself is the eye and the other sense organs. To this, the Sāṃkhyas reply: the eyeball is not the sense organ, because it is impossible for it to travel to the location of the jar and other objects; rather, the sense organ is something distinct from it. Furthermore, it is not composed of the material elements (*bhautika*). For an object of smaller dimension is not perceived by the eye, nor is an unperceivable thing grasped. Moreover, it is impossible for something smaller to pervade something larger, nor can an unperceivable thing be grasped. Therefore, they assert that the sense organs are composed of *ahaṃkāra* (the ego-principle).

This [position] contradicts the scriptural testimony regarding its being a modification of the elements (*bhūta-vikāratva*). Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka assertion that the sense organ is a power residing in the physical orb (*golaka*) is also untenable, because sound is perceived even by snakes and others who lack such a physical orb. Its atomicity (*aṇutva*) is also untenable, because coldness is perceived throughout the entire body. If it were all-pervading (*vibhutva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of all [objects] being perceived simultaneously; therefore, it must be of intermediate dimension (*madhyama-parimāṇa*). (1.53)

"That is not the ear" means that if the ear were of the nature of space (*nabhas*), there would be no destruction of it by disease and the like. "By parsimony" (*lāghavena*) means that when postulating a substratum, it is more cumbersome to postulate both [the substratum and its property]. "Residing in space" (*nabhodhiṣṭhānakā*) means residing in the space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). "A specific property" (*dharmaviśeṣa*) means a property unfit for perceiving sound. "Of that which is derived from *ahaṃkāra*" (*āhaṅkārikasya*).

In the Sāṃkhya system, it is held that "the senses are modifications of *sāttvika* *ahaṅkāra*. This is because the senses perceive the qualities (*guṇas*) belonging to the specific elements (*bhūtas*) upon which they are respectively based; thus, through auditory perception, [sound] is established as having space (*ākāśa*) as its locus. Regarding the nose and so forth: the meaning is that the nose is the quality of the modification delimited by the nasal cavity, and so on. As for the view of the Logicians (*Tārkikas*) that the nose is composed of earth (*pārthiva*) because it perceives odor—that is not so; he says: "They are indeed products of *ahaṅkāra* alone."

The meaning is this: by means of the sense of smell and others, which possess a smaller dimension (*vyūna-parimāṇa*), a large dimension (*mahā-parimāṇa*) is perceived; however, it is impossible for [the sense organ] to pervade what is large. Furthermore, if there were perception without pervasion, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the sense organ is something distinct from the elemental substance (*bhautika*). "From this very reason" means that because the sense of smell is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), it lacks the capacity to travel to another location; thus, direct perception [of distant objects] would not occur. "To that extent" means that for this very reason, the Buddhist position—that the eyeball itself is the visual organ—is refuted.

The first superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of the notion "I am. In the state of dreaming, when there is the conceit of being a tiger, the conceit "I am a man" does not occur; therefore, for the sake of regulating that [conceit], the ego-sense must be accepted as that which pervades its fixed objects. And it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). Because it persists through waking, dreaming, and deep sleep along with the observation of inhalation and exhalation, that which continues to function is the principle of intellect. This is because it is a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The four internal organs—intellect (*manas*), intellect-consciousness (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*citta*)—receive the designation "ego" (*ahaṅkāra*) due to a specific modification consisting of the nature of conceit (*garva*). Regarding the phrase "its modification": this means the modifications of that ego, which is itself a modification of the internal organ, namely the sense organs. An objection might be raised: "It is not that the yogi's sense organs travel to distant places; rather, it is simply the quality born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) that acts as an auxiliary cause for perception. Anticipating this, he says: "But yoga... [and] "...remover of darkness. This is because in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), darkness is observed to obstruct the functioning of the mental states (*vṛtti*).

Consequently, even for yogins, there is perception of both the past and the future through the very connection with the sense organs, by means of the contact with their subtle states. Yoga is characterized by the steady, unwavering concentration and one-pointedness of the sense organs, which are established as being either internal or external. [Objection: If the sense organs were dependent on their respective qualities (guṇas), then it would follow that smell and other qualities could be perceived by the eye and so forth; therefore, he says: "tattad-guṇa... (dependent on those respective qualities).

The meaning is that space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum of sound, which is perceptible by the ear; and since sound is not always manifested (*anudbhūta*), it is not always perceived. Rather, it is perceived only when there is a connection between the ear and the sound. By the term "not manifested," it is indicated that there is no perception of color and so forth by the eye and other senses [when those qualities are unmanifested]. Now, one might object: the connection, or conjunction (*yoga*), exists with the substance (*dravya*) for the sense of smell, but not with the odor itself. To this, he says: "Because of their common locus" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyāt*). "The ear itself," etc.

The meaning is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself, having gone to the location of the object by means of the sense-organ, perceives it. In the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), since the conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*) is also a cause of cognition, the term "mental modification" (*cittavṛtti*) is used. In this system, the contact of the sense-organ is merely the medium for the mental modification. "For this very reason": if perception were to occur only at the location of the auditory organ, then there would be no such experience as "the sound is heard in another village."

Although it is impossible for the auditory organ—which consists of space delimited by the ear-cavity—to travel to another location, it has already been stated that the auditory organ possesses a limited dimension. However, the view that it perceives a subsequent sound reaching the ear according to the analogy of waves and ripples is not tenable; for this contradicts the experience, "I have heard the sound of a drum," and there is no basis for postulating such an error. [The term] "sarvaśaktīnām" means "of those endowed with all powers. "[Of] space and so forth... [is the phrase].

The meaning is that the atoms of space themselves undergo transformation into the state of the sense of hearing at the location of sound. Regarding the phrase "of the atoms": this connects with the statement "due to transformation into the form of the respective sense organs. Now, if the atoms themselves were the sense organs, there would be the undesirable consequence of perception even of an object not in contact [with the organ]; therefore, he says: "at the location of the object. This means: at the location of the object of perception. (1.54)

He refutes [the opponent's position] step by step. He says "Moreover" (*kiñca*). Now, one might object: if the auditory organ were one, there would be no experience of sound being at a distance; therefore, he says "pervading both sides" (*savyāpī*). The meaning is that it is the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) itself that pervades the distant location. Now, if the word-sound existing in all locations were one, then since a genus (*jāti*) cannot exist therein, the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the configuration (*ākṛti*) is perceived" would be inconsistent; therefore, he says "And as... (*yathā ca*). The fact that the ether (*nabhas*) is produced is well-known from the *Taittirīyaka*, whereas its eternity is stated in the *Chāndogya*.

The resolution of this contradiction through the designations "secondary" (*gauṇa*) and "primary" (*mukhya*) is made clear in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*. [The distinction between] "the individual soul" (*jīva*) and "the Lord" (*īśvara*) arises from the difference between the two when associated with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [The term] "conditioned" (*aupādhika*) refers to the superimposition of a distinction residing in the sound (*dhvani*) onto the phonemes (*varṇa*). [The phrase] "because of the apprehension of the form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*) means that in [the sūtra] *aiuṇ* and so forth, the form (*ākṛti*) of the letter *a* and the others is apprehended. "Otherwise" means if there were an apprehension of complete similarity. "By those alone" means by the phonemes themselves. "What is the use of them? means what is the use of the *sphoṭa*? [The word] "of all" (*sarvasya*).

The meaning is: "even for one who has not grasped the convention. Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if that collection of phonemes which is the indicator of the *sphoṭa* were the indicator of the meaning itself, then what is the use of the *sphoṭa*; and if it is not the indicator of the *sphoṭa*, then since an unknown *sphoṭa* cannot possibly indicate the meaning, the *sphoṭa* is useless—this is the meaning. || 1.55 ||

"Ungrasped" (agṛhītā): the meaning is that even when the convention (*saṅketa*) is not grasped, there is still the experience of its being a word (*padatva*). "Of the vowels, etc. (*avarṇādīnām*): the meaning is that because [the vowel] *ā* is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), it is one and the same everywhere; the same applies to other phonemes as well. "Consisting of its parts" (*tadavayavakā*): the meaning is that even a word composed of *ā* and so forth is eternal. Now, if *ā* and the others were eternal, they would have to be perceived at all times; therefore, he says: "The throat, palate, etc. (*kaṇṭhatālvādi*). "Even though there is a difference of location" (*deśabhede 'pi*).

Just as a particular shape delimited by upper and lower regions is recognized as a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) such that there is no difference in configuration despite the difference in location for each individual instance, so too there is no difference in the word (*pada*) with respect to its temporal sequence. This is because of perceptual recognition; for there is the cognition: "This is that same letter *ka*. (1.56)

[Regarding] the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) [and] non-existence (*abhāva*): [an objection is raised]—"But if phonemes (*varṇa*) are all-pervading (*vibhu*) and eternal (*nitya*), how can there be the property of 'being produced in an immediately subsequent moment' with respect to the sound *gha*? To this he says: "The state of being immediately subsequent" (*avyavahitottaratva*). "By its own cognition" (*svajñāna*). "Unconditioned by production" (*utpatty-anavacchinna*). [An objection is raised:]—But since cognition perishes in the third moment, how can the time that is the locus of the third and subsequent phonemes possess the prior cognition? To this he says: "Of cognitions as well... (*jñānānām api*).

The meaning is this: in the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*), there is no difference between the cognitions; rather, as long as the jar manifests, there is only one single modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) having the form of the jar, and not many. This is because it is accepted that the modification remains stable until the arising of a modification that is opposed to itself. Consequently, the consciousness reflected therein, though consisting of the cognition of the jar and so forth, exists only for that duration. Furthermore, if one were to postulate a stream of cognitions, the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*) as "knowledge whose object is an unapprehended thing" would suffer from the fault of being over-narrow (*avyāpti*). || 1.57 ||

He refutes the technical convention of the logicians (*tārkika-paribhāṣā*) that "the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of an all-pervading substance (*vibhu*) are destroyed by the specific qualities of the same substance produced immediately after them. He does so by means of the word "sound" (*śabda*). The sense is that just as the logicians themselves accept that the "apprehensive cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*) persists for three moments in order to account for the perception of duality (*dvitva-pratyakṣa*), so it must be accepted here as well. Regarding the phrase "at this time" (*idānīm*): the connection is "I know now" and "this [word] was uttered now. Regarding the phrase "otherwise": the meaning of "I know now" and so forth would be "I am the possessor of a cognition delimited by this very moment," and so on.

The meaning is that, in such a case, not only the moment (*kṣaṇa*), but even cognition and the like occurring within that [moment] would not be perceptible. As stated in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*: "The time taken by an atom, when set in motion, to leave its former location and reach the succeeding location is a moment (*kṣaṇa*). Because this moment is extremely subtle, it is beyond the senses. According to the commentator (*ṭīkākṛt*), a moment is one-fourth of a blink of an eye (*nimeṣa*). Its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are action and the resulting disjunction, etc. This was stated by Ballabhācārya: "The moment of the sun's vibration possesses a distinction of various moments."
Succession is proclaimed to be the connection with various kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Thus [says] Vardhamāna: "The meaning is that a 'moment' (kṣaṇa) is the motion of the sun as qualified by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the prior non-existence of a division; for a mere motion exists over multiple points of time. Now, one might ask: how can there be a conventional usage of the term 'moment' regarding the motion of the sun, given that a thing cannot reside in itself? To this he says: "Of that" (tasya). The meaning is that the conventional usage of 'moment' therein is metaphorical (aupacārika), due to its connection with a set of four limiting adjuncts consisting of successive divisions and so forth. As for the claim that time is of the very nature of action (kriyā), that is not correct.

Because in the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), due to the absence of activity, the conventional usage of "the production of the great dissolution" would not be possible. Regarding the phrase "but for the other": the sense is that, according to the opponent’s view, since it is impossible [for the same entity] to exist through distinct individual manifestations (*vyakti*) merely by virtue of being spoken of, there could be no cognition such as "this is that very same thing. Regarding the phrase "delimited by *gatva*": the sense is that in the case of different individuals, there exists only a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the respective individuality (*tattad-vyaktitva*) of those individuals, and not even one whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), because *gakāratva* (the property of being the letter *ga*) exists in those [individuals] as well. Regarding the phrase "of two jars": [the meaning is that they are related as counter-correlate and correlative].

The point here is that even in that case, there is no difference [between the two] by way of the form of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Regarding the phrase "if it has an individual as its object": the implication is that, according to your view, the recognition would have to have the universal (*jāti*) as its object. Regarding the statement "the dark one is destroyed": this is because when a color is destroyed, the substratum (*dharmin*) itself is also designated as being destroyed. He demonstrates that contact with the tongue and so forth are causes of sound (*dhvani*). Regarding the phrase "in the utterance of phonemes" (*varṇoccāraṇa*): the meaning is that since sound is observed to be produced in cases where phonemes are not manifested due to contact with the tongue, sound must be admitted to exist even in the case of phonemes.

"tajjanakatve" means "in being the producer of sound (dhvani). "In the production of phonemes (varṇa)" means that if one does not admit the existence of sound at the locus of phoneme production, then one would have to postulate that such factors as the contact of the tongue [with the palate] act as obstacles to the production of sound. "tatsattve" means "when sound is admitted. "That is superimposed thereon" means that the production and so forth residing in the air-contact is superimposed upon that [sound]. "Make a sound" (śabdaṃ kuru)—here too, the meaning is the superimposition of the production residing in the sound upon the phoneme.

[Objection: But surely, since the visual contact with that which is inherent in the object (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samavāya*) is the cause for the visual perception of a quality, how can there be the cognition "the crystal is red" in its absence? To this he says: "It is merely a superimposition (*āropa*). He demonstrates the very sequence [of relations] by saying: "As has been stated. In the case of "the crystal is red," there is a conjunction of the *japā* flower—which possesses the redness—inherently with the crystal. He then says: "In reality," [meaning] that even in the case of colors, production and so forth are merely superimposed, and not through such a sequence.

"Flavor possesses color" [is said] because the property of being inherent in that which is inherent in flavor exists in color. "Because it is not a regulator" means: by this, the definition of relation as "the state of being a particularity that regulates a qualified cognition" is rejected. "What more? means: the conventional usage of "origination" is based on its being perceived for the first time. "From such a cognition alone" means: because there is no cognition [of the form] "it produces. [Objection: But in the case of utterance, there would be the consequence of eternality; therefore, he says: "And the state of being uttered," etc. "By a woman, by a parrot," etc.

The meaning is that it is an inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) of having been uttered by a female, a parrot, and so forth. "That which delimits its being produced" means "that which delimits its being produced by a female, a parrot, and so forth. "Because it is the locus of that" means that because sound is the locus of qualities such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*), it is a substance (*dravya*). [Objection: But if this is so, how is there the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of sound as a quality (*guṇa*)? To this he says: "In the form of space" (*ākāśarūpa*). "[But] by others" is to be construed with "it is impossible to state this. "By another means of knowledge" means "because destruction is observed through perception" (*pratyakṣa*). "Of this very [sound], the *g*-ness" (*gatva*)... [and so on].

The meaning is that [the cognition of dharma] arises from being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Its non-apprehension" (*tadagraha*) means the non-apprehension of its production (*utpatti*). "Misapprehension" (*viparītagraha*) refers to the apprehension of its permanence (*nityatva*). "Its non-apprehension" (*tadagraha*) means the non-apprehension of its production. "Misapprehension" (*viparītagraha*) refers to the apprehension of its permanence. Having raised the objection—"Since it is not accessible through direct perception and so forth, how can there be a cognition of dharma?"—it is stated: "But the connection of the word with its meaning is innate... This refers to the *sūtra*: "But the connection of the word with its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviant because it is not perceived otherwise regarding the object; that is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), according to Bādarāyaṇa, because of its independence. (*JS 1.1.5*)

The meaning of this is as follows: the relationship between word and object is *autpattika*—that is, its origin (*utpatti*) is its very being (*bhāva*), and thus it is inseparable and eternal. By this [word], knowledge is known; by this [word], instruction (*upadeśa*) is taught. Instruction is the cause for the knowledge of that *dharma*; in the injunctive sentence, the word is the means of knowing it. The "object" (*artha*) of this knowledge is its non-deviation (*avyatireka*), which is the absence of error, because it is not perceived otherwise. Therefore, that injunctive sentence is the authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*, since it is independent of other forms of knowledge. This is also the consensus of Bādarāyaṇa.

The prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because the form of the convention between word and meaning is of human origin, injunctions (*vidhi-vākya*) lack authority due to their dependence upon it. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the relationship between word and meaning is beginningless, they do not lack authority through such dependence. This is precisely that.

Its nature is precisely that of being beginningless in its flow. "In this manner here" means: in this section (adhikaraṇa), the connection is with the aforementioned eternity. Now, one might object that just as there is a cognition of oneness in a collection of trees, such as "a forest," [he] says: "in the case of a forest, a heap, and so forth. The sense is that otherwise, even in your own view, the whole would not be distinct from its parts. "Like that which possesses division" means: characterized by division. "That" refers to the word. "Of the phonemes also" is to be construed with the phrase "in the state of possessing parts. "Without distinction" means: [there is no difference].

The meaning is that there would be a resting place in the atom (*paramāṇu*). "A miserable state" means that a jar, which consists of an aggregate of atoms, could not be produced; this is the intended sense. Furthermore, if atoms were partless, there would be no production of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, because of the absence of conjunction of parts. As it was said by Hari: "Due to the lack of contact between parts, neither a letter nor a word would exist. Since they [the parts] are indefinable, what else could be taught?"

The meaning of this is as follows: because there is no sequential conjunction of the constituent parts of the phonemes (*varṇa*), not a single phoneme could exist; in the absence of that, there would be no word (*pada*); and in the absence of words, there would be no sentence (*vākya*). Therefore, what is it that is conventionally designated as the expressive unit? He states that the sentence, like the word, is also partless (*akhaṇḍa*) with the words "the sentence also. Thus, the definition of a sentence should be understood as: a sentence is a word characterized as an indivisible *sphoṭa*. The phrase "having extracted" means having divided [it] through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Furthermore, by means of the analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*) of the words contained within a sentence, the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatā*) of the sentence is demonstrated. Now, one might object: "In that case, the theory of sentence-sufficiency (*vākyasaṃskārapakṣa*) would be impossible. To this he replies: "In some cases" (*kvacid*). This is what is being considered here: in expressions such as "What are they?", simultaneous grammatical sufficiency (*saṃskāra*) is not appropriate, because it contradicts experience that all [words] can simultaneously be objects of cognition. Therefore, when a sentence is explained through its division [into parts], the designation of "sentence-sufficiency" is merely a figurative attribution (*āropa*); however, there is indeed the manifestation of that [sentence].

The meaning is that there is an appearance of the letter *repha* due to the coloring by a sound similar to *repha*. He explains this with the words "as in the case of a word. The meaning is that, just as there are parts of letters, the appearance of letters within a word is merely conceptualized. An objection is raised: "If words are eternal, then the treatise [on grammar] would be useless"; therefore, he says: "But the treatise... (1.58).

The author now refutes the view previously stated, beginning with the words "But others [hold] that there is oneness among the *a*-sounds, etc. He says: "That is not so. Regarding the phrase "of the *a*-sounds": the meaning is that while there is no basis for asserting mutual identity among the various forms of the letter *ā*, there is likewise no basis for asserting mutual identity between the letters *a* and *ka*. An objection is raised: "How can properties such as *katva* (the 'ka-ness' residing in air) be manifested? To this he replies: "By means of the respective places of articulation," and so forth. The meaning is that the nature of the sound is made manifest by air possessing a generic quality (*naijātya*) such as *katva*, just as *katva* itself is. He clarifies what was previously stated with the words "just as before."

"Establishment in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhā*). "By which"—the word "by the sense organ" (*indriyeṇa*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Of the winds too"—the intention is that the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) are perceptible by the same sense organ. "Only taste and so forth"—the meaning is "but not water as well. By the word "only" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of substance (*dravya*), because taste-ness (*rasatva*) and so forth are also apprehended by the gustatory organ and others. "The letter *ka*"—this refers to the phrase "even when the place of articulation is the same," and so on. "Connection with the object"—the meaning is that due to the variety in the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), there is a corresponding variety even in the bliss whose nature is Brahman.

The meaning is that when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) undergoes a transformation into the nature of pleasure, there arises the cognition "I am happy" due to its identity with that [pleasure]. Regarding the phrase "of the qualified object": the meaning is that even though the *sphoṭa* is apprehended as being qualified by [factors] such as the letter *ka*, it remains one. "Its cognition" means the cognition of its unity. Now, one might object: if the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were not perceived, there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of unity; therefore, he says: "not embraced by limiting adjuncts. "That very same" refers to the *sphoṭa* itself. "In the word": the grammatical connection is that the division into stem and suffix is merely imagined (*kalpita*) within the word. "Just like the word" and so forth.

The meaning is that *pra*, *tṛ*, and so forth are also eternal. "In both cases" means in the original element (*sthānin*) and in the substitute (*ādeśa*). Even though individual words are non-eternal, the genus (*jāti*) residing within them is eternal; he speaks according to the view that this very genus is the *sphoṭa*. Regarding the phrase "due to the hearing of 'ra'," the word "phonemes" (*varṇāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Whether included or not included" means that in the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*, the genus *ratva* (the quality of being 'ra'), which is common to both independent and non-independent 'ra', is accepted as the original element (*sthānin*). And "because of the contradiction with his own statement"—the sense is that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is inconsistent.

Regarding the phrase *śrutipada*: this is because hearing (*śravaṇa*) has as its object a specific individual [phoneme]. Regarding the phrase *ityanukteśca* (because of not being stated thus): the meaning is that otherwise the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) would have spoken in exactly this way. Regarding the phrase *samādhānaparā* (intent on providing a solution): the meaning is that it takes the form "the hearing of *r* becomes the hearing of *l*. Regarding the phrase *puruṣamṛgarājābhyām*: "of the limbs of the man-lion" (*narasiṃha*) is to be supplied. *Mṛgarāja* means lion. Regarding the word *rapī* (also *r*): the words "he says" (*āha*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. [Objection]: But since there is no division of phonemes (*varṇa*) within the *sphoṭa*, the previously cited Bhāṣya statement "of the hearing of *r*" is inconsistent; therefore, he says: "And of the word *sphoṭa*... (1.59).

He states another defect regarding the difference between phonemes (*varṇabheda*). "Moreover, in this way" (*kiñcaivam*) means that if there were a difference in time (*kālabheda*), there would also be a difference between phonemes. "Mutated" (*vaikṛta*) refers to the sound (*dhvani*) which, having manifested the nature of the *sphoṭa*, is perceived for a long duration through repeated interruptions. "By this" (*etena*) means that just as the *sphoṭa* manifested by short vowels and so forth consists of one mora (*mātrā*) and so on, likewise there would be a difference [in the *sphoṭa*] due to the difference in its mode of operation (*vṛttibheda*). "By protracted sounds" (*plutaiḥ*); the word "sound" (*dhvani*) is to be supplied. "In this case too" (*atrāpi*).

"Even when there is a difference in the mode of operation (*vṛtti*)," [the compound] "due to the laziness of the speaker" is a *karmadhāraya*. The sense is that because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—namely, "this is that very same [word]"—even across the three modes of operation, superimposition (*āropa*) is not possible. Regarding the phrase "if there were superimposition": in the superimposition "The Vāhīka is a cow," the cause is dullness (*jaḍatva*). Regarding the phrase "in another mode of operation": the meaning is "in a mode of operation other than that which Pāṇini formulated by relying upon. "Striking the kettledrum," etc.

Just as a sound produced from a drum by a particular effort is perceived for a short duration by some and for a long duration by others, so too there is a difference in duration among the perceptions within the mental modifications (*vṛtti*), whereas the object itself remains without distinction. This [object] is termed *dhvani* (sound) and *sphoṭa* (the manifesting burst).

The manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) of sounds—by virtue of being the manifestor of the relationship between the manifested [sounds]—is the modified resonance (*vaikṛta-dhvani*). That very [resonance] is great for some and small for others; thus, in the case of articulate speech alone, both are understood as having the nature of a manifestor. However, in the case of inarticulate speech, it is only resonance (*dhvani*), because that is its inherent nature; the meaning is that it exists by its very own form. Now, since resonance (*dhvani*) is also a sound (*śabda*), how can it be a quality of sound? To this, he states the purpose: "it is an auxiliary" (*upakāraka*).

As for the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*), it serves as an illustration because that [specific] sound is perceived both after a short time and after a long time. Now, one might object that in the case of striking a drum, since there is no *sphoṭa*, the example is inconsistent with the claim that "the *sphoṭa* lasts only so long. To this he says: "even in the form of resonance" (*dhvanirūpeṇāpi*). The meaning is that even there, it is the *sphoṭa* itself that is being expressed. "Only so long" means for a fixed duration of time. "Caused by the modified resonance" (*vaikṛtadhvanikṛta*) means that due to the prolonged utterance, there is merely an increase in the perceptions of the resonances themselves.

He states the very meaning of the phrase "the sound (dhvani) related to words" with the words "but the modified sound (vaikṛtadhvani). Regarding the phrase "this is the remainder": the sense is that since it is established by its own nature, its being accepted as such is indicated by other means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and not that this [establishment] consists of the perception of a yogin (yogipratyakṣa). He says "even though the sphoṭa is undivided" to show that the difference in duration belongs to the sphoṭa only through the difference in the duration of the sounds.

In this regard, because the reality of the self (ātmatattva) is eternal, there is not even the slightest activity of the measure of time during the persistence of the *sphoṭas*. However, the nature of that *sphoṭa* is perceived as conjoined with the sounds (*dhvanis*); therefore, the duration of the sounds constitutes the form of the perception of the *sphoṭa*. Now, one might object: "If this is so, then in the case of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels as well, the sound alone would be the cause of the duration; consequently, for the long and protracted vowels too, the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) would result in them being restricted to that specific duration. To this, he says: "But by its own nature... (*svabhāvatas tu*).

Regarding "also in Kaiyaṭa": taking the Bhāṣya statement that "sound (dhvani) is a quality of the word," the meaning is that sound is a quality of the word [sphoṭa] which assists it by way of being its manifestor (*vyañjaka*). This is because, in Kaiyaṭa's commentary on the phrase "due to a modification of the meaning" (*arthavaikṛta*), otherwise the Bhāṣya statement "the increase is caused by sound" (*dhvanikṛtā vṛddhiḥ*) would be inconsistent. Regarding "of that also": the sense is that at a later time, the modified sound (*vaikṛta-dhvani*) becomes the perceiver of the *sphoṭa* which was previously perceived by the primary sound (*prākṛta-dhvani*). Regarding "and thus": the *sphoṭa* is of two kinds—internal and external.
In that context, the meaning is that the internal [word] possesses primary denotative power; the external, however, is twofold, distinguished by genus and individual. 1.60.

"In this way, the object (artha) is also possible. Just as the internal *sphoṭa* is indivisible and expressive, so too the internal denoted object (*vācya*) is indivisible; that alone is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and its nature is intuition (*pratibhā*). This is the meaning. "The essence of cognition" (*buddhisattā*): the meaning is that it is precisely what has been stated by the Buddhist [logicians]. "Precisely from the word 'jar' (*ghaṭa*)," etc.: for this very reason it is said in the *Bhāṣya* on the *matup*-sūtra: "For every word-meaning (*padārtha*) does not deviate from existence (*sattā*)."

For in cases such as "the cow-possessor existed" (*gomān āsīt*) or "the cow-possessor will exist" (*gomān bhavitā*), which refer to the past and future, there is no external existence; rather, it is merely imagined by the intellect (*buddhikalpitā*). Thus, the sense is that the qualification "exists" (*asti*) is appropriate for the purpose of excluding those [non-existent things] and embracing external existence. Therefore, regarding the statement "the horn of a hare does not exist," it is clearly stated in the *Lāsavatī-śiromaṇi* that "for this very reason, in the cognition of non-existence here, the cause is precisely a superimposed (*āhārya*) cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*)."

"Otherwise, in such cases as 'the lotus is indeed blue,' since the non-connection with blueness is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*) in the lotus, its exclusion could not be obtained"—this is stated clearly in that very same [text]. Regarding the phrase "only by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyenaiva*): because of the rule that cause and effect must occupy the same locus, it is logical that the production of the effect occurs in that very place by means of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This is the meaning.

The sense is this: since it must be stated that only an unaccomplished [object], such as cooking, can be the cause for a desire when an accomplished one lacks such desire, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the cause and its effect must be established in cognition alone. Regarding the word *āvaśyakī*: the term *āvaśyaka* is derived from the root *avaśya-bhavitṛ* (that which is necessarily to be) with the suffix *ṭhak*, due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). If it were formed with the suffix *vuñ*, it would be *āvaśyikī*. The phrase "as for what [is said]... (*yattu*) serves to refute the Logician (*tārkika*), who maintains that the sentence itself is the cause. Regarding the phrase "by way of the relation of objectness" (*viṣayatā-sambandhena*):...

The meaning is as follows: with respect to visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), the cause is the conjunction of the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*) in relation to its object by way of the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), but it is not the conjunction of the eye with a specific jar (*ghaṭa-cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*). This is because, if the object were not included, there would result an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations due to the diversity of objects. Consequently, at the time of the conjunction of the eye with a jar, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a visual perception of a cloth as well; therefore, it is necessary that the objects themselves are causes by way of identity (*tādātmya*). Thus, when the conjunction of the eye occurs with the jar alone, since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—consisting of the conjunction of the eye qualified by the object and related to the cloth by the relation of objectness—is absent anywhere, the aforementioned fault does not occur. This is the intended sense.

In reality, however, it should be understood that causality is postulated by means of the quality of "knowledge" (jñānatva) common to the knowledge of God, based on the force of causes such as the cognition of qualifiers, through inherence (*samavāya*) in the self and through the relation of objectivity residing in the individual. Otherwise, in the case of the perception of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating causality by means of "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*), which consists in residing in all pots while not residing in anything other than pots. Regarding the phrase "belonging to that" (*tadīya*): this is because they [the Advaitins] accept identity (*tādātmya*) between a thing and its own locus. Regarding the phrase "because it does not regulate occurrence" (*vṛttyaniyāmakatayā*): [this refers to the fact that identity is not a relation that determines the occurrence of properties].

For there is no such cognition as "the pot possesses a pot. Regarding the term *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality): the meaning is that coreferentiality—constituted by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) between cause and effect—cannot serve as the basis for the required proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Regarding the term *asaṅgati* (inconsistency): since words such as *kuṇḍalin* (the one who wears earrings) denote Devadatta himself, the use of such a word—which would have two distinct things as its objects—is inconsistent.

In his own view, however, the meaning is that there is no difference between the two, because the word "armlet" (*aṅgada*) and so forth brings to mind a mental armlet (*buddhy-aṅgada*) and the like, which is thus non-different from the external one. Regarding the phrase "Gautama also": for in that [work] there is the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) aphorism, "The non-existent does not become existent. Its meaning is as follows: prior to its production, the effect is not non-existent, because if the non-existent were produced, it would follow that even things like a hare's horn could be produced; and furthermore, oil would be found even in sand and such. Nor is it existent, because production is contradictory to that which already exists.

Now, regarding the objection that because of such cognitions as "the jar has arisen now," the production must be from what is non-existent (*asat*), and that if there were production from the existent (*sat*), there would follow the consequence of re-production—the resolution to that is as follows. Anticipating the doubt that "if there is production from the non-existent, there would be a lack of restriction (i.e., anything could arise from anything)," he provides the resolution: "But that non-existent is established by cognition" (*buddhisiddhaṃ tu tadasat*). That non-existent effect is made an object by the intellect; however, in the case of sand and the like, since it is not known that "a cloth will come to be," one does not act [toward them]. (1.61)

This is because the intention is that what is negated is the thought, "This is not ultimate silver. Since the internal mind does not actually go outside, [the text] says "by means of the senses" (*indriyeṇa*), indicating that it perceives [the object] through the doors of the eyes and so forth. Nor does the departure of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) from the body result in the body becoming lifeless; for even when the internal organ goes to the location of the object—just like the eyes and other senses—there is no contradiction regarding its connection with the body. If it is objected: "In that case, there would be a cognition such as 'I possess silver,' just as there is the cognition 'I am happy,'" we say: No.

If it is argued: "Just as the cognition 'I am right here' has for its object the conjunction with that very place delimited by this body—which serves as the delimitor of the substantive (viśeṣya)—how can the Self, which is not inherently inherent (*asamaveta*) in a substance [other than itself], possess that nature [of being the substrate] through its inherence in that [body]? [Response: There is no contradiction in the inherence of silver and so forth in the Self, even when delimited by the "this-ness" (*idantva*) and other qualities of mother-of-pearl, just as there is no contradiction in the inherence of knowledge and so forth in the Self when delimited by the body. Regarding the word "conjoining" (*saṃyujya*): the word "mind" (*citta*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "transforms" (*pariṇamate*): [the mind transforms].

If it is objected: "But since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is also a sense-organ (indriya), how can [knowledge arising from it] be perception (pratyakṣa)?", we say no. This is because there is no evidence for the status of the mind as a sense-organ; for in the statement, "The mind is superior to the senses," the mind is mentioned separately. Furthermore, the Gītā statement, "The senses, with the mind as the sixth," is consistent even with something of a different category, just like the expression, "They partake of the *iḍā* offering with the sacrificer as the fifth. If it is further objected: "Since it is not produced by a sense-organ, it cannot attain the status of perception," we say no.

For being produced by the sense organs is not the determinant for perceptuality, because it does not apply to the perception of God; rather, it is precisely the non-difference between the consciousness of the object and the consciousness of the knower.

The Sāṃkhyas, however, maintain that because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is transparent, the cognition of jars and other objects arises when their reflections appear therein—just as a face is perceived in a mirror even though it does not actually exist there. Likewise, they say that consciousness also undergoes a transfer into the insentient internal organ and its modifications; thus, the presentation of the forms of all objects occurs only within such a modification of the internal organ. The author refutes them with the words "but not in that [modification]," meaning "conjoined with that [consciousness] within the modification."

The meaning is "connected with the sense organs. Regarding the phrase "in dreams and so forth": according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), however, chariots and other objects perceived in dreams are of a phenomenal (prātibhāsika) nature because they are produced by adventitious defects such as sleep. If it is objected that in a dream there might simply be a recollection (smaraṇa) of chariots and the like previously experienced, we say no; for that is impossible, as it would contradict the actual experience expressed in the form, "I saw a chariot. Furthermore, the quality of being perceivable by the sense organs in the case of the chariot and so forth is also merely phenomenal, since at that time all the sense organs have ceased their activity. [The phrase] "residing in the mind" refers to this.

The meaning is that just as an object, though non-existent [externally], exists within the mind during dreams and so forth, it is likewise at other times as well. When the activity of the external senses has subsided, and the self’s state of being an enjoyer occurs through the mind alone, that is a dream. The mention of "space, earth, and so forth" is for the purpose of including insentient things. Due to the power of primordial ignorance (*avidyā*), the consciousness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—its true nature being obscured—appears in an external form. As they say: "The portions of the attributes of the internal organ are situated externally."

The meaning is as follows: that whose function resides within is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); consciousness (*caitanya*) is its property, and the "parts" of those very internal objects are what are external. This explains the statement that "it is not a reflection of an external object. Regarding the word "error" (*bhrama*), "cognition" (*jñāna*) here refers to a modification of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). Its "form" (*ākāra*) is its transformation into something resembling silver; and this occurs in the case of error just as it does in the case of a real thing.

In that case, since it is impossible for non-existent silver to be the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), illusory silver (*prātibhāsika-rajata*) arises. Furthermore, the identity (*tādātmya*) between the mother-of-pearl and the silver is also merely illusory. To explain: in that situation, because there is no sensory contact with external silver located in another place, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not possible. Nor is the production of silver there possible, due to the absence of constituent parts of silver. Therefore, for one whose vision is impaired by a cataract or similar defect, a mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) in the form of silver arises from its conjunction with the substance present before it.

Thus, according to the Vedānta, ignorance (avidyā), conjoined with defects such as a glass lens (kāca) and the like, transforms into the form of silver and so forth. This refers to the cognition of silver that takes on the form of knowledge itself, regarding its object—the mother-of-pearl and the like. The intended meaning of the statement, "the apprehension of mental silver in that which stands before one," is precisely this: because the modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), upon contact with the object situated in front, transforms into the form of silver. And in this way, it should be understood that the superimposition (āropa) of a cognition having the form of silver onto the mother-of-pearl and the like ultimately results in nothing other than transformation (pariṇāma).

Regarding the phrase "from the established conclusion" (*siddhāntāt*): by this, it is shown that even through sensory contact, there arises only a pair of cognitions consisting of a perception and a recollection—namely, "this" and "silver"—and not a single cognition in which silverness is the qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the mother-of-pearl. This is because, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to deny the rule that a cognition qualified by silverness must necessarily lack a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) that is defined by a qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*) distinct from that of silver.

The point is that even though there is an inclination toward mother-of-pearl (śukti) under the aspect of "silver-ness" (rajatatva-prakāreṇa), it does not [occur] by way of having as its qualificandum the mother-of-pearl qualified by "this-ness" (idantvāvacchinna) and silver-ness as its qualifier; for the non-apprehension of the non-relation of silver (rajatāsaṃsargāgraha) acts as an obstacle to the perception of silver-ness with respect to the qualificandum "this. Thus, the Prābhākara claim—that if the perception "this is not silver" exists, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of an inclination toward mother-of-pearl under the aspect of silver-ness—is refuted. [The word] "proximate" (sannikṛṣṭam) [is used].

In that case, since it has already been stated that neither the production nor the cognition of silver is possible, [the author says] "in the superimposition of silver and so forth. This means: in the acceptance of the appearance of silver that is not in contact with the senses. [An objection is raised: "But surely, by the very nature of the defect (doṣa), even silver located in another place appears. Anticipating this unease, he says: "that is observed [to be so]."

Regarding "from the perspective of its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*): if, in the error consisting of the nature of silverness, external silver itself were the object, then since that [external silver] exists even at the time of perceiving its specific qualities (*viśeṣadarśana*), there would be no cognition apprehending the absence of silver such as "now there is no silver here. If it is argued that the meaning of "silver is not [here]" is "the cognition of silver is not [present]," then it is established that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is indeed a mental state (*buddhi*). If it is asked how a transformation of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) occurs in that manner in the absence of an object, he says: "due to the glittering appearance, etc. (*cākacakyādīti*).

The meaning is that the mere shimmering and so forth is itself the cause of the delusion. For this very reason it is said in the *Paramārthasāra*: "In the case of the rope, which is the cause for the [delusion of] a snake, there is no [other] cause. The sense of that is: in the rope, which is the cause for the delusion of a snake, there is no other cause; rather, it is simply ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting in appearing otherwise. (1.62)

Is it not the case that since the eye-contact and so forth are causes only for ordinary visual perception (*laukika-cākṣuṣa*), extraordinary visual perception (*alaukika-cākṣuṣa*) is established solely through "characterization by cognition" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*)? To explain: in the case of [the cognition] "the jar does not exist," the manifestation of the jar within the portion consisting of the absence (*abhāva*) is impossible; likewise, in the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that," the manifestation of the "that-ness" (*tattā*) portion is impossible; and in the case of "I see fragrant sandalwood" (which is an instance of presented apprehension, *upanītabhāna*), the manifestation of the fragrance portion is impossible due to the absence of a sensory connection. Therefore, the very cognition having that as its object is itself the connection, and such a cognition indeed exists.

The phrase "jñānalakṣaṇā" [refers to] the refutation of the view that the cognition of external silver occurs even with respect to mother-of-pearl. The Logicians (Tārkikas) maintain that since there is the experience, "I cognize the shell as silver," one must accept the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti); and for the sake of accounting for that, one must also accept the "cognition-characterized" (jñānalakṣaṇā) contact. That is not so, because it involves the complexity (gaurava) of [assuming]: the impression's (saṃskāra) capacity to produce that cognition, its status as a cause through a contact constituted by the cognition that produced it, and the postulation of an additional contact. Thus, [the opponent's position] is rejected.

The meaning is as follows: since there is an absence of such cognitions as "I see fragrance" in that case, the status of being the locus of the cause [of perception]—delimited by the property of being visual (cākṣuṣatva)—is not possible through the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā). Therefore, how could the acceptance of *jñānalakṣaṇā* (the characterizing of cognition) be justified for the sake of accounting for that visual perception? Rather, on the basis of the experience "I remember the fragrance," it is more appropriate to accept therein simply the status of being the locus of memory through the relation of objecthood.

Even if there is no proof for two cognitions occurring simultaneously, there is no sublation to the coexistence of both the nature of memory (*smṛtitva*) and the nature of visual perception (*cākṣuṣatva*) within a single cognition. Furthermore, because of the experience "I see this silver," it is necessary to admit a worldly objecthood (*laukika-viṣayatā*) even in the case of an error. If it is argued that, like sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and other factors, a defect (*doṣa*) is also a cause of perception based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [we reply] that compared to this, the transformation (*pariṇāma*) into that very form is simpler (*laghutva*).

[Objection: But if a defect residing in the object were the regulator of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), then even for a person who is not mistaken, the perception of such a mother-of-pearl shell would result in being a delusion. [Response: This is not so, because we accept the causal relationship (the relation between cause and effect) only by introducing the qualification "belonging to that person. However, since the redness of a *japā* flower has a single form for everyone, there is no introduction of the qualification "belonging to that person. This is because it is explained otherwise, as its purpose is already served by the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the mental modification itself.

Furthermore, if knowledge were a means of immediate perception (*pratyāsatti*), then since the direct perception of smoke and so forth would be established by that alone, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the abolition of inference. "That which has those as its correlates" (*tattadanuyogī*): the meaning is that just as the conjunction between a jar and the ground is one where the jar is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the ground is the correlate (*anuyogin*), such an experience does not exist here [in the case of knowledge]. The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) of jar-ness produces the cognition of a jar located in another place; however, the characteristic of cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) is a means of immediate perception only for that very object whose cognition it is.

And thus, the sense is that since there is no cognition of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) and so forth in the cognition of "silverness" (*rajatatva*), it is impossible for it to be a relation. He refutes the Tārkika position—that "the relation of relations is not an object of qualified cognition"—with the words "by means of the relation. The sense is that because the relation in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the same [in both cases], it is necessary to accept counter-positiveness and so forth in the case of the jujube fruit (*badara*) and the like, in order to avoid the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition "the jujube is in the bowl" (*kuṇḍe badaram*). "By way of qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭyena*): the meaning is that it is precisely the conjunction known as having the ground as its locus (*anuyogitva*) that is the cause of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*). 1.63.

He refutes the view that a universal which is being cognized cannot be a "proximity" (pratyāsatti) with the words "of that which is non-existent. The sense is that because silver—which does not exist in the mother-of-pearl shell—lacks proximity, it is impossible for it to function as a proximity.

The proponents of the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti-vāda*), however, maintain that in this case there are two cognitions consisting of perception and memory; for instance: "this" is the perception of the object present before one, and due to a defect, when the nature of the mother-of-pearl is not apprehended, there arises—due to the awakening of a latent impression by similarity and due to a defect—a memory of silver whose specific essence (*tattva*) has been lost. Because the difference between these two distinct cognitions and the non-relation between their two objects are not apprehended, there occurs an activity directed toward a qualified object and the conventional usage of it as a single cognition. This is not correct.

Regarding the process of activity (*pravṛtti*), one must state that the cause is a cognition whose object is the thing present before one (*purovartin*), which is qualified by the memory of the object as qualified by the delimiter of the status of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatāvacchedaka*), and which is accompanied by a non-apprehension of the relation [between the remembered and the perceived]; thus, there is prolixity (*gaurava*). Now, an objection is raised: the phrase "by means of a general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) and so forth means a cognition whose object is a universal (*sāmānya*). And so, since the state of being its object exists even in what is not currently present, he raises the doubt with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

As for the claim that the acceptance of "perception through the character of cognition" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) is necessitated by the appearance of mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) and the like under the aspect of "silver-ness," because there is no appearance of "mother-of-pearl-ness" therein and thus it is impossible for the mother-of-pearl and so forth to appear through "universal-characterized perception" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*); that is not correct, because in that case, the defect itself is what causes the appearance of the mother-of-pearl and the like. Furthermore, as for the claim that "perception through the character of cognition" is required because the appearance of fragrance cannot occur through "universal-characterized perception" regarding the portion of fragrance without sensory contact with the fragrant object; [that too is incorrect].
