That too is not so, because even in that case, one must assume that the causal complex for the mediated presentation (*upanītabhāna*) regarding fragrance and other objects is itself the cause. Regarding the word "cognition" (*jñāna*): the sense is that a momentary cognition cannot function as a means of immediate connection (*pratyāsatti*). Regarding the phrase "the nature of both cognition and the object": if the objective relation (*viṣayatā*) were identical with the nature of the cognition itself, then following the cognition "the floor is possessed of a jar," there would follow the undesirable consequence of no distinction between that cognition and the subsequent cognition "the conjunctions on the floor are possessed of a jar"; it is with this in mind that he says "the nature of both. [The phrase] "only the latent impression" (*saṃskāra eva*)...

The meaning is that [the cognition] has the form of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of silver. Therefore, there is no consequence of its being a memory (*smṛti*) simply because it is produced by a latent impression. In reality, however, even though [the relation] consists in the nature of being an object, the distinction is precisely this: in the case of "the conjunction of the jar and the ground," the conjunction appears as a conjunction (*saṃyogatvena*), whereas in the case of "the ground possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), it does not. The rule that a category other than a universal (*jāti*) does not appear in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*) applies to the aspect of the qualifier (*prakāratā*), but not to the relational objectness (*sāṃsargikaviṣayatā*); it is with this intention that it was stated "in the system" (*mate*).

[Objection: But surely, if a cognition characterized by [both] knowledge [of the object] and memory [of the qualifier] is not accepted, how can there be the manifestation of the fragrance-part, given the absence of sensory contact with it? To this, he says: "It is simply another cognition. The meaning is that it is a single cognition consisting of both perception and memory. There is merely the conventional designation of "memory" for it simply because it is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), but there is no reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I remember," because the aspect of having been previously experienced is not mentioned. For this very reason, the cognition is precisely "I see fragrant sandalwood. Logicians, however, describe it as being a case of "manifestation through presentation" (*upanītabhāna*).

Others, however, say that fragrance is inferred from the state of being sandalwood; otherwise, since the perception of the subject as qualified by the property would already be established, inference itself would be abolished.

The Prābhākaras, however, say: "In the cognition ‘This is that,’ there is perception regarding the ‘this’-portion and recollection regarding the ‘thatness’-portion; thus, it is two distinct cognitions. The same applies to cases such as ‘fragrant sandalwood. Although action arises only from a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), and thus action would not occur if two separate cognitions were admitted, [the Prābhākaras argue that] such action is caused by those two cognitions accompanied by the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*). Therefore, he states another fault: "confusion" (*saṅkara*). This is said as a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*); in reality, there is no fault even if those two [cognitions] are conflated.

Since everything other than Brahman is impermanent, there is no possibility of it being a genus (jāti) characterized by eternality; therefore, that [objection] is a defect. Furthermore, just as in the case of the conjunction with a monkey and its absence, one accepts both mediacy (parokṣatva) and immediacy (aparokṣatva) even in a single cognition through a distinction of limiting adjuncts (avacchedaka-bheda). 1.64.

"Along with the sense organ"—that is, precisely for that which is accompanied by the sense organ. Therefore, because of the accompaniment of the defect of the sense organ, the transformation of the mind occurs as something inherently defective. As for the claim that "only the cognition of a sublation is an obstacle to a cognition not produced by a specific defect," that is incorrect; for since the degree of yellowness is established by experience through the varying degrees of bile, it is necessary that bile itself must be the cause.

[Objection: But how can there be a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having that [yellow] form, given the absence of a yellow conch? To this he says: "And that" (*sā ca*). That is, and the mental modification as well. [Objection: Since these two modifications—the one with the form of "this" and the one with the form of silver—each have only a single object, they lack the nature of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*); therefore, their status as an error (*bhrama*) is not established. To this he says: "Error-cognition" (*bhramapramā*). It is a valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the aspect of the conch, and an error regarding the aspect of yellowness. The point is that the convention of calling it an "error" arises precisely because the single consciousness reflected in the two modifications apprehends the identity (*tādātmya*) between a real and an unreal object.

"Reflection" (*pratibimba*)—this is the sense: the relationship between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the *puruṣa* is a proximity (*sannidhi*) consisting of the state of being the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer. For there can be no other relationship between those two, which are both all-pervading and eternal. This very [relationship] is expressed by the terms "falling of a shadow" (*chāyāpatti*) and "reflection" (*pratibimba*). "The grasping of the mental mode" (*vṛttigraha*) means the illumination of the mental mode. For [it is not] passion... (as in the *Kuṇḍalī-ṭīkā* and *Kappu*).

It does not exist [as a separate entity], because there is a contradiction between being the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and being the seen (*dṛśyatva*), since [the Self] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Regarding the phrase "a particular transformation" (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*): the reflection of a transformation is what is called the coloring (*uparāga*) of the Puruṣa. Because the Self consists of consciousness (*jñāna*), this particular transformation—which is the reflection in the Puruṣa—is of the nature of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*) and is manifested by the Witness (*sākṣin*). It is precisely from this defect consisting of the form of a reflection that the delusion of identity between Consciousness and the Puruṣa arises, such as "I am happy" or "I see," and so forth.

He refutes the Sāṅkhya and other systems with the words "not, however. Regarding the phrase "in a mirror, etc.": for in that case, the state of being a reflection consists in being perceivable by an eye that has been turned back [toward it]. "Mirror" means a looking-glass; for there, due to the proximity of the shadow (reflection) of the face, another shadow arises. "Of both"—that is, of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*). "Because of being formless": for only an impure object has a pure reflection, just as the face has a reflection in a mirror. (1.96)

"Due to the connection with the mental mode (*vṛtti*)" means due to the reflection in the mental mode. This is the underlying point: just as there is the common usage "the iron burns" because of the superimposition of identity with the fire—which is the locus of burning—even though the lump of iron lacks the power to burn; so too, the Self possesses objectivity through the superimposition of identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which has transformed into the form of the object. "Proceeding from that" means proceeding from the mental mode. "Connected with that" means: due to that connection—namely, the connection with the Person (Puruṣa)—there is the illumination of the mental mode by the consciousness of the Person.

By such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge," etc., Brahman alone is primary knowledge; however, because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is an insentient attribute of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its status as knowledge is merely figurative. The sense is that, just as in the case of a hibiscus flower and a crystal, when non-difference is perceived due to proximity, the attribute of the person (the self) is superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*). (1.97)

In expressions such as "he knows the jar," the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the activity (*vyāpāra*), which is knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*); the result produced by that is manifestation (*prakaṭatā*). Thus he says, "produced by the modification" (*vṛttijanyā*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the modification" (*vṛttidvārā*): the sense is that [the object] is reflected only within the mental modification (*vṛtti*). In the "pure consciousness"—that is, in the Self whose nature is knowledge—there is [manifestation]. Regarding "of that"—meaning of the object—and "due to its connection": through the connection with the modification, the object possesses the status of an objective case (*karmatva*) because it is the locus of the result produced by an activity inherent in the person (the Self). For here, the action inherent in another is precisely the mental modification (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the term "agency" (*kartṛtva*): the meaning is that agency belongs to the Self (*puruṣa*) as well, due to the identification with the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which is a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). If it is objected: "Since the 'I'-sense (*ahamartha*) alone possesses the nature of a knower, and since the non-Self lacks that [nature], [the Self] would incur the state of being insentient (*jaḍatva*)," we say no. This is because it is of the nature of consciousness (*jñāna*) and is therefore not insentient. If it is asked: "In the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), there is no manifestation of objects; how then can it consist of knowledge? [The answer is: Because knowledge is precisely the light (*prakāśa*) characterized by an object.

Now, since the self (*puruṣa*), whose nature is consciousness, lacks the status of being a substratum for knowledge, it would follow that it cannot function as the agent in expressions such as "he knows"; therefore, the author says, "of the verb *jānāti*. He explains how the stick (*daṇḍa*) possesses the status of a qualifier (*prakāratva*) within the cognition "the man with a stick" (*daṇḍī*) by stating, "residing in the mental modification (*vṛtti*). This expression—"residing in the modification"—is used because object-ness (*viṣayatā*) is defined in relation to cognition. Only the stick and so forth, when conjoined with the mental modification, are said to reside in the modification, because they are perceived [through that modification]. In that case, the very relationship that resides in the stick is itself the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*). [The phrase] "having the mental modification as its relatum" (*vṛttyanuyogika*) [is used].

The relation of consciousness that resides in its occurrence (*vṛtti*) is itself what constitutes objectivity (*viṣayatā*) here. For this very reason, the relation of knowledge with its object is objectivity; and that [relation], residing in the knowledge, has as its nature the knowledge qualified by the object—so says the *Dīdhiti* on the *Bauddhādhikāra*. And thus, even when the object has perished, [objectivity] still occurs because the knowledge remains present.

Otherwise, since objective relations (*viṣayatā*) are distinct based on the difference between qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) and qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*), if one were to posit the causality of a cognition having "pot-ness" as its object toward a cognition qualified by pot-ness, then upon the inclusion of only one [type of relation], there would be no comprehension from a cognition possessing another objective relation. Therefore, the meaning is that one must accept a single, unitary nature of objective relation (*viṣayatātva*). (1.99)

Regarding the phrase "according to the method of Nyāya": in the cognition "the ground is possessed of a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), the meaning is that the objective qualifier (*viśeṣyatā*) consists of the cognition qualified by the jar. If objective qualifiers and the like were of the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhajñāna*), there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I am one who possesses a cognition having the ground as its qualifier. Therefore, it is said: "qualified by their respective objects. Thus, the point is that in the aspect of the jar, the cognition takes the form of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*), while in the aspect of the ground, it takes the form of being an objective qualifier (*viśeṣyatā*).

In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is an elliptical expression for "desire" (*icchā*); otherwise, if one were to accept that desire possesses objectivity (*viṣayatā*) only by way of knowledge, then when that knowledge ceases, the desire would no longer possess an object.

As for the claim that the objectivity of desire consists simply in its being produced by a knowledge whose object is a jar or the like—that is not correct. Since the desire of God (*īśvarecchā*) is eternal, such a definition would fail to apply (*avyāpti*).

In reality, because it is necessary to distinguish between the nature of a relation as a specific instance (*tadvyaktitva*) and the state of being related (*sambandhitva*), it is logical that objectivity itself is distinct from knowledge.

Regarding the term "tritaya" (triad): it means the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), the qualifier (*prakāratā*), and the relation (*saṃsargatā*). Now, one might object: since only the pot and so forth—which are the objects of the word's function (*vṛtti*)—are the objects of cognition, how can an external object be such? To this he says: "precisely through non-distinction. This means because of the identity between those two [the external object and its mental representation]. || 1.100 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the person" (puruṣe): the meaning is that through the connection with the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā), the shadow of the person (puruṣacchāyā) appears within the sattva of the intellect (buddhi). The underlying idea is that the person, as the object of the mental modification (vṛtti), is also an object of perception (dṛśya), just like a jar or other objects. "The establishment of knowledge" (jñānopapatti) means the logical possibility of the self being an object of cognition; it refers to the logical possibility of a single entity simultaneously possessing the status of both agent and object, as in the expression "one knows oneself."

If it is objected: "If the self is admitted to be an object of knowledge, its self-luminosity (svayaṃprakāśatva) cannot be established, as it would then be like non-self; yet, if its state of being unknown is admitted in accordance with the experience 'I do not know,' then its nature as self-effulgent light (svayañjyotiṣṭva) is undermined," we reply: True. For, according to the Śruti—"That is indeed other than the known, and moreover above the unknown"—the Self is distinct from both the known and the unknown. If it is asked what the status of the empirical experience "I know myself" is, [the answer is]: because the pure Self alone is self-luminous.

Although it is the very nature of knowledge, desire, and the like to possess objects, nevertheless, this "object-possessing" character is a relation with an object; and that [relation] is not real (tāttvika), but rather superimposed (ādhyāsika). There is no contradiction, however, in the fact that [the self], when qualified by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), becomes the object of knowledge.

Thus he says, "the self," and so forth. Consciousness qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), while that which is conditioned by it is the witness (*sākṣin*). Although the synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*) of the senses and the cognitions produced by them is indeed the knower (*pramātṛ*), the witness is nevertheless accepted for the sake of synthesizing even the knower. The witness, however, being non-different from Brahman and self-luminous, synthesizes both itself and other objects independently; thus, cognitive states (*vṛtti*) and their resulting validity (*prāmāṇya*) are its objects.

Now, one might object that if the person (*puruṣa*) is also an object of cognition, its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) would be compromised; to this he replies: "Of the original and the reflection. Its self-luminosity consists in being illuminated by itself alone.

The meaning is as follows: just as a lamp that illuminates objects such as a jar does not require another lamp for its own illumination, so too cognition, which illuminates an object, does not require another cognition for its own illumination. For the nature of cognition consists precisely in its distinction from the insentient; thus, even though it is an object of illumination, there is no consequence of its being insentient like a jar or similar things. Furthermore, at the time of illuminating an object, if the illuminator itself were not illuminated, there would be no awareness of the object at all. Indeed, an unilluminated lamp does not illuminate a jar or other objects.

"Manifested by the witness" (sākṣibhāsya) means "to be known by the witness" (sākṣivedya). "Residing therein" (tanniṣṭhā) means "having as its qualificandum that which possesses potness, with its qualifierhood delimited by potness. "To be grasped intrinsically" (svatogrāhya): intrinsic graspability consists in being graspable by whatever causal complex grasps its own substratum, provided there is no specific defect. Its own substratum is the cognitive state (vṛttijñāna); that which grasps it is the witness-consciousness (sākṣijñāna). The meaning is that when the cognitive state is grasped by that [witness], the validity residing in it is also grasped.

If it is argued that if the validity of a cognition were apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then there would be no occurrence of doubt regarding invalidity in a cognition produced during a state of non-habituation (*anabhyāsadaśā*), we reply: True; for in that case, validity is not apprehended due to the presence of a defect (*doṣa*) that generates doubt. It is for this very reason that it was stated [in the commentary] "provided there is an absence of specific defects. It is for this same reason that he says "subsequent" (*auttarakālika*). The meaning is that when there is a determinate sublation (*bādhaniścaya*) such as "this cognition is invalid," the erroneous nature (*bhramatva*) of the preceding cognition is then inferred. [The phrase] "he also [infers] himself" [is explained as follows].

And thus, in the cognition "I know the jar," the triad consisting of the jar, the knowledge, and the self is made an object by that knowledge. This alone is the "triplicate perception" (*tripuṭī-pratyakṣa*) of the Prābhākaras. For the Naiyāyikas, however, knowledge is apprehended through the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form: "I am possessed of the knowledge having the jar as its object. If it is objected: "How can the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—consisting of the contact of the eye and so forth—which produces knowledge, generate the state of being an object of knowledge within that very knowledge? For [according to you], the substratum (the knowledge itself) does not yet exist [at the time the complex operates]," we say: no.

Just as the conjunction of potsherds produces a jar characterized by specific qualities, so too there is no obstacle to the production of knowledge characterized by luminosity (*prakāśatva*). Thus, sound also [is luminous]. The connection with the preceding [statement] is that it illuminates itself as well. He provides the reason for this very point: "because of its luminosity" (*prakāśatvāt*). The meaning is that all three possess the nature of luminosity. Furthermore, the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of knowledge is due to its not being an object of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). (1.101)

For this very reason—that is, precisely because of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). Regarding the phrase "when cognition exists": the meaning is that when an object such as a jar is manifested in the form "this is a jar," the cognition whose object is that jar is also manifested; therefore, doubt and so forth regarding that cognition do not arise. With the words "by means of after-cognition" (*anuvyavasāya*), he refutes the position of the Logicians (*Tārkika*) who hold that the apprehension of cognition occurs through an after-cognition in the form "I am possessed of a cognition having a jar as its object. The meaning is that if the first cognition were to be manifested by a second cognition, and that [second] cognition likewise by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

The point is that it is impossible for an unmanifested *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness) to be a manifestor [of itself]. And [it is so] because of the absence of experience [of such a process]. Thus, cognition is not graspable by another cognition. If it is objected: "In cases where something is perceived as an object (*viṣayatayā*), there must be a requirement for the object and its contact (*sannikarṣa*) in the preceding moment; how then can there be self-graspability?"—we say no. This is because we do not accept that the contact between the cognition and the sense organ is the cause of the perception of the cognition; rather, we accept a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not constituted by the object and its contact.
Now, one might ask: if the self alone possesses the sequence of agency and the relationship of object and subject, how is this so? To this he says: "Even though there is non-difference."

For just as even in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), in the cognition "all is knowable" (*sarvaṃ prameyam*), there is the status of being an object (*viṣayatā*) of that very [cognition] itself; or just as the linguistic usage of "existent" (*sat*) with respect to substances (*dravya*) and so forth is caused by "existence" (*sattā*), yet with respect to existence itself, the linguistic usage of "existent" occurs despite the absence of an existence distinct from itself—so too, the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) of a thing to itself is not contradictory. Likewise, in such cases as "I know myself," the same single entity possesses the status of both agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*).
The sense is that, just as in the case of the relation of identity for logicians, it is possible for a thing itself to be related to itself.

"Having the form of the pervaded" (*vyāpyākāra*) means that the modification (*vṛtti*) which has the form of smoke is itself the cognition of smoke. Therefore, inference (*anumiti*) is the reflection of an external form. "The pervader" (*vyāpaka*): the meaning is that whatever is of the nature of the pervader is that category (*padārtha*), and whatever is of the nature of the word-meaning is that category; [inference] is the modification having that form. "And verbal comprehension" (*śābdabodha*): thus, verbal comprehension from a word also occurs in the manner described. Now, one might ask: since there is no external object in cases such as "the horn of a hare," how can there be meaningfulness? To this he says: "The horn of a hare," etc. This was stated by Hari:
"In the designation of objects, external existence is metaphorical;
it reveals the nature of the self of all things in all states.

Regarding the "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) of external objects for the sake of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), there is an existence distinct from the external that is "metaphorical" (*aupacārikī*), meaning it is entered into by the intellect and possesses the purpose of superimposition (*āropa*). By the phrase "in all states," it is shown that even past and future things have a manifestation through the intellect. By the word "of all" (*sarveṣām*), it is shown that the relationship between word and object is eternal (*nitya*), because linguistic usage occurs even in the case of words such as "the horn of a hare" through the conceptualization of that [non-existent] object by the intellect.
For this very reason, with reference to a rabbit's horn by means of the intellect, one employs the expression "it does not exist" in order to exclude its external reality. 1.102.

[Objection: But surely, since the object in words such as "hare's horn" is imaginary, there is no proof for the existence of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding it. To this he says: "It is cognition itself. If it is asked how a latent impression is produced in that case, he says: "By the previous [cognition]. If it is asked how this was so even at a prior time, he says: "Because of beginninglessness. There is no fault—that is, there is no impossibility of the latent impression.

Some maintain that in cases such as a hare's horn or nacre-silver, because even what does not exist externally becomes an object of the intellect, this is called "the appearance of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*).

The Sāṅkhyas maintain that it is the *sadasatkhyāti* (apprehension of the existent and non-existent), because the object present before one exists in its own nature (*svarūpa*) but does not exist in the form of external silver.
For the Vaibhāṣikas and others who accept that the continuum of cognition (*jñānasantāna*) alone is the self (*ātman*), the conventional term used is *ātmakhyāti* (apprehension of the self).
The logicians (*tārkika*) hold that it is *anyathākhyāti* (apprehension otherwise), because there is the cognition of mother-of-pearl as being silver.

Regarding the phrase "or the object" (*yo vārthaḥ*): the word *vā* indicates an alternative position. The meaning is as follows: the object (*artha*) that is superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is itself superimposed upon the word—is the external object (*bāhyaṃ vastu*) that, having been superimposed [upon the internal], becomes the referent of the word (*śabdārtha*). The point is that just as the internal *sphoṭa* is the signifier (*vācaka*), so too the object is merely internal. Now, one might ask: what is the basis (*bīja*) for this superimposition? To this he says: "due to defects such as passion" (*rāgādidoṣa*). The sense is that activity proceeds solely by virtue of those [defects]. As stated in the *Pātañjala-sūtra*: "Passion (*rāga*) is that which lies latent in pleasure. (*sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ*)

The meaning of that is: attachment (*rāga*) is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) for pleasure or its cause. "Precisely from this" means precisely from superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the external. "Correspondence" (*saṃvāda*) means identity. "In this very way" means by means of correspondence and non-correspondence alone. In the case of cognition, "correspondence" means having an object that accords with reality. "Valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) means that which corresponds to the external object. || 1.103 ||

[Objection: Since words such as "Nala" are modern [in origin], how can there be a latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding them, or how can there be a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of both the internal and external? To this, he says: "Nalādi... and "Bauddha...". For there exists an beginningless latent impression whose object is the mental form (*ākāra*). [Objection: But how can even the form of that which is unknown reside in the intellect? To this, he says: "And that (*saca*). The sense is that the general form resides in the intellect everywhere through inference and other means. "Of those"—that is, of words such as "Nala. "The apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) also... [is likewise possible].

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the phrase "in the form grasped by the intellect. Regarding the phrase "on the occasion of [its] exposition": for in the case of paintings, puppets, and the like, the expression "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" is established through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a relationship between the instigator and the instigated within the form of the representation. However, when—through imitation of the actor (*saṃsādhya-anukāreṇa*)—there arises in the spectators the perception of the actors as having that very form due to similarity (*sādṛśya*), the question is raised: "How is this so in the case of the primary [actors]? To this, the answer is: "Because of their production [as such]."

Narrators who describe the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of Kaṃsa and others reveal objects that are within the scope of the intellect; because these objects do not exist externally after a long time has passed, they reveal them as existing only as the domain of the intellect. Thus, since the narrator generates in the listener a cognition bearing the form of Kaṃsa and so forth, it is logically consistent for the Buddha to be considered the "instigator" (*prayojaka*) in the sense of "causing Kaṃsa to be killed by Vāsudeva. Therefore, the point is that since this is already established by the Sūtra itself, the Vārttika need not be commenced. And thus, it follows that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is based solely on the existence [of things] as objects of the intellect. 1.104.

"Superimposed by words" means having the form of an object of cognition presented by words. "As a means" means as the killing and so forth that are objects of cognition. Thus, having established linguistic usage through the intellect (*buddhi*), he states [the verse beginning with] "by the intellect" to show that even for a single entity, the multiplicity of powers is conceptual (*bauddha*). The activity or operation of the intellect is characterized by determination; its form is its aspect (*ākāra*) appearing through ignorance (*avidyā*). Having superimposed that upon external objects, the multiplicity of their powers is imagined.

And thus there is a distinction of mental (bauddha) powers. In this way, due to the difference in activity, the very object is determined to possess manifold powers. Regarding the term "qualifier of the action" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇam*): the sense is that one determines the object with a clearly manifest form by means of a cognition caused by the senses; such is the intended meaning. He states the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*) with the words "produced by the senses" (*indriyajā*): the word "as if" is employed because this cognition is not actually produced by the senses; such is the meaning. Regarding the word "visible" (*dṛśya*): it means external. The object of the cognition is mental (*bauddha*).

For this very reason—from the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) in the universal form alone—there occurs the cognition "Devadatta is not in Kāśī" for a man staying in Kāśī who has heard of Devadatta as being in another country, even though Devadatta is actually present in Kāśī. The meaning is that there is no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the mental universal form onto the external form. "In a state of confusion" means as non-different. "Of him" refers to the one staying in Kāśī.

[Objection: But how can there be the cognition "this is that" based on instruction? To this he says: "This is that. [The reading] "vijātīyetyarthaḥ" (meaning "of a different class") does not exist in the Kuṇḍina and Kapardin manuscripts. And this is the cause of its being indistinct. "Delusion" (moha) means ignorance. Thus, the meaning is that due to delusion, there is no apprehension of the identity between the two forms. "That" refers to what is situated in another place; the meaning is "this very same thing. "Cognitive" (bauddha) means that immediately after the instruction, the cognitive form becomes an external form. "Past time, etc. [is the meaning].

The apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) regarding a past object such as Nala, having "Nalatva" (the property of being Nala) as its qualifier, is not possible because Nalatva was previously unknown; rather, it can only be an apprehension having "knowability" (*prameyatva*) as its qualifier, in the form "it possesses knowability. In the experience "it possesses knowability," there is already a prior experience of that which is qualified by Nalatva under the aspect of knowability. Thus, the ancients maintain that since no awakening factor (*udbodhaka*) need be postulated for the aspect of knowability regarding a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), there occurs a mere recollection qualified by Caitratva (the property of being Caitra).

That is not so; for after the experience "possessing a genus" (jātimān), there arises the recollection "jar" (ghaṭa). In that case, there is no regulating factor as to what serves as the awakener [of the latent impression] and what does not. Therefore, the moderns hold that in such instances, recollection occurs solely through the postulation of a stream of latent impressions (saṃskāra). ||1.1.05||

"Bhāvī" refers to a compound of those who are past, such as Nala and others; those who are yet to be, such as Caitra and others; and those who, though well-known and present, are not in close proximity. "Because the reason is unestablished" (hetvasiddheḥ) means that since there is no specific cognition [of the word], it is impossible to postulate a latent impression (saṃskāra) based upon it. "Gṛhītā" means that just as one remembers the word "jar" upon seeing a jar, one would consequently have to remember the word denoting Caitra and others even upon seeing them for the first time. "[Cognition] having the word as its qualifier" (padaprakāraka).

The meaning is that there was someone denoted by the word "Nala. Similarly, regarding the phrase "the word 'pada'": the ellipsis is "such usage [is observed]. Regarding the phrase "in the case of known [objects]": according to the view of the logicians (Tārkikas), however, since the referent is also known once the word "Nala" is known, the question would be untenable. Regarding the phrase "of analogy" (upamānasya): it connects with the word "validity" (prāmāṇyam) in this context.

For in that case, from the analogy "the gavaya is denotable by the word *gavaya* because it is similar to a cow," there arises the apprehension of the linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*) that "the gavaya is denotable by the word *gavaya*. By the phrase "through similarity and so forth," dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is included; for example, through the dissimilarity to other animals—such as having an exceedingly long neck—one apprehends that the camel is denotable by the word *karabha*.

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is, because they function with respect to a single object by virtue of being denotable. [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of grasping the expressive power" (*śaktigrahāsambhavāt*) means that the form as *nalatva* (the state of being a *nala*) was not previously present [in consciousness]. [The term] *moṣe* means "in the absence of apprehension. Regarding the part [of the object], the experience does not serve as a cause for a memory that has a different qualifier in that same part, because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāvāt*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, if one experiences a jar, etc., in the form of "possessing a genus" (*jātimattva*), then a memory of "jar" would result even when no stimulus (*udbodhaka*) is obtained for the other parts [of the object].

The meaning is that the occurrence of the awakening [of a latent impression] and its capacity [to produce a memory] are to be determined by the force of the result (*phala-bala*). Regarding "those respective universals and so forth" (*tattaj-jāty-ādi*): the meaning is "such as Caitra-ness" (*caitratvādi*). Regarding "indeterminate perception" (*nirvikalpaka*): the meaning is that just as for children, when there is a recollection of a previously experienced state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatā*) regarding breast-feeding and the like, a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*) alone is the regulator, so too is it in the case of the recollection of previously unexperienced Caitra-ness and so forth. Regarding "residing in the self" (*ātmavṛtti*): the meaning is "subsisting in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭha*). The sense is that in cases such as "I see fragrant sandalwood," this [recollection of fragrance] is the cause of the memory of fragrance.

"There is no consequence of [the self] becoming omniscient" means that even though there is knowledge [of the self] by way of its being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), there is no consequence of omniscience because there is no specific knowledge [of its individual characteristics]. "In such a manner" means that while there is experience in the form of being an object of cognition, there is recollection in the form of being Caitra. "Only of the aspect of the experience," etc. [is the meaning].

And thus says the *Pātañjala-sūtra*: "Even for those [experiences] separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of a single nature. Separation by birth occurs through connection with another life; in that case, the recollection of what was experienced in another life occurs through means such as collyrium and the like. Separation by place and so forth occurs through distance and the like. Nor should it be argued that the recollection—expressed as "I slept happily, I was not conscious of anything"—is untenable because there is an absence of experience during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

For this very reason, it is accepted that sleep is indeed a specific modification (vṛtti) [of the mind]. By this, the claim of the logicians—that sleep is the mere absence of all cognition—is refuted. 1.106.

[Objection: "But surely, in order to avoid a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the fact that an experience having a certain object is the cause of a memory having that same object, one must include either 'immediate succession' (*avyavahitottaratva*) or 'a specific class-distinction' (*vaijātya*) [in the definition]. Because of this unease, he says: 'Furthermore, in the case of that portion,' etc. The meaning is: for someone who has had a specific experience of something, it is precisely that person who has knowledge of it even through the *jñānalakṣaṇā* [type of perception]. "But not," etc.: the connection is that for those things not so experienced, there is no such knowledge even through *jñānalakṣaṇā*. "Even of Brahman," etc. [This refers to the following objection: "If the *jñānalakṣaṇā* were the cause of the knowledge of Brahman, then since Brahman is eternal, its knowledge would also have to be eternal; and if that were so, liberation would never occur. To this he replies: "The knowledge of Brahman... and so on. The meaning is that the knowledge of Brahman arises from the *śabda-pramāṇa* (scriptural testimony), which is distinct from the *jñānalakṣaṇā*. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptures. Furthermore, the word "even" (*api*) implies that this applies even to the knowledge of Brahman, let alone other objects. The meaning is that, because even Brahman is experienced by people such as ourselves through its general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇā), it would follow that Brahman also attains liberation. ||1.107||

"In many ways" (*bahudhā*): because the qualificand appears in multiple forms from words such as "Nala" and "pot. In the case of comparison (*upamiti*), there is a multiplicity of forms, such as "this is denotable by the word *gavaya*," and so forth. "Because of the sublation of the object" (*arthabādhe tu*): because it is impossible for the object [itself] to be uttered. "Mere word" (*śabdamātra*): in that case, there is simply no cognition of the object. "Precisely for that reason": the meaning is "precisely because of the non-difference between word and object. "Pervaded" (*anuviddha*): because, given the non-difference between word and object, it is logical that the object is preceded by the word. "The subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) is the means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that since words and the like cannot be objects of perception, the word is the object in the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective cognition) produced immediately after [the initial perception]. It is stated "in the latter half" because it is precisely in the *anuvyavasāya* that the cognition itself appears. "Precisely for this reason"—that is, precisely because of being permeated by the word (*śabdānuviddhatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "not known as a signifier": this refers to that whose signifier or designator (*vācaka*) is not known. Since the object appears only when permeated by the word, the conventional usage of "not knowing the object" occurs even when the designating word is unknown. (1.108)
"Jewels, mantras, and so forth"—this is the intended meaning:

following the certainty that "the lake is devoid of fire," the cognition that "the lake possesses fire" does not arise; therefore, the certainty of the absence of a thing acts as an obstacle to the cognition of its presence. In this regard, even though [the jewel] does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped (fire), just as a jewel and the like act as specific obstacles to burning, so too, through the apprehension of power (*śakti*) by way of specific qualifiers such as "being Caitra," there arises understanding (*bodha*) and the like. This is the sense.

"Stated by us": because it was previously stated that [the object] has the form of a cognition (*buddhyākāra*). "In the apprehension of that"—that is, in the apprehension of its meaning. "Of that"—of the word. "Because there is no sublation": because there is an eternal relationship between the word and its meaning. He states another defect regarding the non-appearance of the word with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Name" (*nāma*): the meaning is that it would have both the name as its object and the relation as its object. Even in visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), there is indeed a qualification by the name; for, as in the case of "fragrant sandalwood," it is possible for the name-component to appear through "presented appearance" (*upanītabhāna*), or else there is recollection (*smaraṇa*) regarding the name-component.

Just as in the cognition of non-existence there is the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), so too [here] there is the absence of a denotative word (*vācaka-śabda*). This means that the cognition of categories such as substance (*padārtha*) lacks the status of being denoted by a word. Consequently, cognition is not permeated by words, because there is no relationship of connection between the cognition and the word. Regarding the term "itikaraṇa": it means that the conventional usage of the cognition occurs through a word such as "jar" joined with the particle *iti*, which denotes the object "jar. Regarding "indriyārtha": it means produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object.

Although all knowledge is produced by the sense organ in the form of the mind (*manas*), nevertheless, what is intended here is that which has as its causehood that which is delimited by the nature of a [specific] sense organ. In the case of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), however, the causehood is by way of the nature of the mind (*manastva*). As for the perception of God (*īśvara-pratyakṣa*), although it is unproduced (*ajanya*), this definition applies only to produced perception. "Non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārī*) means distinct from error (*bhrama*). He divides perception [further]: "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) means non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). "Expression" (*vyapadeśa*) is the employment of words.

And since that [determinate perception] arises only from a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is designated as "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) because it is unfit for such a designation. The phrase "of the nature of determination" (*vyavasāyātmakam*) means "having the nature of a qualified cognition. The term "sensory" (*indriya*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to verbal valid knowledge (*śābdapramā*), which is produced by a compatibility (*yogyatā*) consisting of the relation between the meanings of two words within a single sentence. The term "object" (*artha*) is included to exclude over-extension to inference (*anumiti*) produced by the contact of the skin with the mind (*tvag-manoyoga*).

The term "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*) is included to exclude the over-extension (*avyāpti*) [of the definition] to non-worldly perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*), such as the cognition "the maiden is in every respect [beautiful]," which lacks being produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object. The term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is included to exclude the over-extension to the conjunction of the eye and the jar (*cakṣurghaṭasaṃyoga*), which is produced by the conjunction of the eye and the potsherd (*kapāla*). Nor should it be argued that even so there remains an over-extension to inference (*anumiti*), which is produced by the contact of the self and the mind (*ātmamanoyoga*); for by the power of the word "cognition," what is obtained is the state of being produced by the contact of the sense organ and the object, as delimited by the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*).

Now, in the case of the sentence "one eats jaggery" (*guḍaṃ bhuṅkte*), since sweetness (*madhuratva*)—just like the state of being jaggery (*guḍatva*)—also functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*), one must assert that for a verbal cognition having a particular property as its qualifier to arise, the knowledge of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) having that same property as its qualifier must be the cause of that verbal cognition.

And thus, since the knowledge of such a power (*śakti*) is the cause for a verbal cognition characterized by a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), how could "the word 'pot'" (*ghaṭaśabdatva*) appear as the delimitant of the mode? For there is no apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) in the form: "The word 'pot' has power with respect to that which is denoted by the word 'pot'. As for the claim that the word appears [in the cognition] by way of being a cognition of a related entity (*sambandhi*), that is not correct; for it would follow that even an elephant would be cognized from the word "elephant-driver" (*hastipaka*). If this is argued, [we reply]: because we accept that the cognition regarding the word-component is indeed of the nature of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

"Elsewhere"—that is, in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). "The non-apprehension of its non-appearance"—the meaning is that the apprehension of the non-appearance of the word [in perception] would be futile. By Vātsyāyana—the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*.

For there, in response to the objection that perception takes the form "one knows the color" (*rūpam iti jānāti*), and since words such as "color" are names of objects, perception would consequently result in being verbal (*śābda*) because it is designated by a name-word, the portion of the sūtra "indescribable" (*avyapadeśyam*) was introduced.

The meaning of this is as follows: at the time of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of color and so forth, the word for the name has no function whatsoever; rather, it functions at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), such as when one thinks, "I know this as 'color,'" and so on. Therefore, direct perception is non-verbal (*aśābda*). This has already been largely explained: for this very reason, after defining inference as "that which is produced by the knowledge of a word while being produced by a cognition," the logicians (*tārkika*) also state that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the true knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) produced by reflection (*manana*), because [the latter] has as its object words such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). However, they do not say "being produced by a word" [as the definition], because that would result in over-extension to the direct perception of a word itself, where the word acts as the objective condition (*viṣaya-vidhayā*).

As for the objection that when there is a desire for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), a verbal cognition arises by the force of that desire at a time when the causal complex for an inference with a different object is present—and that in such a case, it is impossible for the word itself to be the object [of that cognition]—it is not so. This is because a desire of the form "let there arise a verbal cognition of the word" serves as the excitatory factor (*uttejaka*); thus, the causal complex for inference, when qualified by the absence of such a desire, acts as an inhibitor. Consequently, in that situation, no verbal cognition occurs.

If it is argued that even the desire [of the speaker] acts as an excitatory condition (*uttejaka*), then there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) because, in the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified among the sets of absences of those various desires, there would be no determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*). This is not so; for since verbal cognition in general has the word as its object, it is a single type of desire alone that serves as the excitatory condition. (1.109)

"Or rather, not this"—the meaning is that the sūtra "its own form" (*svarūpam*) need not be stated. "'For it is preceded by the word'"—the meaning is "for it is preceded by the cognition of the word. The point is that only a word that has been perceived causes the understanding of its meaning; it does not cause understanding by its mere existence, as is the case with the eyes and other sense organs. This is the underlying intention: because it is internal, because it is not to be discarded, and because it is unique, the own-form (*svarūpa*) alone is the primary meaning. Furthermore, due to the non-difference between the word and its meaning, the genus residing in the word is superimposed upon the meaning. For this very reason, it was said by Bhartṛhari:

"Likewise, through the connection between word and object, the universal (jāti) resides in the word; it serves as the basis for the function of the universal when designating the universals of objects. Thus [it is said]. "And preceded by the word" means "for it is indeed preceded by the word. "The negative concomitance" (vyatireka) refers to the sense that in the absence of knowledge of the word, there is an absence of knowledge of the object. "It is precisely another argument" means that the phrase "since it is preceded by the word" should not be explained as a previous reason [for the same point]. "In the mantra... [refers to the following].

Anticipating the objection that the prohibition "aśabda-saṃjñā" (not a word-designation) is intended to exclude the apprehension of mantras and sounds, the author of the *Bhāṣya* says: "Since the apprehension of mantras as words is impossible in the actual examples (*lakṣya*), there will be the apprehension of their meaning. Kaiyaṭa expresses this very point by saying "and through association" (*sāhacaryāt*). Regarding the phrase "that cognition": it is observed in verbal comprehension that the cognition of a jar has the word "jar" as its object. "That cognition" refers to the cognition of a jar; "having the word etc. as its object" means having the word "jar" etc. as its object; "that" refers to the cognition of the jar. [The phrase] "produced by that word" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is "other than the word 'pot'. This means that it possesses the same objective referentiality (*viṣayatā*) as the objective referentiality present in the cognition produced by the word "pot. And thus, even in perception, the objective referentiality of the word is necessary; the point is that objective referentiality itself is indeed possible [in perception]. Regarding "the same" (*samāna*): the meaning is that as many objects as there are in verbal cognition, those very same ones are present in perception as well. (1.110)

[Objection: But surely, just as the perception of color is established through the force of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), so too the manifestation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) is established through the force of being a qualifier-of-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*) alone; for what purpose, then, is the "denotability" (*vācyatva*) of objecthood asserted? To this, he says: "But by means of contact and so forth... The point is that while at one time color may function as a qualifier and at another time as a qualificand, there would likewise be no fixed rule regarding its status as a mode (*prakāratva*) and so on.

By this [argument], it follows that when words refer to themselves, there is only indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and not primary denotation (*śakti*), because [the meaning] is obtainable through other means. Furthermore, the claim that "because it is presented through perception, the word itself also appears [in cognition]" is not tenable; for if there were no linguistic function (*vṛtti*), it would contradict the maxim that "suffixes denote meanings connected with the base-meaning," resulting in the impossibility of the suffix-meaning being syntactically integrated. Therefore, the view that "the appearance of a word even without a linguistic function is due to its own nature" has been refuted; for one cannot maintain that "a linguistic function is required to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in making another object known, but not even for making itself known."

"Regarding the phrase *ghaṭarūpe* (the form of the jar): the meaning is that when there is prior cognition of something, that thing possesses the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase *viśeṣyajñānasyāpi*: likewise, if the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) were known first, it would result in its becoming a qualifier. Regarding the word *kiñcit*: the meaning is that it would be perceived even as devoid of a qualified object. Regarding the phrase *na tu ghaṭa ityādi*: the meaning is that the cognition "the jar has color" (*rūpavān ghaṭaḥ*) would not occur. He states the reason for this very point in the phrase *viśeṣyāgraha*: by the non-arising of that [cognition], i.e., by the non-arising of the cognition of a jar qualified by color."

Regarding the term "of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭasya*): in the cognition "the ground has a red staff," the qualifiedness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the staff as qualified by redness appears in the ground. In that case, the cause is a certainty (*niścaya*) having redness as its qualifier. The point is that such [qualified cognition] does not arise immediately after a doubt, such as "Is the staff red or not? Now, if it is argued that [cognition] is a cause merely by being a certainty, then following the doubt "Is the staff red or not?", there would be no subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) regarding the qualified object, such as "I am doubting the red staff."

True. Such a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) has precisely the form, "I am doubtful regarding the redness in the staff," which apprehends the absence of redness in the staff. However, in the case of a qualified cognition such as "the ground possesses a jar," the cause is simply the knowledge having the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*) as its mode, and not one that includes the element of certainty (*niścayatva*). This is because such a cognition arises even immediately after a doubt, such as "Is this a jar or not?"

[Objection: Surely, the perceptual establishment of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) follows from the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I am the possessor of a cognition having potness as its qualifier and the pot as its qualificand. However, there is no evidence for the acceptance of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). To this, he says: "For this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because the cognition of the qualifier is a cause [of determinate cognition]. The point is that without the cognition of potness, a cognition having potness as its qualifier is not possible.
[Objection: But the cognition of the qualifier is not a cause because it is superfluously established (*anyathāsiddha*). [Reply: No.

This is because the cognition of the qualifier is established as a cause: since the knowledge of "pot-ness" in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*) is the cause for the qualified cognition "it is not a pot in its own form," and the knowledge [of the universal] as "universal-ness" (*jātitva*) is the cause for the cognition "it possesses a universal."

Regarding the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*): in the cognition "the red-stick is the object of knowledge" (*prameya*), there is the cognition of the qualification of knowability (*prameyatva*) residing in the stick as qualified by redness. Regarding "the jar and jar-ness": since a universal does not appear without its individual instance (*vyakti*), the individual instance also appears. However, the point is that the relation between those two does not appear due to the force of the resulting cognition (*phala*). If it is argued that the appearance of the relation itself is unavoidable due to the causal factor of "inherence in what is conjoined with the eye" (*cakṣussaṃyuktasamavāya*), then [we reply]: in that case, its being indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) follows simply from its being devoid of any qualifying mode (*niṣprakārakatva*). (1.111)

Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*): since a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) arises precisely through the simultaneous sensory contact with both the qualifier and the qualificand, there is no evidence for the knowledge of the qualifier being a cause [of that cognition]. Thus, the point is that the indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is accepted even as a means of producing the knowledge of the qualifier. Now, one might object: "Since recollection is impossible at a time devoid of the knowledge of the qualifier precisely because of the absence of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), let the mere recollection of the qualified object itself be the cause; what is the need for an indeterminate cognition?"

[The opponent argues that] because there is no recollection of "being Caitra" (caitratva) and so forth as something previously unexperienced, there could be no qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*). [The author replies: "By means of contact alone. This means they maintain that contact itself is the cause. [The opponent says: "There would be an impossibility. This means that in the absence of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be a lack of restriction.

However, the Naiyāyikas (*tārkika*) assert that in perception alone, a certainty (*niścaya*) having the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) as its mode (*prakāra*) is the cause. This is because, according to their acceptance of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) by way of the "crows-on-a-roof-peck" maxim (*khalekapotanyāya*), it is only the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) and so forth that serves as the restrictive factor for verbal comprehension and the like.

[Objection: Since the purpose is already served by the fact that the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause [of the qualified cognition], there is no evidence for the claim that the cognition having the delimitor of the qualifier as its mode (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakārakajñāna*) is the cause. [Reply: True. However, this is because it would be overly complex (*gaurava*) to postulate that the cognition having the delimitor of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvacchedakaprakārakajñāna*) is the cause, in order to prevent the perception "the jar does not exist" immediately after a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), etc.

[Objection: But surely there is no cause for the manifestation of "objectness" (*viṣayatva*) when it is not presented by a word; therefore, he says: "In the manifestation of objectness... The meaning is that, like the pot itself, the objectness residing in the pot also manifests. [Regarding the phrase] "residing in potness": the meaning is that if a property consisting of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) and so forth is denotable, then being a qualifier and the rest are also established as denotable. [Regarding the phrase] "having objectness as its object": this refers to [cognitions] such as "I am one who possesses a cognition having potness as its qualifier. [Regarding the phrase] "in its own form" (*svarūpataḥ*):...

The meaning is: "even when an object-entity appears [in cognition] though it is not the object of the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*). Regarding the example "the hunchback and the lame": here, the modehood (*prakāratā*) resides solely in the state of being hunchbacked. Now, one might object that if the objective status (*viṣayatā*) itself appears [as an object], then another objective status would have to arise there as well; therefore, he says "in its own nature" (*svarūpa*). The meaning is: "but not through another relation. Regarding "by force alone" (*balādeva*): the meaning is "by means of [the causal chain] beginning with the verbal cognition having 'pot-ness' as its mode. Regarding "for the sake of knowing that": the meaning is that for the sake of knowing the modehood in pot-ness, the word's power (*śakti*) must necessarily reside even in the portion consisting of modehood itself. (1.112)

"Of its own meaning in the form of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). This is the intended sense: the meaning of the word *rājan* (king) is delimited by that qualificandness which is determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in kingship. In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, because the meaning of the word *rājan* functions as a qualifier, there is an abandonment of its own meaning in the form of being the qualificand. But since there is no abandonment of the meaning in the form of the entity "king" itself, the term *jahatsvārtha* (abandoning its own meaning) is not applied on that account. "And its being the denotable object (*tacchakyatva*)" means that appearing [in cognition] as an object of awareness and being the denotable object are established by experience. (1.113)

Regarding the phrase "individual and configuration" (*vyaktyākṛti*): if one were to accept that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in an individual qualified by a genus (*jāti*), then there would be the consequence that the relation (*sambandha*) itself would also possess that power; furthermore, there would be the consequence of an inability to determine which factor is the qualifier and which is the qualified (*vinigamanāviraha*). Therefore, both of these [the individual and the genus] have their own distinct status as the denotable object (*śakyatva*). Since there is no rule that a genus is necessarily manifested by a fixed configuration (*saṃsthāna*), the configuration has a separate status as the expressed meaning. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of qualification" (*viśeṣaṇārtha*): qualification means differentiation (*vyāvartana*). He asks, "What is differentiated? and "What is qualified? He provides the answer: "The primary [element]. (This refers to the individual.)

The meaning is that because there is no fixed rule regarding the status of genus (*jāti*) and the others as either secondary (*gauṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*), all three possess the status of being word-meanings (*padārthatva*). Others have explained that the word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the status of word-meaning for each one individually; otherwise, there might be the occasional presentation of only one of them. Therefore, it was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*.

For when there is an intention to express distinction and a comprehension of particulars—as in "the cow stands" and so forth—then the individual (vyakti) is the word-meaning, while the genus (jāti) and other factors are merely subordinate. When distinction is not intended and there is a comprehension of the universal (sāmānya), then the genus is the word-meaning; as in "A cow must not be touched with the foot. But when the form (ākāra) is predominant, as in "cows made of flour," [the form is the meaning].

Regarding the term *prajñāpanīya* (to be made known): in the statement "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), the property to be understood is fire (*vahni*), and the property qualified by that [fire] is the mountain (*parvata*). This is the *sādhya*—that which is to be established. In the case of "sound is impermanent" (*anityaḥ śabdaḥ*), sound as qualified by impermanence (*anityatva*) is what is being established; therefore, the sense is that sound qualified by impermanence is the *sādhya*. For this very reason, the venerable Patañjali stated: "The subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property sought to be known (*jijñāsita-dharma*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*)."

This is the explanation of the sūtra: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*). For this very reason, the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) there states: "The proposition is the statement that apprehends the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by the property (*dharma*) to be made known. He explains the function of the term "to be made known" (*prajñāpanīya*) with the word "impermanent" (*anitya*). In this context, since sound (*śabda*) is already established, its status as a probandum (*sādhya*) is not possible [if it were merely the subject].

Nor is impermanence (*anityatva*) itself the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is already established in things such as a jar. Nor is it the case that impermanence residing in sound is the probandum; thus he says "nor" (*nāpi*). For in the inference "impermanence resides in sound," if one were to take impermanence as the subject (*pakṣa*) and prove its residence in sound, then the reason (*hetu*)—namely, being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—would be absent from the subject, which is the property-bearer (*dharmin*) consisting of impermanence. Regarding the phrase "of the probandum": this means of the subject (*pakṣa*), which is to be understood as possessing a particular property. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of connection": this refers to the passage beginning with "therefore, [it is] to be made known" (*tasmāt prajñāpanīya*). Thus, it has been well said.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. "Succession" (*paramparā*) means "subsisting in its own substratum. If it is asked: "How then is there the common saying that in cases such as 'one color' (*ekaṃ rūpam*), since a quality is not admitted in a quality, oneness is perceived in the color by way of inherence in its own substratum?"—the answer is no; for in that case, oneness is accepted as being of the nature of the absence of number (*saṅkhyā*). As for the phrase "nor... (*na ca*): the sense is that even the non-eternality established in jars and the like is not to be proven here, precisely because it is already established; this is the meaning. In some places, the reading is "furthermore, non-eternality also" (*kiñca anityatvam api*).

[Objection: If the property (*dharma*) is that which is to be made known, then how can a property that is not yet known function as a qualifier? To this he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). [The phrase] "as another property"—that is, as a property of a jar or the like. The sense is that even though the property and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) are known in a general way, inference exists precisely for the sake of understanding the specific relation consisting of the qualified and the qualifier (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*). And [the word] "it" (*sa*) means the relation of the qualified and the qualifier. Being dependent on both, he establishes what has been proven with the words "the property," etc. [The subject is] the mountain and so forth; the "property" is fire and so forth. (1.114)

"Distinct from that" means that a substance (*dravya*) is not perceived apart from its genus (*jāti*) and other attributes. The point is that if one were to superimpose non-difference between a word and its object, then even the genus of a cow (*gotva*) would potentially possess the nature of being a word. "How so? [is asked]. The point is that when a new form arises in a single fruit through the destruction of its previous form, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—"This is that very same fruit"—establishes that the substance is logically distinct from its qualities.

Regarding the position that "substance is a collection of qualities" (*guṇasamūho dravyam*): since the collection is denoted by the word, the meaning is that the constituent parts are also denoted by the word, and thus [the collection] possesses the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). Regarding the phrase "particular constituent": the meaning is that substance is precisely that collection of qualities in the form of general and particular characteristics which follows those constituents that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). Inseparable establishment means being experienced as non-distinct.

The nature of the elements is as follows: solidity is the common property of earth; moisture that of water; heat that of fire; the quality of motility that of air; and omnipresence that of space. Furthermore, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the specific qualities of earth and the other elements; the collection of these is substance (*dravya*). To clarify that a mere collection is not substance, it is stated that it must be "inseparable" (*ayutasiddha*). This very point is further explained as being characterized by "contiguity" (*nirantaratva*).

For just as the parts of the body and so forth are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), the parts of forests and the like are not thus inseparably established; therefore, they do not possess substantiality (*dravyatva*). As for qualities (*guṇa*), color and so forth are the universal (*sāmānya*) and white and so forth are the particular (*viśeṣa*). What is the understanding here? The meaning is: what do you consider a substance (*dravya*) to be composed of? [The answer is: A substance is a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*).

The Sāṃkhya tenet is that the five objects, such as sound and so forth, which are specific transformations of the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas, consist of those very qualities themselves; a jar or similar object is merely a collection of them, and there exists no composite whole (avayavin) distinct from them. This is because, even when an animal is cut into hundreds of pieces, nothing whatsoever is perceived apart from its form, taste, smell, and other such qualities; thus, substance is simply a collection of qualities.

In this regard, the conventional usage of the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is intended with reference to individual members, whereas the conventional usage of the term "substance" (*dravya*) is intended with reference to the aggregate. The difference in weight between iron and cotton is produced solely by the aggregate and not by a difference in the substance itself. The intention behind the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "tasya bhāvaḥ" is that the conventional distinction between substance and quality is likewise produced by the aggregate and its constituent members. In that context, because there is no difference between the aggregate and its members, the perception of that [aggregate] is what constitutes the "substance"; however, in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the word "quality" denotes merely a property (*dharma*). As it has been said in the *Hiraṇya*:
"Whatever is perceived as having an operation that differentiates the related [members]..."

"Its status as a quality (*guṇatva*) is declared in the treatise because of its dependence on another. That which distinguishes the related substratum (*saṃsargin*), being perceived through an operative form of delimitation (*avacchedaka-rūpeṇa*), is a quality; for in common worldly usage, that which is dependent is called a "quality" (*guṇa*). The technical definition of the Vaiśeṣikas is that "substance" (*dravya*) is the locus of those [qualities]. However, in this system, the definition of substance is "fitness to be referred to by pronouns" (*sarvanāma-parāmarśa-yogyatva*) or "the state of being distinguishable" (*bhedya-tva*), and so forth. For this very reason, the position is held that "substance" is the meaning of a word (*padārtha*). And for this same reason, since a term in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa-śabda*) denotes the same substance, the compound *sarvarasa* ("all tastes") is formed.

If it is objected that, in this way, even in the rule "vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇavāci" (Pāṇini 2.4.13), because qualities and so forth are excluded, the singular collective form would not apply in cases such as *śītoṣṇam* (cold and heat) or *sukhaduḥkham* (pleasure and pain)—we say no. In that case, by the force of the specific statement, well-known substances (*dravya*) are understood. Furthermore, in the rule "voto guṇavacanāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.44), since there was the possibility of including things qualified by genus (*jāti*) and so on—because the term "guṇavacanāt" refers to a substance where a quality is subordinate—the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) "that which enters into a substance" (*sattve niviśate*) was adopted.

Regarding the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*, the position of the Vārttika is that "quality" (*guṇatva*) consists in being distinct from compounds and the like. In the rule *tṛtīyātatkṛtārtha*, however, only [qualities] such as "curvedness" (*khaṇḍa*) and so forth are considered qualities.

In the expression "the rope has three strands" (*triguṇā rajjuḥ*), the word "quality" (*guṇa*) signifies "constituent part" (*samavāya*), because the term "quality" includes parts as well. He establishes that even the collection [of parts] is a substance (*dravya*), and intending to show that color and the rest are also parts by virtue of being constituents of that collection, he says "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*). It is with this very intention that he says "by the word 'quality'. This is stated in the *Bhāmatī*.

For there, having cited the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* as stating "partless," it was said: "Just as in the case of rice grains, a portion called a 'refinement' (*saṃskāra*) is admitted through sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), no such portion exists in Brahman that could be produced by action."

[Objection: But if substance (*dravya*) is merely an aggregate of qualities (*guṇa*), then the relation of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) cannot exist between a thing and itself; to this he says: "between the aggregate and its constituents. For this very reason, it is said that [substance] is the substratum of qualities. The meaning is that because the difference between the collection (*samūha*) and the members of the collection (*samūhin*) is also accepted, this conventional usage [of "substratum"] is possible. "[It is] not something additional": the meaning is that the forest is simply the collection of trees, not something distinct from them. [Objection: But if substance is merely an aggregate of parts, how can there be its destruction? To this he says: "only disjunction (*vibhāga*) is its destroyer."

For this very reason, the destruction of the effect results from the destruction of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and not from the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for since atoms are eternal, the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would otherwise be impossible—so say the logicians (*tārkika*). Now, one might object that if the whole were imperceptible, there could be no perception of a jar or similar objects; therefore, he says: "by means of many parts" (*bhūyovayava*).
